div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. TO Tlf E ELECTORS. LADIES AND GENTLENIEN,—You will be called open on Thursday next, :September Ist, to Elect Five Members to represent your Interests on the Board of Commissioners. I be most respectfully to offer myself as a candidate for your suffrages, and can assure you, should you do me the Irrnour :to elect me. it will be my constant endeavour to dischargo my duties to your satisfaction.
Vehicular Bridge across the Atersey.—l am Intuit sympathy .with the schemata unite Runcorn with Widnes by means of a .cart and toot road.
itridge across Canal.—l am also in favour of the -pro- ' posed bridge across the Bridgewater Canal near she Crane in -Halton road.
`Roadway to Weston Point.—l would support the making.of a direct vehieularrocd to Weston Point.

Waterloo Bridge.—l am greatly desirous in common with most ,of my fellow townsmen for the completion of Waterloo Bridge,•and would gt•ve the matter my best attention.. Sanitary Condition.—Believing the sanitary condition of the town to be far from what it ought to be. in vlewof the out break ,of .cholera and of other infectious diseases throughou- the country, this mrearer would have my especial attention. Improvement Contracts.—l am strongly of opinion that all contracts for town improvements should be Carried out by local ArmE, and I would give such lontracts my prior con- sideralen. 'd nstitute.-1 am in fell rthy no

Technice, sympathy with Me pro- posed Tee Lance Institute and woufd strongly support this matter. Recreathas i.carrids.---I would support any well considered scheme for the establishment of Recreation Grounds or Baths, said pledge myself if returned to bring fox ward and support mewures to secure the greatest comfort and convenience of the ratepayers, and make it ray duty to rerve to the best of my abcity all -.lasses of the rarbepayers, and give my test attention. to all matters to improve cur town.
I remain. ,E,z.clies and 43-entlerom. Yours faithfully-, THOMAS LEA.

_ Tea ei 14 Sir Andrew Clarke. For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep. and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke. the London Physician, corroborates opinion.
• Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital :

"Tea is a blessed beverage. I donot know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about tivessVock, when I got into a place, the lady of the house will say to me ' Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup ottea.' I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call It positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea. to be useful, should be first of au Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which Is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Slack China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person alld one for the blessed pot. Then nuir on briskly boiling water, and, within five minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned ea is like.

- The colour of the (ea after it is erevv-ed will be found lobe mach paler than that now la use, and the taste may not be ao;eptable at first owing Wits apparent insipidness ; but if it use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much I more tmitable for the system. aril if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you wcii wonder howevcr you could have nueu using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. Although-VOrd—RibblB4lll/e—taa been apperinted. Master of the Buckhounds, there is no intention of permanently retaining the office. It will be dis- continued as soon as the necessary arrangements for transferring the formal duties to,other depart- ments can be made. The censures passed upon the Government for keeping it up are therefore entirely beside the mark.

Mr. Welton Dale, the young actor ho appears at the Criterion in ." Betsy," has been the victim of a curious accident. A young lady at the buffet ad- joining the theatre was opening a soda-water bottle when the cork shot Mr. Dale in the eye. Grave consequences were at first feared, hut Mr. Dale has now recovered the use of his eye—and 1,50 compensation from Messrs. Spiers and Pond.

. , Lord Salisbury has again been elected president of the Angfo-French Tennis Club <the society chro- nicler of the "Gazette de France" says), which meets three times a week during the autumn months on the at shore near the Grand Hotel des Bains, at Dieppe.. The members, who principally belong to the English and French aristocracy, have alreaay arranged for a series of matches, and Lord and Lady Salisbury have promised to take part.

Mr. John Morley, the man of the hour, lives in Elm-park-gardens, off the Fulham-road. His house is wholly unpretentious outside, and simplicity is the note within. In the entrance hall quite *num- ber of portraits of notable men are hung. Few of the portraits are of politicians, however. Mr. Mor- ley's study.which is upstairs, is simply packed with books. Perhaps it is as true to-day, as it was long ago, that Mr. Morley is never more happy than when among his books.

Mr. Morlers first official duty as Chief Secretary for Ireland was to give a word of eneourageinent to the evicted tenants. The secretary of the Evicted Tenants' Association called on Mr.Morley,and urged that an autumn session should be held to do some- thing for the victims of Coercion in the South of Ireland. Mr. Morley admitted that the case of the evicted tenants deserved attention, and indicated that something would be done for them. "The question now was," he said, "how to discover a sound way of securing an object of public policy which was held to be urgently desirable." It will be me of the first subjects which Mr. Morley will consider when he gets through the turmoil of his election.

•(During the past year the average cost of the maintenance of Board schools per child in average attendance in England and Wales has considerably increased. In London the increase was 15.51 d., and in the remaining Board schools in England Is. 3d. per child. The average cost of voluntary schools this year also shows an increase of 80. per child. Further, it appears that 52.79 per cent. of the scholars in England and Wales paid less than 3d. a week; that 38.53 per cent. paid 3d, and less than 6d. a week; that 3.72 per cent. paid 6d. and ever; and that the free scholars were 4.93 per cent.

Mr. LabouchereY:lisely narrative' in' Truth recalls a story which Lord Beaconsfield used to tell with great gusto. It Was about a member of his party who ranked his services higher than the leaders did, and was always •hinting about his reward. At last the time came, and the expectant member suggested a peerage. Lord Beaconsfield pleasantly evaded the subject, but the request was persisted in, and at last the Tory Premier tried to effect a compromise on the following terms :—" I can't make you a peer," he said,' but if you like you play say that I offered you a baronetcy, and that you refused it."

The- Right Hon. George Osborne Morgan, who has just been made a baronet on the recommendation of Mr. Gladstone, has been nearly a quarter of a century in Parliament. He is a tall man, with silvery hair, regular features, and brown eyes. He was ,called to the Bar at Lincoles-inn in 1853, and took silk" in 1869. Ile was, however, more of a jurist than a practisingi barrister: having obtained the Winerian Scholarship at Oxford. Mr. Morgan was Judge-Advocate-General in Mr. Gladstones Administration from 1880 till 1985, and was Under- Secretary for the Colonies in the Home Rule Government o1;1886. '

The iirst-class pension of £2,000 a year, which was at the disposal of the Government when they quit- ted office, has, been bestowed upon him. On the whole, it is a, cheap arrangement for the country. The six yearBe, naval expenditure for which Lord George Hamilton is responsible has been a petiod of extravagant,.Qutlay where saving was possible and petty cheeseparing where it was the duty of a Government tcp,begenerous. The outlar.,3ak of cholera:at Hamburg is an unplea- sant fact, Dr. Koch—whose authority is certainly not of the Ugliest—de:flares the epidemic to be Asiatic cholera; and whether this be so or not, the outbreak is certainly a deadly one, for out of three hundred and forty persons attacked, a hundred and thirty died. This is a .terrible proportion. Bo frightful have been the ravages of the disease that Certain streets have been closed to traffic, most of them in the neighLourhood of the harbour. This fact must not be lost eight of in view of the con- stant communication betvceen Hamburg and our ports. Every individual rcay in some little way help to keep the epidemic Lway from this country by strictly observing the ;Anitary requirements of the authorities. Now is the time to urge the suprenae importance of cleanliness. Cholera has no more chance than any other epidemic with a clean people.

The news of the marriage of the Duke of Devon- shire with the • Dowager Thichess of Manchester, which in the bygone time would have fluttered the pulses of society, has been recefiect with perfect in- difference. The inevitable sotrietithes occurs,as well as the unforseen, and- the fatt that both the con- tracting parties ere elderly, and to a certain extent, demodea, robs the event of-its-charm. The romantic, story which appeared in the Btar is simply a farrago, of foolish and absurd fabrications. It is utterly tin- true that before the Duchess married the late Duke! of Manchester she was etigiiged to marry her pre- sent husband. As a matter of fact there was no ac-: ctnaintance between them until she had been for; many years married to the: Duke of Manchester.l When the marriage of the Duchess took place; the Duke of Devonshire (then Lord Cavendish) was- an undergraduate at Cambridge. It may be in-: teresting to recall the fact that Christ Church, May-: fair, where the Duke of Devonshire was married, was the -scene of Lord Rosebery's wedding, when. Lord 'Beaconsfield gave the bride away. The crowded state of the church on that occasion con- trasted strangely with its -almost perfect empti- ness on Tuesday, the secret having been wonder- fully well kept.
NTS FIRST BATTLE.

-40 0 4 The borne or Dttrosigr deserves to be historic as thlit-Ordne -61—thirtirMst of French soldiers;--al-' though the‘noble young fellow who bore it saw but one battle. Timoleon Durosier was one one of the first students admitted tdAhe ikElo .Pplytechnique, and at the period of (be Irev'asionlwasvgazetted to an ensignship. At the battle of Montmirail, he chanced to bin attendance on the Emperor at the moment when it became essential to dispatch an order to one of the generals of the division. Napo- leon, summoning him to his side, gave him instruc- tions to deliver it without delay. "Spare neither yourself nor your horse, sir,", he said sternly, "for there is not b. moment to lose, and return at once to report to nie that my order has been obeyed." Du- roster galloped away amid a shower of shot and shells, and within a quarter of an, hour,w,as again beside the Emperor. ''You have behaved well, monsibur," said Napoleon, when he had received his report. "You have a stout heart and a clear bead, though you are still only a youngster. I give you your captain's brevet, and attach you to my person. What is your name?" Durosier, sire." "On what occasion have I before beard it?" "I was the colenel of the boy battalion your Majesty." "I re- member. Well, that is an additional reason why I should attach you to my person." "It is too late, gee." "Too late, Captain. 'Durosier? And why?" " Sire, they have hit me;" and he reeled in his sad- dle and fell heavily forward, dead. "So young, his first battlefield !" exclaimed 'the Emperor, bending over him. "Poor boy."

He wrote :--" A little before the conclusion of the late war in Flanders, one who came from thence gave us a very strange relation. .i.Tonathin Pyrah was a member of our society. .I:knew him for some years to be a man of unblamible character. One day he was summoned to appear before the Board of Gen- eral Officers, who said, 4` What is this.that we hear of you, that you are turiked,prophet and fortell the downfall of .the bloody House of Bourbon and the haughty House of Austria?? We should be glad if you were a real prophet, but what sign do you give to convince us that you are so?'' He readily answered. '-Gentlemen, I .give you a sign. To- morrow, at 12 o'clock, you shall have Aluch a storm of thunder and lightning as you have not bad before since you came into Flanders. I. give you a second sign—as little as any of you wect it, you shall have a general engagement with the. French within three clays. I give you a third sign. A farmer's wife dreamed that she was walking I near the houde of a rejected lover, one 01Flanagan, attended by a beautiful bound, of which she was fond, when a raven dashed at him, killed him, and tearing out his heart, flew away with it. She next imagined that she was running home, and, that she met a funeral, and from the coffin blood :flowed upon the ground,' .The bearers placed it at her feet, opened the lid, and exhibited her husband mur- dered, and his heart torn out. She awakeras, might be expected, in great terror. But here follows the most incomprehensible part of the narrative: her husband entertained an idiot cousin in the 'house, sand he, in doggerel thyme, repeated the you same dream to a gossip, towhom the farmer's wife- had 'related hers. That very night the farmer was murdered; and the next morning the poor idiot, td thetborror of all, exclaimed as he•rose from his bed. •",Ulick "—Ulick Maguire was the farmer's same— "is atilt ! Shamus dhu More kilt him." (Shamus • dhu More OTlanagan—big black James) "and ,Iniried him under the new ditch at the back of the ,garden I dreamed it last night—every word ef,it." Search was made at the spot inditated by -the dream, rand the body was found with the .skull r nearly cleft in two. In the meantime, O'Flanagan absconded and enlisted, but was subsequently wrested, confessed the crime, and was executed.

Numismatists or coin collectors have interesting objects of search in two coins which belong to the transition periodi,between the French Republic and the Second Empire, says tt e " Youths' Companion." One of these is al) extremely rare coin which was struck off just at the moment of the assumption of the reins of empire by Napoleon 111. Only the die for the obverse or head of a new Imperial nein had been .completed, and-by some accident, or possibly by mischievous design} &coin was struck off which bore the head of "Napoleon 111., Emperor," on one side, and "French Republic" on the other. This contradictory coin is of interest to others than numismatists, for' it symbolises in a striking way the many sudden' changes which have taken place in French.politics in the past century. With the other coin a singular story is connected. While Louis Napoleon was "Prince. President," and just betore,he made himself Empsror, a decree was is- sued ordering a live-franc silTer piece to be coined bearing his image. The dies were inade, and one coin was struck off as a sample, and sent to the Prince President for approval. But some time passed before he,examineci it. When at last he gime it his attention he was annoyed to find that he hijd been represented on the coin With a "lovi-loa," or hooked lock of hair on the temple, which he did actually wear at that period,' but which he thought unsuitable to SO dignified and permanents represt n- tation .of himself as an effigy. upon, a, coin. The Prince President sent for the director of the mint, and ordered him to remove the "love-lock." Then he found that his silence with regard to piece had been taken for approval, and that the stamping of the coins had commenced. The work was stopped. and the image deprived of its undignified lock; but the twenty-three coins that had already been struck off were not destroyed, and are now regarded as of great value.

div.head: AN AWKWARD MISTAKE.
div.p: AN AWKWARD MISTAKE.

_ -- Mr. Blank had been a missionary in Brazil for some yearivend,spoke the Braiilian ',Spanish. But he foresaw that there was going to be trouble on the score of the langnage when he came home to the United States tOget his bride and dike her back to Brazil." But the bride -anticipating trouble studied Spanish for a time there was some hesitation and embarrassment but no trouble. Thinking,she was getting along famously, she soon gained more confidence., So all went well .until the young couple set up an ,establishment and secured a man-servant with the fine manners of a Spanish grandee. The young *He stood in awe of him from the start, and her greatest trial was when her husband would be detained from home during the Pinner hour, when she had to dine alone, except for that grand man-servant. One. day that functionary was standing, elegant and impressive, when she had occasion to ask him to band ,her the cheese. The man stood immovable, like a lay figure in a tailor's shop, but she noticed a carious twitching of his mouth. She detected that.he had hetad her,and she began to get angry but he didn't move to de her bidding. She repeated her r, command as she thought :--" Give me the cheese." This tithe the grandee of a man-servant perceptibly laughed, but was immovable. In indignation, supposing him to be impertinent, or worse still, crazy, she rushed to" the front door to call assistance, when she met the belated missionary, her husband, and , ttollaptly ex- plained the situation:" Whit 'did you siy,liy dear? was his smiling query. "Dive me the cheese,"was what I said. "Yes, but the word; :he insisted. "I said beso," replied the Wife, still puzzled. Then the unfeeling missionary fairly roared with laugh-, ter. His wife began to think that he too had gene mad, when he managed to keep calm , long enough to explain. It was only& ,mistake in the sound of one letter that she had made, but it was a funnily fatal one that time. She should have said" queso instead of" beso,'' and instead of asking the man- servant for the" cheese," she had asked him with- out any qualification for M a kiss."

div.head: JUDGES AND .TILEIR NOTES.
div.p: JUDGES AND .TILEIR NOTES.

There is a great difference in judges as regards the quantity of their memoranda. Like the wily Eldon, who, when writing letters in court to his private friends, always folded the paper to deceive the Bar,some only make a pretence of taking notes. Judges, indeed,, have even sketched while profess- ing to follow the evidence closely. Xi ce-Chancellor Bacon often thus killed time, and once, probably, regretted that he had not adopted some other method. He heard an action for damages claimed for injuries done to shrubs and trees by chemical fumes from a chimney. A witness stated that he ascended the particular chimney stack and put his nose over the top, when he smelled the fumes ascending. The decision is immaterial. Enough that, whatever it was, an appeal was made. The Vice-Chancellor was then asked for a copy of his notes of the action. He at first refused this request, but even- tually complid with it, and it was thereupon band that his " notes " consistel of a single rough drawing representing a chimney emitting dense smoke, and with a long-nosed man hanging over it. Other judges, however, made voluminous abstracts of evidence. If these occupants of the Bench took their notes in shorthand the saving of time would be enormous. Frequently when a wit- ness is giving evidence has the judge to ejaculate "Stop ! " in order that he may catch up with the person under examination. These interruptions are at times very irritating, but nobody now at the bar nas thought of treating a judicial slow coach as a counsel treated Sir C. Cres- well. That judge was once making notes of a wit- ness's evidence, when he had occasion frequently to call out "atop !" in the approved way At last counsel went on without attending to the coma- and. Sir Charles accordingly addressed the barrister by name, complaining that he had not time to take down the evidence in writing, and asking if he did not hear the call to stop. The counsel blandly replied, "Oh, my lord, I thought your lordship had been calling to the usher of the court." To get down anything like tip-eels of the evidence judges are obliged to use abbreviations. That these are liable to misconstruction is shown by the fact that Mr. Justice John Williams, in reading out the notes of evidence taken by another judge, made hash of this sentence.: "When the plaintiff was asked to pay for the goods he said he would see them dd. first." The ,contraction means delivered ; Justice Williams interpreted it to mean something else. Much that would be interesting might be written about the way judges consider their notes. Justice Allude. for example, was fond of reading a novel both before and after studying his memoranda with a view to summing up. The president of the Par- nell Commission had Ins notes of that inquiry bound, and considered them on board a yacht. In this his lordship followed the example of Lord Chief Justice Cockburn, who prepared the Tichborne charge so.—" Cassell's Saturday Journal."

div.head: lONIE,
div.p: lONIE,
TEE
PRIDE OF THE MILL, A THRILLING LOVE STORY BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.

CHAPTER VII. A FALSE LOVER AND A BROKEN LOVE-DREAM. " lonie I can you mean it? You—you are really, to marry Mr. Lyons?" Mrs. Gregory gasped, in dis- may. "Yes, I shall marry him," murmured lonie, a swift blush covering her lovely face. "You do not wish me happiness, Mrs. Gregory. Why 7" "Because I fear you will have little enough of it with that man, my dear. I hope you may never rue it—that's all I can say. Why, I'd almost as soon see you lyin' in your coffin as standing ,at the altar with Frank Lyons l" "You grieve me to hear you speak like that," said lonie, turning away with quivering lips, "for I love him." _ _
" More's the pity." commented Mrs. Gregory. lonie walked into her own room and sat down by

the window to think. In a little while this life of toil would be over; she would be released at last from the grim poverty which she had known all her young life, and, what was itest of all, she would have a young husband, whom she fairly adored, to love and protect her. Ah I such rosy, happy, girlish dreams I What a pity it was that they were to be shattered so soon. How long she sat there she never knew. She was startled from her reverie by Mrs. Gregory coming into the room with a white, terrified face. "Oh, Miss lonic I" she cried, "would you mind doing a favour for me? My little Jamie is ill, and I have no one to send to the drug store for Dr. Judd, who always attends us—unless you would go. It is so late—after eleven—but—" "I'll go for you, of course, Mrs. Gregory," she Interrupted. "Go back to little Jamie; I hear him calling you. I'll be off in a minute." "You won't be afraid ?" questioned Mrs. Gregory. "You'll have to cut through the Park, and the way is lonely, so near midnight." " Afraid I " laughed lonie. "Oh, no," and throw- ing on her long cloak, and drawing the hood well over her curly head, she hurried out into the street. It was lonely, as Mrs. Gregory had said, though the streets of New York, even at night, are never deserted; and many a pedestrian turned to look after the little, dark figure with the beautiful face hurrying so rapidly away. 1 lonie executed her errand promptly, and it was on the homeward trip that an event happened that changed the whole current of her life. Hurrying down the street she ran almost directly into the arms of a gentleman, who, with a com- panion, was advancing around the corner. She drew back with a little cry of surprise; for, despite the darkness, she had recognised the face of Frp.nk Lyons at the first instant, and she noticed, too, in dismay too great for words, the fumes of strong wine on his breath. He drew back with a laugh, crying out, inso- lently: "Whither away so quickly, pretty one?" "Come, come, Lyons, none of that," said his companion, impatiently. "Never mind the girl— we are discussing an affair of more importance." Too shocked and horrorstricken for words, lonic had hurried on—noting, however, that he had not recognised her—and feeling the force of the remark that it was too late and too dangerous for a young girl to be walking the streets alone, lonie signalled a passing street car which would take her at least within a block of her home.

She was the only passenger, and sinking back in the nearest corner and drawing her dark veil closer over her face, she gave herself up to a good cry, all unseen. Heaven help her, was this the lover • she had idolised A moment later the car stopped again, and, to lonie's dismay, Frank Lyons and his companion entered, seating themselvei directly opposite. "Same little creature, by Jove l" commented Lyons, in an unsteady voice; but, as before, his I friend silenced him, and rim next instant both I seemed to forget the little; dark-robed, dark-veiled figure shrinking back among the sh,tdows. "You say you can pay this debt," said Lyons's companion, energetically. " You've said the same thing often enough before; now I propose to know when and how. I've done trilling—l mean business now. Remember, a debt of honour should be the first to be liquidated. W ben I loaned you that sum, which you lost at the gaming table, you prom- ised me it should be paid at once, and now it must be paid, or a grand exposé will tollow." "Enough of this dunning ; it shall be paid," declared Lyons, angrily; "and if you must know, I will tell you how and when. I am expecting to marry an heiress, and as soon as the knot is tied and she comes into possession of her wealth—which Is upon her marriage settle your bill." The words had been uttered in a low cautious voice, but they seemed to the girl sitting opposite them to have been fairly shrieked through the car. He was soon to be married, and to another: this man who, not forty-eight hours ago, had clasped her own hand, asking her to be his wife, breathing words so eloquent, so full of love and deathless devotion, that they had fairly taken her heart by storm! Had she heard aright? or was this some horrible dream from which she should awaken presently? • By a violent effect she collected her scattered senses and listened spellbound. Heedless of a third party's presence, his brain 'fired by wine, Frank Lyons went on boisterousy : "The whole affair, as the novelists would say, has been rather romantic. You remember meeting me one afternoon with ' that pretty little mill girl,' as you called her, and how you chaffed me about it the next time we met? Well, she's the heiress I'm referring to. Don't ha! ha! and interrupt me until You've heard all, for there's more back. "You have heard about that accident at the Nottingham Milrs, of course, and how lonie Law- rence, one of the girls, came near losing her life, for the papers were full of it, and the affair was copied far and wide. "It appears that a copy fell into the hands of an Iron merchant from the West, wbo had gone to Philadelphia on business. Well, to make a long story short, the name • lonie Lawrence' riveted his attention. He called upon a lawyer at once to in- vestigate whether or not this girl was the child of his only sister—lonie—who had married a man by the name of Lawrence, who had come North years before, and whom he had lost track of, though he had made several attempts to discover their where- abouts. Once he had beard of her through an old friend who chanced to meet her; that she had two children—lovely little girls—one named Barbara; the other named after herself—lonie.

"The merchant had written immediately to the address given, only to find they had recently moved away, and all trace was lost. "Now he requested this Philadelphia lawyer to ascertain if this orphan mill girl is one of his nieces, declaring that if it be provgd so, she shall inherit the whole of his immense fortune, one half to be paid down on her wedding-day.

• 'The Philadelphialawyer caned upon is my room-mate, and he wrote on immediately to me, stating all the facts, asking me to find out beyond a doubt if this girl was the one sought for, and had bad a sister named Barbara, knowing I could easily ascertain the required information, as I was acquainted with young Rochester, the mill-owner's son.

"Imagine my astonishment upon learning all this, for I bad quite an acquaintance with the bewitch- ing little mill-girl, with whom I had been flirting desperately to kill time. Why, it was as good as a novel, I say. You can depend upon it I lost no time in proposing to the charming nymph, saying never a,word just yet of my wonderful discovery. You understand, I want her to think I wooed and won her.in all her poverty, for herself. She will never know gold was the bait, not love.

"Colonel Whitney, this wealthy old uncle, is stopping at the K— Hotel, in Philadelphia, awaiting patiently the result of the investigation. So there's the long and the short of the whole story. You may be sure I shall push the marriage forward as rapidly as possible;" adding with a laugh: "There'll be no time spent on wedding trousseaus from Paris, and all that sort of nonsense." "But the girl," responded his friend—" are you sure she will accept you? Proposing and being accepted are different matters." "Beyond a doubt," returned Lyons, twisting his moustache about complacently with his white fingers. "Wish I was as sure of five millions of dollars." "Well, under those circumstances, of course, if it will oblige you, I'll wait on yon for that little amount, Lyons." "I knew you'd see the natter in the right light. If you had, in common parlance, blowed on me, the whole affair would have ended for me; for, although this charming lonie is only a mill girl, as she believes herself just now, yet she would never marry me if she knew what a reckless fellow I am; that's the sort pf_a. girl she is. It wouldn't do for

her to hear that I have run through two fortunes already, at my age of life." "And are waiting to run through a third," sup- plemented his companion, dryly. "Upon ray word, I actually pity the girl so unfortunate as to get you. iknd that little girl I saw you with has a sweet face, 'tender and true." ; The little veiled figure in the dark cloak rose quickly to her feet, and with a swaying motion, like a leaf in the wind, left the car; and it rolled on, leaving her standing there on the snowy pavement, her face white as it would ever be in death, her eyes heavy with unshed tears. CHAPTER VIII. A HEART CAUGHT IN THE REBOUND. lonic did not cry out, nor utter any moan, great as the shock had been. As she listened to the words that fell from Frank Lyon's lips, all the love in her heart turned instantly to loathing. The scales fell from her eyes which had been blinded so long by love. She saw him in his true character at last. Her idol was shattered—her love dream broken; but she thanked Heaven it had happened before, instead of after her marriage. Mrs. Gregory was dismayed at lonie's white face when she returned. "You look ill yourself, my dear," she declared. I would really advise you to see the doctor, too, when he calls." All that night the dark, curly head tossed rest- lessly on her pillow; but if lonic shed bitter tears of girlish disappointment over the loss of her hand- some, fickle lover, the world never knew it. Frank Lyons was at the house at the appointed hour the next day. Mrs. Gregory admitted him, and he could not fail to see the dislike on her honest face.
He was shown into the plain little parlour, and, to his surprise, it was some little time before lonie put in an appearance, which was quite unusual.

•At length the door opened, and f ome, flushing and paling, hesitatingly entered the room. " lonie I my darling l" he cried, springing eagerly forward, and attempting to clasp her hands with his outstretched ones. "It seems to me I have been waiting here an age for you, dear." lonie drew back from him in scorn, the delicate bloom deepening on her dimpled cheeks, her dark eyes blazing.

"You play the part of an anxious lover capitally, Mr. Lyons," she said. "Allow me to compliment you on your perfect dissembling." "mule," he cried, "what can you mean? Last evening I left you with the light of love shining in your face for me and kind words on your lips. Now I find you suddenly changed toward me. I ask you again: What can it mean? Have you forgotten why lam here to-day ? Is it to gain the promise that you will be mine, dear? You were to give me your answer to-day."
She held up her little hand with a gesture of silence.

"lam here in accordance with that agreement," she said. "I have brought you your answer." "And that answer, my darling," he cried, breath- lessly, "is—" "No," she replied. "lonic," he cried, hoarsely, "surely you are jest- ing. You cannot—you do not mean it." "I can and do mean it," she retorted. "I will never be your wife, Mr. Lyons. Please consider the interview at an end."

"You shall not leave me like this, lonie," he cried, fairly beside himself with rage.. "You have led me on to hope that my suit would meet with favour in your (3 es, and new you would coolly throw me over. You would make rue the laughing•stock of all my friends. It must not be. lonie. You must marry me." _

The girl drew back and looked at him haughtily. "Pardon me. The word 'must' was ill chosen," she said. "I am not used to coercion. I will not be forced into marriage. I told you all along I was not sure of my own heart whether I cared for you or not. Now I have analyzed my true feelings toward you. • I-I—would not marry you if you were the last man in the world." Frank Lyons started back in amazement. He had been so sure of her. For an instant keen dis- appointment and rage got the best of his judg- ment.
A sneer fell from his lips—his eyes blazed wrath- fully.

"'One would think to hear you that you were an heiress instead of a poor factory girl," he cried, "who should deem it a grand honour to be asked in marriage by me." The girl's lip curled. Without deigning him a reply, she turned like a young queen and walked away.
In vain he sougiht Mrs. Gregory, and pleaded with her to implore lonie to return to the parlour; he had so much to say to her, and that he could not leave her like this. '
But lonie was inexorable. She would not return.-

In utter despair, he seized his hat at last and hurried from the house, muttering that this was some enemy's work, and that he should win the girl in spite of all the fates that could intervene. Aye, in spite of herself; for she had loved him once, and love could not die in a woman's heart so easily.

Ma'n-like—when he found he could not get lonie —he discovered how much he really cared for her aside from her fortune. "She shall not know about that fortune until she is my wife," he said, grimly. And that night he wired the following message to his friend in Philadelphia: "To WALTER STANHOPE, No. Chestnut-street Have made diligent inquiries concerning the girl you wrote me about, and have learned that she has left the city. "(Signed) FRANIC B. LYONS."
The telegram was duly handed over to his patron, Colonel Whitney, by Mr. Stanhope, the lawyer. - -

Slowly the colonel read it through. "Left the city l" he groaned—" her whereabouts unknown I lam beginning to believe I shall NEVER be able to trace lonie's child. To-morrow I will go on to New York and see for myself if all clue is hopelessly lost." The next afternoon, just as the colonel stepped out upon the piazza, he was met by one of the bell- boys who had been searching for him, with the information that a young lady who was in the recep- tion room wished to see him.

" A lady I" ejaculated the colonel, surprisedly. "Now what in the name of all that is wonderful can a lady want with me ?" he muttered, under his breath, adding: "The best plan obviously is to go and see. No doubt it 's some book agent ; and with a look of resignation on his ruddy face, he stepped into the reception room. A slim figure in a brown dress rose from the depths of a cushioned arm-chair, and fluttered down to meet him. A ' little brown hand was stretched out to him, and a pair of great, childish dark eyes were raised timidly to his face, and a voice, as sweet as a silver bell, said: "Please welcome me, Colonel Whitney. I am tonic Lawrence, your niece." -Bless my soul," exclaimed the bewildered Colonel, "can it really be true 7" But there was no need to ask that question, for the first swift glance into that lovely girlish face, so wonderfully like his dead sister's, was conclusive proof to him that this was her child. The letters she had brought written by the colonel to her mother, and the locket she wore round her neck containing her father's and mother's portraits, were conclusive evidence.

The colonel's delight at finding her knew no bounds, and he listened intently when she told him briefly and truthfully just how she had heard of him at the cost of finding out the falsity of her lover.

You have escaped one of the worst rascals society ever tolerated, my dear," he exclaimed. "I have known this Frank Lyons for years, and never knew any good him. You say you were in the Rochester Mill," he added, suddenly. "Then, of course, you saw young Arthur Rochester. If there was ever a man who ought to be called a king among men, he is the one. I hope, lonie," he continued, energetically, "if you ever fall in love with a young man, it will be some one like him." He did not understand why the girl's face flushed so deeply, then turned so deadly pale. lonie did not realise then, but she knew after- ward, why it gave her such keen pleasure to hear her uncle speak so kindly of Arthur Rochester. She could not tell the colonel that he had asked her to be his wife, and that she had refused him— thrown away a golden heart for one of tinsel. A strange truth was dawning upon her. She was beginning to care for Arthur Rochester; she was learning to prize the love she had cast aside. Ah, how blind she had been to have even imagined she cared for Frank Lyons. She had not mourned his loss as she had imagined she would; his face was blotted all too quickly from her memory, and another filled her thoughts, waking or sleeping. But would she ever see Arthur Rochester again? she asked herself, and her heart beat more quickly at the thought. Ah, if he would but come to her ajd ask that momentm queation again, she would

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup
skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: not send him away, and she thought of beautiful, pathetic lines : "She told him 'No,' and he went away; But neither could she forget ; • And many a time in the long still night. Her eyes with tears were wet— -- For she missed the love that she cast aside. 'Why does he not abk me again?' she cried." Colonel Whitney informed lonic that they should start for Pittsburgh, his home. His immense foundry interests, required his constant presence there. The colonel had behaved in a most munificent manner to lonic. He took her at once to a modiste and ordered a wardrobe for her that was as elabor- ate as a princess's trousseau. It was a novelty for him to have charge of a young and beautiful girl, whom he constantly impressed with the fact that she was to be his heiress. lonie was troubled at first when she heard of the magnificence of the home that was to be hers. She imparted her fears frankly enough to the colonel,. but he smiled at them. "It is like a fairy story," she said; "from a New York tenement house to a mansion—from a mill girl, searching the streets for work, to an heiress. The famous story of Cinderella is not more startling and strange. How am I ever to fill such a position, uncle? It bewilders me even to think of it.' "My dear lonic," he said, "there is that happen- ing aroun;i us every day which could scarcely be 'believed if written up by a novelist, xerifying the old adage that 'truth is indeed stranger than. I fiction.' You will soon be accustomed to the new mode of life ; you will adapt yourself to it naturallY• If there is a little deficiency in your knowledge of society matters, you will meet it by studying attentively the habits and manners of those about you."

SHE WILL NEVER TELL THE SECRET. , Here is a piece of glass ; it is cut into facets ; pure white glass ;it is fit to be one of the pendants hanging from a chandelier in a millionaire's drawing- room ;it is about as big as a hazelnut. How it sparkles as I hold it up between my thumb and finger ! Yet it, is merely glass and scarcely worth a shilling, oh ! if I onlY knew how to turn it into a diamond ; a blue or a rose diamond. Why, there are thousands who would give all their health, and then mortgage their souls to buy it cif me. Then good-bye to work and care, for I should be rich beyond the dreams of avarice. Who will show me the process ? Alas ! nobody. Who will tell in how to transmute tin or copper into shining gold ? Alas I nobody. A bit of coal is carbon. A diamond is also carbon. Where is the link bet xeen them ? We yearn to know. Thousands of men have burned out life's Can- dle in the effort to ascertain. How vainly ! In the bosom of her hills Nature hides that secret, as she hides the secret of man's destiny under mountains of ashes and crumbling bones. On our bended knees we beg her to break one unbroken seal,to speak one unspoken word. She only regards us with contemptuous pity arid re- mains for ever dumb. Yet, is there no other mystery,just as deep,that conies home to your thoughts in a way to frighten you? Thinic a minute, man. What builds and repairs the house Yon live in, that is, your body ? What changes a loaf of bread into nerves, flesh, skin, and muscle? What does this mean ? as when a lady says of her daughter," She took food but got no strength from It means that in her case the base products of the ground were net turned into the diamond called the burn° body. What does that mean in familar English ? Sie- pro, ply that the process of digestion is interrupted, a into gold cess stranger than the trausmutation of copper would be. The lady proceeds to say that her daughter was seven- teen years of age when she was taken ill. This is the age of h cpe, brightness, vigour, and enjoyment, and, by rights, illness ought to be unknown to it. Still, she lost her strength, and languished as though stricken bY time. She grew tired anti weak, and could keep nothing on her stomach. She would, so her mother say-s, often throw up a quantity of green fluid as bitter as gall' This was bile, the fluid which in health nature takes from the blood and sends to the bowels to aid digestion there. The liver failing to do this work, the bile re- mains in the blood, and is returned to the stomach,which rejects it as a poison. That is a part of it. the rest saturates the body, producing headache, nervous de- pression and debility, bad dreams, cold hands and feet furred tongue, yellow eyes and skin, dizziness, had taste in the mouth, and the gulping up of a nauseating gas and slime, with loss of appetite and ambition for labour or pleasure. This state of things is often called a bilious attack, and is part of the results and sy roc" toms of indigestion and dyspepsia. This affected life' to young or old, is one constant mjsery. It is the copper, the glass ; not the gold or the diamond. "This was my daughter's condition," adds her mother, " for nearly two years. She took various clues, and and was treated by a physician, but without benefit. She grew daily weaker, and with her decline our anxiety increased. We knew not what to do, net where to look for help. " It was at this worrying time that we first heard of the preparation called Mother Seigel's Syrup. and read the statements of different persoNis who said they had derived great good from it. Thinking, or rather hop- ing, that it might avail something in my daughter's case, I procured a Dottie from Mr. Rogers, Drug Mullinear. To our great joy she found relief after tak' lug the first bottle, and before she had finished the third one she was completely cured and has had no return of the complaint. I have since recommended Seigel:6 Syrup to many friends and neighbours. The facts 10 my daughter's case are well known to Mr. Rogers and to others in the vicinity. I append •my initials° and address. R. J. M., Slanemore, near Mullingar. Storee, Ireland." Mr. Rogers certifies as follows : " I remember the lady above named informing in' d the cure of her daughter by taking Seigel's SyruP, an can vouch tor the accuracy of the statement. " RICHARD G. ROGERS, " Mullingar, June 4, 1591." To recur to our illustration, we may say that tire remedy employed assisted nature to resume lie.r work e producing the most precious of all her jewels--healtn and happiness. •

THREATENING THE WARRINGTON NUISANCE INSPECTOR. Mr. Browne appeared for the Prn,r. cution and Mr. P. Davies for, the defence. Ze Browne said his client was talking to Mr. PS manager for Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, oppOSite 111. s shop, when Martin, who somehow had got it into lue head that Mr. Norman had a grudge against him. ca!!„ close to them and used some filthy language, shoal; • out with foul oaths " There's a slaughter-house dnv. there (pointing to that of Mr. Charles at the corn, er4. and if it is not moved I will have it done for a nu;ri Bence." div.head: NEW ST. HE LE IV3 RAT [MAY.
div.p: THE NEW ST. HE LE IV3 RAT [MAY.

A few days ago a rept esentative of a Liverpool newspaper.along with a brother journalist, had "the singular privilege" of -travelling - over the entire line of the new St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway as far as at present constructed, and load the opportunity of viewing not only ' the actual Work accomplished, but of witnessing the further operations now going on.- The' two pressmen met Mr. S. Pilling, of the firm of MPSBr$. S. W. Pilling and Co., of Manchester, the contractors for the new line, at the Haydock offices of the firm, and that gentleman courteously consented to accompany them on the proposed trip. The locomotive " Bamboo." was immediately signalled, and on its tender Mr. Pilling 'and 'his two visitors were soon apeeding along high embankments Or through deep cuttings' in the direction,of Golborne and Lowton., Chatting on the way Mr. Pilling explained that the delay in the completion of the railway was not due I to any'fault of the contractors,a fact which has long been known to all interested in the new railway. I There were at present about 500 men engaged in the construction of the new line,and the movable plant in I eluded two immense steam navvies,four locomotives many portable engines, a couple of hunolred of ' ballast waggons, and some four or .five aides of tempor- ary rails. After a smart rollicking run of half an hour ; " Sambe." drew up at the junction with the Manchester , and Wigan Railway (Cheshire Lines), at Lowton, St. , Mary's—Station, and, in the few minutes " breathing , time" which was allowed, the press representatives ' " viewed the landscape o'er." Perhaps the most strik- ing fact forced upon their attention was the vast import- ance of the new railway connection. The new line pas See through the centre of the extensive coalfield covered by the 16 or 17 collieries of Messrs. Rd. Evans and Co., and it is stated that there are smile 400 million tons of fuel available for immediate removil. The pre- ; sent annual report of the firm is estimated to , be about : million tons and the new St. Helens railway, when , completed, will open out to the colliery proprietors , direct communication with the eastern, midland, and seethern counties now served by the M S. and L., the Gfeat Northern, and the Midland Railway Companies. To tbe chemical and glass manufacturers of St. Helens, the new line is expected to prove an unmixed blessing. As in the case of the Haydock coalfield, a new outlet will be found for the staple industries ot the town, and as an important competitive line for goods traffic, it will secure for the trades of the district more equitable ratesof carriage and less of the annoying delays, petty hindrances, and heavy charges to which they have hitherto been subject. After the brief stoppage at Lowton the return journey was commenced, and along the line plenty of time was allowed for noting the progress of the workm The line from Lowton to Golborne—a distance of nearly two miles—was constructed some three or four years ago, and is now in a thorough working condition. The first mile is a perfectly straight cutting from three to seven or eight feet below the surface of the land, and the line then enters upon an embankment some 20ft. high until Wigan-road, Golborne, is reached. At this spot the pro- posed Golborne passenger station will be erected, and the surrounding land is now being drained, levelled,and in other ways prepared for the intended buildings, in- cluding a goods warehouse. Leaving the site of the station, the line is carried, on three massive bridges,over Wigan-road and the adjoining four sets of rails constitut- ing the main line to Scotland of the London and North- Western Railway Company. These bridges, whith formed the heaviest work of the kind to be encountered in the construction of the new railway, are now com- pleted, and the permanent way generally for a con- siderable distance in the direction of St. *Helens is in a highly finished conditien. When the London and North-western lines have been crossed, the embankment is continued towards Ashton-m-Makerfield, and with the exception of a atzetch of about 200 yards the lines and working arrangements for over two miles of the track ere fully completed. Over this portion "Sambo" had a rattling uninterrupted run. Approaching the well known Ashton Heath the line skirts, on the left, the estate of the Haydock Park Coursing Company, and it has been arranged that a platform station shall be erected at a convenient spot for the use of visitors during race and coursing meetings. From' here the railway enters a deep cutting, which when finally completed will be three miles in length • the trains entering at Ashton Heath not emerthing until the ' village of flaydock is reached. The cutting first winds , along the north side of the grounds of Haydock Lodge , Asylum, and the site of the station for the thriving vil- lage of Ashton-in- Makerfield is reached at Lodge-lane. The main road between Warrington, Newton-le-Willows, ' and Wigan, under which the railway will pass near to I the entrance of Garswood Park, the residence of Lord Gerrard. Here large numbers of navvies were at work ' completing the cutting or preparing the site of the sta- tion for the intended buildings, and the scene of ac- tivity betokened that the undertaking is being vigor- ' ously prosecuted. Up to this point the cutting has been made through a soft red sandstone material, but from ' Lodge-lane to Kenyon's-lane, Haydock, a distance of about a mile, solid rock has been met with and blasting ' operations have been necessitated. The track, how- ever, bas been laid through the rock cuttings, but pend- ing the final completion of the other work in that ' locality the continuation of the cutting in the direction of Haydock has been suspended. A steam navvy is in position at the face of the cutting, ready to resume its operations at any moment, but at the present time I the surface of the land for about 2,000 yards has not ' been disturbed. An interesting feature of the new railway works was I observable in the cutting near Garwood Park. A mis- sionary connected with *the Church of England Navvy Mission was holding one of his daily gatherings during the dinner interval, and the " congregation "—about half-a-dozen labourers—seemed deeply interested in the simple service of concertina music, Sankey's hYrnn-sing- ing, and a few words of prayer and exhortation. It may be noted that the expenses of the missionary are borne by the contractors,and, as if to emphaeise the fact that if men won't be honest and good by persuasion, force will be employed to prevent their wrong doing, Police-constable Rothery was to be seen a short distance away in the cutting. The officer is on special duty" protecting the property of the contractors, and for his services the contractors have to pay certain charges and demands of the county constabulary authorities. Our pilot engine "Sarnia)," indifferent to these sur- roundings of navvy life, mounted, with a spurt,- from the level of the permanent way in the cutting to the top of the embankment, and a rattling spin along the private temporary line of the contractors, crossing on a level Kenyon's-lane, at the spot known as the Withins, and one or two small occupation roads, took the party to the centre of Haydock, where all the varying forms ef labour necessitated by the making of railways were in full operation. The principal work here has been the construction of a strong, substantial covered way under- neath the extensive sidings of Messrs. Richard Evans , and Co., the well-known colliery proprietors. This covered way'la in close proximity to- the King, Queen, and Princess Pits of the firm, and is about 100 yards in length. Its sides are of solid cement, six feet thick, lined with glazed blue • bricks and the rails belonging to Messrs. Evans will be car- ried over the 'cutting by Hobson's patent steel floors, .of exactly similar design to that used for the Liverpool Overhead Railway. The covered way is not vet finally completed, but the work has reached an ad- vanced stage. On the Ashton side of the covered way one of the contractors' steam navvies was in full work. It is said that one of these machines can accomplish as much work as 25 men,and certainly to see the ponderous machine in operation will obviate the necessity of dis- putipg the assertion. The massive scoop of the navvy works its way up the face' of the earth, and in a few seconds gathers into an immense iron bucket a heap of , dirt suffieient to almost fill one of the ordinary ballast waggons. These waggons are being continually shunted and receiving their loads, and when a train is got toge- ther off they are taken by one of the locomotives in the direction of St. Helens, where the contents are tipped and used in the construction of an embankment near the Sankey Canal. About 300 yards from the covered way; approaching St. Helens, the line passes under Clipsley-lane at a spot near the Wesleyan Chapel and schools, and Lout' mid- way between the extensive offices of Alisra.. Evans and Co. and the Haydock Cottage Hospital. It is here that the Haydock passenger and goods'statioh will be erected and there cannot be the slightest doubt as to the admir- able site which has been selected. flaydock generally consists of one straggling thoroughfare tome three miles in length, and the new station will not only be at its very centre, but it will be in close proximity to the terminus of the St. Helens tramway. It will practically adjoin the headquarters of the great firm of colliery pro- prietors, and it will be within a few minutes' walk of the residences of the great bulk of the population. At this spot Messrs. Pilling and Co., the contractors, have put up a number of wooden huts for storerooms, stables, and blacksmithing purposes, and fronting a new road which has been constructed to meet the requirements of Messrs. Evans and Co., two handsome semi- detached houses bave been built for the new railway company. From the site of Haydock Station the line runs along the surface of the land for half a mile and then enters upon an em- bankment and viaductp which will finally be over two miles in length, and carry the line to the central station of the compan, , in Corporation-street, St. Helens. This embankment has been formed down to the Sankey Canal at Double Locks, and the water will be crossed hg a massive bridge of two spans, one of the latter being 80 feet. This bridge is partially constructed. On the ap- posite side of the canal the line will enter the borough of st. Helens, and will gross in a direct line the field used last season by the St. Helens Association Footbalit: Club, whose members have had under these conditions to seek fresh fields away from possible interruptiou by energetic railway promoters. Herd he main road be- tween St. Helens and Haydock grill he crosseet. by another bridge, the foundations of .which have•been built, and a hundred yards further en the canal, which in this locality makes a wide sweep, is again covered, by a bridge similar to the

one at Double Locks. A series of similar arches will next carry the line to Merton Bank-lane, where a heavy brick bridge ip now in course of erection, and from this point a wide sweep will be made past the Globe Alkali Works and the Gcrard's Bridge Chemical Works, both " btlenging tother Unitifd. Alkali Company. This will be accomplished by altiaduct' of brick and iron arches, Which will pill-over aisoition II of the Globe Works yard, near,the bleaching chambers, land on to the Central Station. This viaduct will be from 20 to 25 feet in height, and will necessitate the platform 'of the Central Station being reached by a flight of steps. The vacant land surrounding the site will be partly occupied by goods warehouses, to be erected by the railway company. It is understood that plans for the proposed stations are now under the consideration of the directors and the company's architects, but have not yet been finally adopted. The station will have a fron- tage to Corporation-st., and, if , present intentions are carried out, it will be worthy, of the,prominent position it will occupy in a thoroughfare already containing such handsome buildings as the Town Hall, Free Library, and Municipal-offices, the new Theatre Royal and Opera House, the Wesleyan Chapel, and the Holy Cross Catho- no Church. It cannot be ascertained at the present time when the line will be carried forward from St. Helens to Liverpool. All the energies of the contractors are being devoted to the completion of the first section from St. Helens to ' Lowton, and Mr. Pilling informed our representative that be hoped to have that portion ready for passenger traffic by the end of next year. Everything is being hurried forward, and in view of the vast number of bricks which will be required in the construct,on of the viaduct from Merton Bank-lane to the Central Station, the con- tractors have started brickworks and kilns on their own account in Merton Bank-lane. The present arrange- ments for the Liverpool line, are that, starting from the Central Station, St. Helens, a viaduct some 250 yards long will carry the railway over Corporation4st., Baldwin-street, Ormskirk-street. New Cross-street, Rigby-street, Hamer-street, Lowe-street, Napier-street, Talbot-street, Kirkland-street, Hope-street, Grant-street and Boundary-road (near Spray's Bridge), and this will necessitate the removal of about 200 cottages or other buildings. ..From Boundary-toad the line will pass through Denton's, Green and Eecleston, then skirt the north side of Knowsley Park, passing close by the water- works of the St. Helens Corporation at Knowsley, and afterwards join/ the Cheshire Lines Railway at West Derby ; passenger stations being provided at Denton's Green, Knowsley (Longborough-road), and Croxteth Park.

THE EXAMINER, SATIJRDAY. AUGUST 27; 1892. I GAS STOVES EXHIBITION AT 1 .. THE NEW MINISTRY. WARRINGTON. An exhibition of gas stoves, &c., held under the abil :vices of the Mayoress ( drs. Greenall) was in'ed in ;the Gymnasium; Palmyra square, 'ifif •Winflay etening. The Mayor and Mayoress add' hfr. E. W. T. Richmond of the firm of Messrs 4ictimond and Co.. Limited, were present on the platform, as also was Mks Owen, of South Ken- sington, the well known lecturess on cookery, with her juvenile assistant. There was a pretty numer- ous attendance, principally composed of ladies. The MAYORESS addresNed the meeting as follows : Ladies and gentlemen,—The pleasant task .devolves on me this evening of introducing to you Miss Owen,,, who has arranged with Mr. Richmond to deliver a course of lectures this week on gas stove cooking. As good cook- ing is, as we all know, of the first importance in every household these lectures cannot fail to be interesting and instructive to all here present. Personally, I have no experience in gas stoves, but will call on Mr. Richmond, to explain more fullythand'could the usesf them, after which Miss Owen will show us how cooking can be done by the use of gas stoves both eceromically and well. I hope these lectures may prove most interesting and suc- cessful, and be a benefit to all. (Applause.) Mr. W. T. Rierrirosna, then delivered an address on "Gas as a domestic servant." He said he was sure it would be the feeling of those present that Mrs. Greenall had performed a very pleasing duty in opening the exhi- bition; and thus lending her very valuable services to an object which was for the amelioration of the conditions of their households, or that in any way tended to reduce the troublesome labour that occurred in them on every hand. When those who were placed in positions of honour 1 amongst them took such evident interest in the welfare of those who had done them the honour of electing them to those positions, he was sure it was a very gratifying matter r and they all thanked Mrs Greenall very heartily for her kindness that evening in coming there to promote the objett of that exhibition. They would all be aware that it waa held for the purpose of making clear the ad- vantagesof the use of gas for other purposes than that of lighting. They were all familiar with gas as an illumin- ant in their buildings. They wished to make them equally familiar with gas stoves. It had been their object by exhibitions and lectures to make gas stoves so St,ell understood throughout the length and breadth of the land that the first wish of the public who had not yet adopted them would be to try them. In Warrington the home, as it might be termed, of gas stoves, the system, stranse to say, had not been adopted to the extent that it deserved. There were, he believed, in the town some 4000 consumers of gas, and yet, strange to say, only 150 of these cooked by gas. He thought that fact alone proved that an exhibition of that kind was urgently wanted, in order to show them that the system of cooking by gas was, at any rate, worthy of a trial. It was with very great pleasure that they were able to come beore that audience supported by the Gas Committee of the Cor- poration. It was his privilege on the previous Friday and Saturday evening to be speaking on the same sub- ject at Brighton, and he could not now help comparing the terms on which stoves were supplied there, where they had to be purchased according to the maker's list of prices. In Warrington the Gas Committee had taken steps for the hiring out of stoves costing £7 or £8; exclusive of cost of fixtures, £1 to £1 10s., .at the rate of 6s. or 7s. the half year ;or as. a year, and if at the end of that time the hirer was not satisfied with the stove and it did not fulfil its requirements he was at liberty to return it to the Committee. Surely such con- ditions as these—and the cost of fixing Was included— ought to make everyone who had not adopted the stove an inunediate user of it. It appeared to him that there was another, reason apart from that of economy why the , gas stove ought to be used in the household. The aver- age business man was not always certain as to what time he could get home to his meals. Sometimes he came in late, and the consequence was that some tasty dinner, the preparing of which had cost much trouble, was spoilt. Not so with the gas stove. If a man was late for his dinner his wife could turn the tap back, and the dinner could wait art hour if need be ; and at the 1 end of that time be as good as if it had been served up' the moment it was cooked. On many points theni it was almost a necessity that they should have a gas stove in their households. Who would ever think of makings journey to Glasgow at the present day by stage coach. Gas was as much in front of coal as travelling by rail was of travelling by coach. It was as much in front of cooking by coal at the sewing machine was in front of stitching hy hand, as the telegraph was in front of the special messenger of bygone days. It was as much before coal as the speaking trumpet Was eclipsed by the telephone. Its conclOsion he hoped that many of those present would see the utility of having a stove in their respective households. (Ap- plause.' , . Miss Owen then gave a lengthy and practical exposi, tion of cooking by means of a gas stove, giving as she went on, clear explanations of her method of procedure. The comestibles cooked by her were short paste, Cor- ni.h pasties, Swiss roll, and an omelette, many of the ladies present taking profuse notes of the details given by her. ' The exhibition and lectures have been continued throughout the week. The exhibition includes princip- ally a large number of stoves,, from the establiqh- ment of Messrs. Richmond and Co. Probably the ex- hibit to which most attention was directed was the famous model range gas cooking stove manufactured by the above mentioned firm, which was much admired for the beauty of its construction and ita scientific work- ing.—Mr. J. S. Garland, Bridge-st., Warrington, ex- hibited Stott's patent gas governor and reflex light, and Messrs. Skelton, of Warrington,a variety of cooking and other appliances.—Messrs. Webb, of Leicester, exhibited a number of lamps of improved construction.

div.head: CYCLIST KILLED ST WARRINGTON.
div.p: A CYCLIST KILLED ST WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Dispensary adjoining the Infirmary concerning the death of Joseph Abrams, aged 21, chemical works labourer, who resided at 15, York- et., Runcorn, and was killed on Saturday, under the circumstances hereafter detailed. Mrs. Sarah Abrams, the deceased's mother, said he left home between two and three on Saturday afternoon, and she heard no more of him till Sunday when she learnt he was at Warrington Infirmary. He was a steady man. John Dickinson. chemical labourer, deposed that they came to Warrington together on Saturday afternoon, on safety bicycles. They left them at the Norton Arms, Warrington, about three o'clock. They then went round the town, but had no drink except several lemon dashes. They started from the Norton Arms to return home about 9 p.m. They had gone about a quarter of a mile along Wilderspool road, witness being in the middle of the road,and the deceased on hisleft, when thsy saw a float 20 yards in front. He saw no light on it. It was on the proper side of the road. The deceased was about two yards from the parapet. There was a 'bus on the right side of the deceased behind the float. Witness shot ahead of the deceased to pass the float and the bus, and was riding ahead of them, when someone shouted to him to draw his atten- tion to his friend, and he turned and found to his sur- prise that he had got injured. The deceased he found, had been placed in the 'bus. The float was goine at the rate of ten miles an hour. The night was not very dark. Mr. Bailey told witness on the other side of the Norton Arms to look after Abrams, as he was riding very awk- wardly, but he was right enough, in his estimation. John Bailey, 200 Wilderspool-road, corroborated as to the caution given to Dickinson, and said the deceased made two unsuccessful attempts to mount his machine' and he assisted him. Ile made the remark he did to Dickinson knowing the dangerous state of the way, it being badly out of repair, and thronged with 'busses on Saturday night. It was very lumpy too, throu2h the traffic to and from the Agricultural Show. He did not consider the deceased a culpupetent rider. The driver of the float appeared te be sober. Witness knew his horse well, and it could not go much more than five miles an hour. _

Alfred Edward Brooks said he saw the accident. Owen was on his right side, and driving five miles an hour, and had a light right in front on the right side of the float.. The deceased ran with his bicycle into wit- ness's horse's chest, and was knocked off. Arthur Fitzhugh, a lad, said Owen was sober, and called to the deceased as loudly as he could four times before the collision. _

Ella Smith, nurse at the Infirmary, deposed to the deceased being admitted to the institution unconscious, never recovering consciousness, and dying there about four o'clock next morning. Alfred Owen deposed that the deceased was riSing very awkwardly and witness 'pulled up, and shouted to him" Heigh up " several times. Dickinson rode past, and Abrams attempted to 'pass bat rode clean into the horse. Witness was driving at the rate of 4to 5 miles an hour. The deceased was conveyed from the Norton Arms to the Infirmary in the float. The Coroner in summing up said he should las very sorry if this accident should bring any disrepute on the pastime of cycling, beconse he had very strong opinions that cycling was one of the most enjoyable pastimes that anyone could indulge in. He was also strongly of opinion that the benefits of it if not seen at present, would be seen later on, because though they might come in contact with young men who knew nothing of any place six miles out of- their district, yet those young men who were cyclists were enlightened, because they travelled ibout and saw the cuuntry. Of course there were cyclists and cyclists. A great many of them could improve their manners, both in their ways and their riding. It was perfectly ridiculous to think they could come on to the highway and use it as a play- ground. They had no prior right on the road as they seemed to imagine, and had no right to run races on if, but could only use the highway as those driving con- veyances could, in a fair and legitimate fashion, to go from one place to another. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and exonerated Owen entirely from blame.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. R. Heaton presided; and there were also present Messrs. Balharry, Davie, Shaw, Piling, A. Jolley, Muir, Gill, A. J. Jolley, Smith, W. Houghton. Huniphrefs, J. Houghton,- Ratcliffe, -Turton,-Auk- land, Hibbert, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and other officers.

div.head: PADOATS SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE PADOATS SCHOOLS.

• The Padgate Schools Committee reported that a speci- fication of repairs to the boundary wall of the schools prepared by Mr. J. G. Wright, bad been before the Com- mittee, and they recommended that the tenders be ad- vertised for and submitted to the Committee at their next meeting. A letter was read from the Rev. T. P. Williamson, of Thelwall Vicarage, offering for the use of the children at Padgate schools a ".Itavenscroft May Pole" for indoor amusement, and it was recommended that • the offer be accepted and the thanks of the Guardians given to Mr. Williamson for his kindness. The Committee having considered the desirableness of fixing upon arrangements for occasional absences from the school of female officers, they recommended that, exclusive of any arrangement for attendance at divine services on Sundays, each fetnaie officer be entitled to one absence per week and that such absence upon no occasion exceed six hours. The Committee regretted to hear of the illness of Mr. Mines, superintendent of the schools, and they wished him speedy recovery, and were pleased to hear of an im- provement in his condition.—Mr. W. Houghton, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that the reso- lution with regard to the absences of female officers was passed in order to strengthen the hands of the superin- tendent in reference to applications for leave of absence. —The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: RUNCORN BREWSTER SESSION&
div.p: RUNCORN BREWSTER SESSION&

The annual licensing sessions for the Petty Ses- sional Division of Runcorn were held at Runcorn Police Court on Monday. Mr. Alfred Thomas pre- sided, and the other magistrates on the Bench were Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele.

div.head: SOP'ERINTENDENT'S REPORT.
div.p: THE SOP'ERINTENDENT'S REPORT.

Mr. Superintendent Atherton read his annual report as follows I have the honour to submit my annual report with reference to the conduct of the License,il Victuallers and Beer Retailers in this division during the past year. There are 44 licensed victuallers, 51 beer- sellers—and 6 others who sell off the premises, total 101; which gives an average of 248 of the population to each license. 2 licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year, both of whom were convicted; against 2 proceeded against and one convicted last year. 2 beersellers have been proceeded against and one con- victed; against 5 proceeded against and 3 convicted last year. 293 persons have been convicted of drunkenness during the year against 492 last year. The population at the 1891 census was 24,886.

div.head: BLACK LIST.
div.p: THE BLACK LIST.

The list of publicans and beersellers proceeded against for the year ended 31st July, 1892, and results, were as follows :—James Ditchfield, Royal Hotel, fully licensed, permitting drunkenness 10th November,lB9l,dismissed ; for selling drink to drunken pessons on same date,he was fined 203. and costs 335. 6d. ; Fanny Lee, Clarendon Hotel, fully licensed, permitting drunkenness 7th Nov., 1891, fined 203. and costs 183. 6d. ; a charge against the woman of selling drink to drunken persons was with- drawn; James Woods, Bridge Inn, beerhouse open dur- ing prohibited hours 7th February, 1892, dismissed; charge of refusing to admit police on same date was dis- missed ; Charles T. Bridgeman, Bird in Hand beerhouse, supplying drink to Constable Dickinson whilst on duty on Bth April, 1892, fined 40s. and costs Bs. 6d ; a similar penalty was imposed upon Bridgeman for supplying drink to Constable Dutton.

THB BIRD IN HAND. Superintendent Atherton said he should ask the Beach to adjourn the application for the renewal of the license of the Bird in Hand fot one month.—Mr. A. Linaker said he appeared in that case to apply for the renewal of the license. His client was in bed suffering from a serious complaint. He handed to the magistrates a certificate from a medical man to that effect.—Supt. Atherton said he objected to the renewal of the license for one month only.—Mr. Linaker said his c'ient had been served with a notice of objection which had been withdrawn, and under these circumstances he thew,ht the renewal ought to be granted.—Mr. E. Wynne Hump- hreys said at the adjourned hearing lie should represent the Chief-constable, and if it were necessary he should appear for him now and ask that the Superintendent's request be granted. A second notice had been served upon the applicant.—Mr. Linaker said the first notice was served on the 11th August, and the Superintendent would oppose the renewal of the license on the ground that the license was not necessary for the requirements of the district in which the house was situated. On the 18th Mr. Bridsreman received the second notice in which the Superintendent stated that it was not inten- ded to proceed on Monday neat with the notice of opposition to your license served upon you on the 12th., but you are hereby required to attend the Sessions when objection will be taken to the renewal of your license on the ground of the convictions obtained against you on the 25th April, and an adjournment if necessary will be ap- plied for to the adjourned licensing sessions.—Mr. Lina- ker contended that that notice would not be good.—Mr. Humphreys agreed that the first notice was bad be•muse it was one which could not be sustained having reg rd to the Beerhouse Act, 1869 ; but another notice had been served and he urged that the Bench should follow the invariable practice of the Court and adjourn considera- 1 tion of the renewal of these licenses against which a conviction had been recorded.—After consulting with his colleagues the Chairman announced that the whole of the licenses would be renewed with the exception of those against which there had beea convictions, the Bird in Hand and the Royal Hotel.
TB E ALBION INN, NELSON-STREET,

Mr. Hislop, of Manchgster, on behalf of the Assignees of John Massey, applied for the transfer of the licence of the Albion Inn, Nelson-street, to George Johnson. He said the application was made under unusual circum- stances. It appeareA that the holder of the licence, along with several other people, was brought before the Court in connection with stealing and receiving certain goods. The offence was considered a very serious one, because the magistrates fined the parties £1 and costs. In consequence of this, according to the Licensing Act,a, person who was guilty of such a matter was renderedi incapable of conducting the business of a pliblicaa,, Provision, however, was made by the .isame Act. Sy which an owner of the premises could come before the Court and obtain power to sell. That was made and granted. The applicant was of good character, auk he had two witnesses who had known him for 20 years who would speak to that. Be was a fit and proper person to hold the licence.—Superintendent Athertma said ba. had been in possession of Mr. Johnson's character for some time, and it was good .—Granted.
