MR. S. WOODS, M. P. , AND THE PAY

MENT OF MEMBERS. Mr. Samuel Woods, M.P., speaking at a meeting of miners held in the Ince Division, on Saturday evening, said working-men of all political faiths had assisted in his return to the House of Commons. and so long as he was a member of that body he would know no section of working-men. He had tried to labour for the work- ing-classes as a body, and he unhesitatingly said that the future of his career should be in keeping with his past life. An endeavour had been made to divide the miners of the Ince Division, but he trusted they would be strong against the sophistry and cunning arguments which had been advanced by their opponents. Speak- ing on the question of the payment of members, he stated that the labour members and the advanced sec- tion of the House of Commons were determined there should be no dissolution of Parliament until the pay- ment of their representatives became an accomplished fact. The measure of one man one vote would also be passed within a short time, and when the two reforms were carried the working-men of this country would have attained the means which would ultimately lead them to a noble and final Ntictory. MR. LABOIJCHERE'S EXCLUSION, FROlf OFFICE.
A PERSONAL EXPLANATION.-

Mr. Labouchere says in " Truth" :—.When Mr. Gladstone was making his Cabinet I was away from London. On my return on August .15 an emissary from Canton-gardens came to me. After a lengthy exordium', in which he dwelt upon our mutual admiration frir Mr. Gladstone and upon the difficulties under which. he was labouring, and after explaining how in a monarchical country it is always well to consider the wislass-of the monarch, he told me that I was one of Mr..Gladetone's difficulties. I was asked to get him out of this diffi- culty by writing to him a letter in which, I was to say that I did not wish to juin his Government, as Lthought that I should be more useful below the gangway. and I was informed_ presumably as a Quid pro• qua.,-that Mr. Gladstone would always be glad to consult with me on public matters:, .This letter I declined to write,, and, to my thinking, my refusal was a proper one.. I certainly understood that the Queen had. in some way, direct or indirect, led Mr. Gladstone to arrive at the fact that my being one of his administration would not be pleasing to her. I think that most people would have agreed with toy conclusion. Such a letter would have been a Radical surrender. Was anyone else asked to write such a letter during the formation of the present Ministry? .1 may. boa political leper, but I hardly could be asked to admit it. Assuming, that. the Qpeen had conveyed to Mr. Gladstone any such exptessioa of dis- favour, it is to be regretted, for, although I may not see eye to eye with her Majesty, I have always regarded her as strictly constitutional, and as I understand the Con- stitution, the Queen selects as her Prime Minister that man who is the head of the party that has.theconfi- derma of the House of Commons, and .leaves !Urn a free hand to choose his colleagues. The real fact is,.l never waste my time in the barren amusement ofr deciding what I shall do in hypothetical .cases that may never occur. If I had . been asked to join a Ministry I should have first asked who composed it., Had I.been satisfied on this head it by.no means follows that:Lsbould have I joined it. On the one hand it had been put to me by Radicals that a Radical had no right to refusein the interests of good government. On ; the :Nattier hand, strange as it may appear to some..l like my independ- ence, and I have no great liking . for the trammels of office, even if they involve the • right to airear a uniform and to be addressed as right hon. Tastes differ. So that the good ship " Democracy".sails prosperously into Joppa I care not whether my,- berth is in the officers' quarters or in the forecastle. Whether Jones or Jonah, it is all the same `to me, and ill thought my being thrown overboard would render the success of the voyage more certain, overboard I would go with pleasure, all the more as I can swim. Royal smiles and Royal favours may affect some. Henry VIII. cut offthe has of those who did not find favour with him, „Oharles 11. cut off their ears. I thank heaven that, eome what may, my head and my ears are safe .under-Aneen. Victoria. Anxious as I am to secure the .approbation of her Majesty, for whose many excellent qualities and habi- tual regard for the constitution I have-the sincerest res- pect, I am afraid that my conscienceforbids me to do this at the cost of my being false to the-stalwart Radicals of Northampton, and to those who dwell outside that Mecca of democracy and honour me with their approval. Radical approbation weighs more with me than all the emperors and empresses, kings and queens, lords and "lickspittles "in the universe. If !ties matter had been a purely personal one, the slightestlint that a lady did not wish me to enjoy the privilege of kissing her hand would have been sufficient.

To sum up, so far as Mr. Labouchere'a personal state- ment is concerned, this quotation may be given : During the last ten years I have taken a somewhat leading part in opposing Royal grants in Parliament, and I have not infrequently protested in the Press against vrhat I have, in my humble, judgment,, considered in- jurious to the public interests.in regard f to members of her Majesty's family, Fatally (but possibly erroneously). it would be thought that memhers of Parliament or pressmen must henceforward pursue this-course at their peril.

div.head: LETTER rROM MR.-GLADSTONE.
div.p: LETTER rROM MR.-GLADSTONE.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATUBDAY, AUGUST 27, 1892

Labour in strikes in the United States, Troubles. n the iron trade, and on the rail- way, resulting as they have in blood- shed and loss of life, are indicative of a troublous state of things in the labour world, and point to the crisis which has long been predicted. It is difficult, on this side of tho Atlantic, to get at the facts on both sides ; but, broadly speaking, the situation may be summed up in the statement that the workers are determined to have a larger share than they have hitherto had of the fruits of industry. They perceive that the number of millionaires is steadily increasing, while, as they contend, there is no corresponding increase in the wages of the workers. Indeed, in the large cities of America the struggle for a bare existence has become as hard as it is in the crowded centres of England. Matters are being made worse in America as a consequence of the numerous rings and syndicates which have been formed during the past ten years. It is stated, on what appears to be good authority,that, at the present moment, two-thirds of the capi tat employed in the manu- factories of the United states is under the control of these syndicates. Further, it is alleged that, as a result of these combinations, prices of goods have gone up from ten to fifty per cent., while wages have either remained stationary or have had a tendency to fall. The McKinley Tariff, 'protecting" these syndicates, as it was intended to and as it did, has intensified the bitterness of feeling amongst the workers ; hence,the beginning of a labour war, the end of which no man can fore- see. In the haste to get rich in America, longer hours of work than in this coun- try have been the rule ; and the toilers are now disposed to seek relief in restrictive legislation. An Eight Hours Bill has actually passed the United States Congress ; and it applies to all workers employed directly or indirectly by the State, through contract or sub-contract. The penalty upon employers who deliberately break the law is a heavy one, being no less than a fine of £2OO, along with imprisonment for six months. If this measure be enforced, it will have no small effect in stimulating the eight hours agitation not only in America, but in Europe. At home, in the cotton trade, the demand for an eight-hours day has suddenly become a burn- ing question. This is the more surprising as it is well-known that the operatives' representatives opposed the eight-hours proposal, when it was brought before the Trades Union Congress, as calculated to injure if not destroy the textile in- dustries of this country. It would now seem that the leaders spoke without sufficient authority; for in Blackburn, as in other Lancashire towns, the vote which has been recently taken has resulted in a majority of more than two to one in favour of reducing the hours of labour from 54 to 48 per week. It is because of a proposal on the part of employers to reduce wages that the question has so suddenly come to the front. The workpeople admit that trade is bad; but they contend— and they back their contention with official figures—that the depression is duo to over-pro- duction. " Let us," they say, " reduce production by reducing the hours of labour; and trade will revive." They object to have the rate of payment reduced ;but they show their willingness to take a share of the burden by accepting less wages as the inevitable outcome of fewer hours of work. The employers' objection to this proposal is that a reduced output, with interest on capital and , standing expenses remaining the same, is not to

be thought ,of, as it would immediately increase the current loss. They plead, too, that it is hope- less to attempt to compete with foreign manufac- turers who work longer hours, if the hours of labour in this country are still further shortened. It looks as if matters would ,soon come to a dead-lock, and result in a great strike such as that of 1878, which was so disas- trous alike to employers and employed. Is there no way out of the difficulty? There was a time when, under similar circumstances, the workpeople suggested that they would be willing to submit to a ten per cent, reduction in wages, along with " short-time " hours, on the understanding that full vages should be given the moment "full-time" hours were resumed. Why should that plan not be adopted now? It' is fair all round. Granted that it would be a loss to employers, it is still to be observed that the loss is in part met by less wages being paid. As for the workpeople, they would be making a double sacrifice they would, while the depression lasted, have less work, and less pay for the work to the extent of ten per cent. It would be meeting the employers more than half way ; it would have the effect of reducing stocks; and, with an increased demand, there would be im- proved trade, resulting, in due course, in full time and full wages.

Lord Cross THE late Lord IDDESLEIGH once ac wrote a paper on " Nothing " which Bacup. was in every respect admirable. Lord CROSS has a way of making political speeches which suggest that he has" nothing " for his text; but it cannot be said that the result is admirable, either as to style or matter. Ile was one of four, on Saturday afternoon,in laying foundation stones for a Conservative Club at Bacup ; and delivered himself of what he doubtless thought was an im- portant speech. There was a time when the Duke of DEVONSHIRE—then Lord FIARTINGTON —took pleasure, in a mild way, in poking fun at Vicount CROSS; but the Vicount had his revenge on Saturday in patronising the Duke as a person that the electors of Rossendale had not been ashamed to send to Parliament. It is true those electors had rejected that other great Liberal Unionist Sir Thomas BROOKS ; but what of that ? If Sir Thomas could not get • into one House he could be pitchforked into the other; and they could thank God that they still had a House of Lords. Referring to the fact that the Govern- ment of Which he was a member had—like Sir THOMAS Baooas—been rejected by the,, people, Lord Cnoss said the new Government "would find the Irish members the hardest of task-masters, who would have their pound of flesh or know the reason why ?" Perhaps he speaks feelingly. There was a time when the Tories went down on their knees to secure the Irish vote; and having secured it, and got into office by it, payment for "value received " was given the Irish in the shape .of "a bill" to make Coercion perpetual. The Irish members would not stand that ; they were betray- ed ; and they 'have punished their betrayers by turning them out of office. Even Lord Caoss admits that they have thus far succeeded. He says :—" If any party had won at the election it was the Irish party. The Irish members were not only to have their own Home Rule, but they were at the present moment the governors of the United Kingdom." This is a piece of refreshing if not blundering candour. We commend to Ulstermen, and to the Tories generally, this frank admission that the Irish are to have Home Rule. It would save a deal of trouble and a deal of time if other ex-Ministers would accept the inevitable in the easy-fashion of Eord CROSS. And yet he thinks the Home Rule Bill will be a terrible thing ; for, he said, "his impression was that one half of the Gladstonians would say that if they had known that was what they were voting for nothing would have induced them to do it." Holy charmingly simple this old-fashioned mode of trying to frighten people! It ought to have succeeded at the General Election; but somehow it didn't. But if it is to be a case of giving impressions, we will venture to say that our impression is that the bill will not be brought in, as was the Irish Local Government Bill of the late Government, with ill- disguised contempt for it on the part of its authors, and with a desire that it shall never be- come law. Mr. GLADSTONE will have no nonsense of that kind ; he is in earnest.; he means to carry Home Rule because he believes it will be for the benefit of Ireland; and the Irish members will assist him because they can trust him. He is not an echo, like Lord Cnoss ; he is a living voice—a living power moving in the direction of the rightemmsness which exalts the nation.

EXCEPT in Warrington, Brewster Brewster Sessions. Sessions have come and gone, and little or no change has been made in the matter of licensing. The almost universal polic of Licensing Justices throughout the coun- try is to grant no new licenses, because in the first place, there are already too many licensed houses in the country; and, secondly, because it is unwise to take action in view of the fact that the Legis- ture is likely to make important changes during the next few years. In the Prescot Petty Ses- sional Division, on Wednesday, the Bench, in refusing an application for a new license, said "Those people who required a public-house could go and live where there were public-houses ; and certainly people should be able to go and get a house without the annoyance of having a public- house at their doors." That is a sound view to take of the matter ; but, unhappily, it is not the view taken by the Licensing Justices of Warring- ton. They have made a new departure by grant- ing Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company's applications for two new public-houses without tailing into account the wishes of the inhabitants. It is true that these big brewers have presumed to make what may be called a bargain with the Bench by offering to surrender six other licenses of little or no value to them. But the bargain is bad on the face of it; for, now that the highest courts have determined that there is no such thing as a vested interest in a license, the magistrates are under no obligation whatever to consult Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company, or any other firm of brewers, in re- ducing licenses in congested districts. What the town really needs is not a reduction of six with an addition of two licenses; but a reduction of at least sixty with no additions at all. The magis- trates have taken upon themselves a grave respon- sibility in thrusting new drink shops upon new dis- tricts; ani,by callously disregarding public opinion they have once more demonstrated the necessity of all power as to licensing being taken out of the hands of " the great unpaid." It would be interest- ing to know if there is a single one of the jus- tices who voted for these two additional public- houses who would like to have one of them at his own door; and, if not, it would be still:more inter- esting to hear him explain why that which would be:objectionable to a magistrate should not be ob- jectionable to a working-man. Again, where is the

justice of giving Messrs. Greenell, Whitley and Company a new field of operations to the exclusion of license-holders already in the field?, we. have before observed, if a fully licensed house wile required in the Battersby-lane district, Councillor Bovrore has the first claim, .seeing that he bag beer-house there, and has repeatedlymade applige" tion for a full license. Unto them that have much a monoply is being given, altogether unjustly, I over Mr. BOLTON'S head; and he has right to complain of unfair treatment. Attu so with regard to the Bewsey 'district. The fan license, if granted at all, should have been granted to" The Grove," which already possesses an, off• license, and has again and again applied for a full license. Mr. Wagstaffe, the owner of theY premises, paid over £3,000 for them; it is sixteen years since he first applied for a full licen• se; and, further, he has offered to spend to meet, if need be, the wishes of the magistrates. We repeat that it is nothing to the porP°s€' that Messrs. , Greenall, Whitley and CoroPellY have offered to surrender other licenses. TheY were not theirs to surrender; it was within the power of the magistrates to refuse not only these but many other licenses in these congestedA_ tricts, and it is a power which they he" ought to exercised. They have utterly failed in their &II in this matter ; and it is to be hoped that the fus, bench will refuse to confirm an arrangement whie' is bad in itself, and will constitute a raisobievo4B precedent.

The Ditton Wesleyan Chapel has been rat ovated at a cost of nearly £3OO, and was re-opened on Sunday by the Rev. D. Jones, ex-secretasy of the Liverpool Baptist Association. The collections amounted to nearly £9. On Monday evening a tea and public meeting were held, and addresses given by the Rev. D. Jones and W. Prit- chard, and Mr. G. Davies. The chair was taken by Mr. A. Clarke, of Haugh Green, who presided in the absence of Mr. Benjamin Brown. The work of renova- tion and decoration has been done by Messrs. T. Sadler and Sons, Widnes, and reflects great credit upon them. If you wait a lucky wedding ring go 1051, Illcw-or.,where you will gets present with it.—Advt. PICNIC FROM RuNcortsr LIBERAL CLUB. About 170 members of Runcorn Liberal Club formed a picnic party to Hawarden on Wednes- day. The party travelled by the 1.33 p.m. train at a cheap fare, and on arriving at their destination visited the various places of interest in the village and subse- quently went to the Horticultural Show and Fete in the grounds of Hawarden Castle. There were also present a large number of excursionists from other parts of the Northwich Division and Mr. J. T. Brunner,M.P.,also put in an appearance during the afternoon, and conversed with many of his supporters. About half past six Mr. Gladstone and his son, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, came upon the lawn of the Castle, and they were greeted with a tremendous cheer by the thousands present. The G. 0. M. did not make a speech. DROWNING CASE AT ST. BEMIS, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held au inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday forenoon, on the body of an unknown man, who was found drowned in Sankey Canal, near Latharn's timber yard, Parr-st., on Friday afternoon.—P.C. Peters gave evidence that the body was removed to the mortuary, where many people had ex- amined it, but no one could identify the man. There were no marks of violence upon the body, which was that of a well-built man, 30 or N years of age. It was sft. 91n. in length, with lull features, dark brown hair, and a long brown moustache. It was dressed in black worsted coat and vest, grey striped tweed trousers, blue check cotton-shirt, red flannel singlet, grey stock- ings, and an almost new pair of elastic-side boots.— Inspector Goodall said the body, which had been photo- graphed, seemed to be that of a respectable working man. There were no letters or papers in the pockets, but he had in his possession a small sum of money and a penknife.—The jury returned an open verdict of "Found drowned." The body was on Monday evening identified as that of Michael Byrne, a labourer, thirty- three years of age, who lived at 72, Byron-st., Garston, and who left home on Saturday, the 13th inst., to go to St. Helens in search of work. Mrs. Byrne and her mo- ther saw the photograph and clothing and pocket knife and recognised them. They said deceased had no trouble beyond being out .if work, and was not likely to commit suicide. Josrpn PRITCHARD is prepared to wind and keep in repair, private clocks from 10s. per aanum.—Advt. GOSPEL UNION MISSION, RUNCORN. On Friday evening under the auspices of the above Union Mr". Nicola Eyoub Tams, the converted Arab, concluded his series of services by giving a lecture in the Ship Canal Mission-room, Irwell-lane, Runcorn. The chair was occupied by Mr. Daniel Bisbrown. In intro-. during the lecturerthe Chairman said that he was in full sympathy with the work, as their object was to extend the Redeemer's kingdom among them. He Was glad to be associated with them. He proceeded to state that Mr. Tams had proved himself to be a true soldier of the master and had gained for himself the esteem of all parties. He had conducted the mission • with conspicu- ous ability, and the speaker teusted that the cause would receive a fresh impetus as the result.—The lecturer then proceeded in an interesting manner to describe Fel- )aheen marriages, or marriages in Caucian Be referred Ito the selection of the bride, to the negotiation, the Parents' consent, the inquiries made, the private official and clerical requests, the dqwry settlement, presents, marriage preparation, joyous times, shaving the bride- groom, musical assembly, great torches, grand proces- sion, processional customs, the bride's duty, her first outing, &c. The remarks of Mr. Tams were listened to with deep attention. A feature that added interest to the evening's proceedings was the lecturer being dressed in the costume of the people, with whom he dwelt, as well as two ladies and gentlemen who illustrated the marriage ceremony. At the close, on the motion of Mr. Moorfield, a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, the Chair- man, and to the Hon. and Rev. Mr. Grimston for the use of the room.

JOSEPH PRITCTIARD, Watchmaker 'tad Jeweller, 51, High- at.. aiti 4, Bridge at.. Ittincera.-4dv4. ASSAULT ON TUE POLICE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, John McCabe, of Widnes, was charged with assaulting P.C. Johnston on the preceding night. Patrick McCabe, was similarly charged, and Mary Ann Walsh, of Widnes, was charged with aiding and abetting the aforesaid. John was also I charged with assaulting P.S. Carter.—P.C, Johnston said that at 10-30 on the date named, he was at Simms Cross when he found the male prisoners fighting. Patrick fell to the ground, while John struck witness a blow on the nose. Patrick by that time had jumped up, and kicked him in the back. He then took hold of the prisoner Patrick, and endeavoured to drag him to the station. The female prisoner then came up, and struck witness with a brick or other hard substance on the back of the head. The blow broke his helmet at the back. He had only been in the town a week. The men were under the influence of drink. He was black and blue all over, and was not fit for duty.—P.S. Carter proved arresting the prisoners. John McCabe struck him a blow on the side of the head, The men were drunk.— P.C. Eians and other officers corroborated, and proved that the prisoners had not been ill-used by the police, the prisoners having stated that violence had been used. —Mrs. Walsh called a number of witnesses to prove that she knew nothing of the row, nor that she was present. The case against her was dismissed. Patrick bad been convicted 21 times for various charges and John 16 times.—The Chairman : The assault is a very brutal one. The police have a difficult duty to perform, and such roughs as you loafing about prevent the proper discharge of that duty. John will be sent to prison for three months with hard labour, and Patrick for two months with hard labour. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —.T. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Adv. SOUTHPORT CENTENARY. The Southport Centenary Exhibition continues to be a great draw. Grand concerts and displays of fireworks are among the advertised attractions. Amoug the artistes at the concerts for next week are Miss Vadini (late of Carl Rosa's) and liidlle. Vacua. The Probyn Orchestra is also announced to take part. ALLEGED BIGAMY AT FRODsIiAM. At Frodsham on Wednesday morning, Caroline Hoperoft was charged with committing bigamy. In December 1873, prisoner was married at Llanwen- arthaltra, Monmouthshire, by the Rev. George Grove, to Edwin Hoperoft. In 1890 she went through the form of marriage at Prodsham Parish Church, under the name of Alice Evans, with John Hughes, her first husband being, it was stated, then alive. Prisoner was committed to Chester Assizes. Lawn Mowers—GARLAND, horticultural ironmonger, War- rington. THE SHIP CANAL OUTRAGE.

. - On Wednesday morning, at Frodsham Police Court, a navvy named Charles Bund, of Chesterfield, was charged with the attempted murder of Emily Duke, a widow who kept a lodging-house at the Ship Canal works, Frodsham Marsh. The prisoner had battered in the woman's head with a poker on the 15th inst. through jealousy. Her condition has improved, but she is still in a critical state and not out of danger. The prisoner was again remanded fora week. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-3. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington .—Adv. THE GLASS BOTTLE MAKERS UNDER NOTICE. Messrs. Cannington, Shaw, and Co., the largest glass bottle manufacturers in St. Helens, have just served notices, which will terminate this week, on upwards of seventy of their workmen. They attri- bute this to the overstocked condition of the market consequent on bad trade and foreign com- petition. It is understood that Messrs. NEWTON FLOWER SHOW. As will be seen from vur advertisement columns, the annual show of the Newton Floral and Horti- cultural Society will be held on Saturday, and should the weather be favourable, will doubtless be largely patronised. During the week the judges have inspected the cottagers gardens in the Society's district, and have made their awards as follows ;-Ist T. Howard, Asliton-road Newton ; 2nd W. Boardgian, The Vulcan; 3rd A. Catterall, Low- ton Junction. There were ten entries against two last year. THE CATASTROPHE AT A WID4ES CHET...MAL WORKS. . .

Yesterday afternoon was the time fixed for the adjourned inquest on the bodies of Henry Stone, Dominic Kelly, and John Routledge, three men who were killed a fortnight ago by the collapse of a vitriol chamber at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., Waterloo-road, Widnes. As the five men who were also injured were unable to attend, Mr. Brighouse the County Coroner telegraped adjourning the inquest until Friday night. The men are pre- greasing satisfactorily at the Accident Hospital.

STRIKE OF THE WEAVED. WATERHEN. Toe subjoined memorandum from the Salt Union, on the subject of the dispute between the watermen and the Salt Union, has been issued :—Further pro- gress is being made by the Salt Union in the or- ganisation of its river traffic. Craft manned by men newly engaged have been sent to and come from the salt works. The directors have not manned the craft so quickly as they might do, so that the places might not be closed against some of their older and more experienced hands. Some of the watermen who had refused to move from one craft to the other in order to make up crews appeared at the Middle- wich Police Court, on Wednesday, and it was de- cided by the magistrates that a case should be stated for the superior courts. The dispute is caus- ing much excitemtnt and some ill-feeling in the neighbourhood of Northwich. On Thursday night, as a steamer worked by non-union hands and with a barge in tow was proceeding in the direction of Winsford, a crowd ot people hooted the crew and threw stones at them. At Northwich on Thursday night, a meeting of the Saltl"Union hareholders' Association was held and arbitration was proposed. A suggestion that Mr. Burt, M.P., and Mr. Brunner, M.P., should nominate the arbitrator was favour- ably received by both sides. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J. and W. Dn'TTOB, Sankey-et. Warrington.-4 dv.

A. MAD DOG AT EARLESTOWN. A case of rabies doubtless brought on by the heat developed itself in a dog at Earlestown, on Sunday morning. Mr. M. McCoy was walking along the Mesnes footpath in the direction of Newton, accom- panied by his dog, a black and tan terrier, when it suddenly turned upon him and attempted to bite him. He struck it with a stick, but it returned to the attack, and he then lifted it some distance with his foot. The dog then began to bleed and froth at the mouth,and turning round set off at full speed in the direction of home, Mr. McCoy following in hot puisuit. On the way it snapped at everything in Its path, and with the short yelp peculiar to dogs suffering from rabies, it raced on. In Wargrave- road, it attempted to bite the iron palisading of some houses, and being foiled in an effort to get through the window of a house it made several circuits. It darted • across thq road towards the grocery shop of Mr. Taberner, and finding the cellar window open. it made its way into the cellur. Mr. McCoy immediately warned Mr. Taberner of the danger, and the latter secured the cellar door to prevent the dog getting into the house. During its confinement in the cellar, the'dog bit at everything within reach,but ultimately McCoy,who had rushed home, returned with a Martini-Henry rifle, and two rounds of ball cartridge. At an opportune moment Mr. Taberner fired•on the dog andkilled it instantly the bullet passing clean through the body. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-1. and W. DUTTON. Sankey-it.. Warrington.—Adv.

THE DAVIES MEMORIAL FUND AT RUNCORN. With the object of adding to the fund which is being raised for the widow and children of the late . Mr. T. H. Davies, the popular three-quarter back of the Runcorn team, a sacred concert was given in Runcorn Public Hall,on sunday evening. There was a very large attendance. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presi- dent of the club, occupied the chair, and in opening the proceedings said the occasion was .a solemn one they were assembled to do something for the widow and children of one whose death they deeply lamented. He understood that some people objected to their having a sacred concert on the Sunday evening. So far as he was concerned, if he had the slightest idea that it was wrong they would not have found him supporting it. They had the highest authority for assisting the widow and or- phans, and he was firmly convinced that G ,c 1 intended that they should help them to the best of their ability. Be was not there to discuss the question of Sunday con- certs, but if it were necessary to do so he could find an ample defence of their laudable proceedings. In London, at St. James's Hall, he found the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes and a splendid orchestra doing their utmost to elevate and improve the condition of the masses of the people, and as a result many sinners were being brought to repentance. The Salvation Army were also doing the same thing. In Llandudno and other places there were sacred concerts attended by thousands of people of all conditions, and the programmes submitted proved not simply enjoyable but truly elevat- ing. In conclusion Mr. Speakman asked the audience not to interfere with the solemnity of the proceedings by applauding.—The Mill Brow Brass Band played several selections of music most admirably and Mr. R. W. Pierpoint gave the cornet solo " Star of Bethlehem " with his accustomed style and finish. Miss Heathering- ton contributed the songs" Calvary "add "Angels ever bright and fair " in a manner that appealed to the sympathies of the audience. Mr. H. Morris rendered the song "King David's Lament and but for the rule against applause would have received a recall for his fine vocalisation. A pleasing feature in the programme was the recitation of Carleton's " Out of the Old House Nancy." which was given by Mr. Cyril Chantler, who displayed elocutionary abilities of great merit. The duties of accompanist were efficiently fulfilled by Mr. C. C. Le.Coateur, and Mr. T. Outhvraite conducted the Band with credit. There was a balance of £ll us. 9d. left from the proceeds of the concert after the expenses had been paid and this sum has been paid into bank to the credit of the fund.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, J. Brundrett, J. M. Williams, T. Lewis, J. Whitlow 11. E. Heywood, J. Whitlow, J. Ashton (clerk) G. Ashton (deputy clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector). FRODSHAM PROTESTS AGAINST TELEGRAPH POLES. At a meeting of the Frodsham Parochial Committee on Saturday, the 20th inst., Mr. Linnell the road sur- veyor and the Post Office engineer attended. Tke latter pointed out the route and position of the telegraph poles proposed to be erected between the Prodsh,m Post Office and the Frodsham Bridge Post Office and were carefully examined and considered by the Committee who unanimously resolved that a strong protest be made against the erection of poles in the Main-street, and being of opinion that the necessity therefore might be obviated either by taking the wires along the line of railway or by laying them under the greund. The Committee further resolved that a copy of the resolu- tion be forwarded to the Clerk a the County Council and to Mr. Baxter, the representative of the Frodsham electoral -division of the County Council, and that the County Council be requested to urge by all the means in their power the adoption of the Committee's views. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. J. M. Williams.

THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. Mr. E. Marshall, secretary to Runcorn Board of Im- provement Commissioners,wrote under date August 20th as follows: " Vehicular Bridge across the Mersey. I am directed by my Mersey Bridge Committee to advert to a copy of the memorial which has been presented to the Cheshire County Council with regard. to the above named matter, and which was sent to you on the 18th January last. My Committee will be having another conference with the Committee of the Widnes Local Board towards the ehd of September. I am directed to ask if you will be good enougii to instruct your clerk to attend such conference with a view to supporting the object referred to."—Mr. Aaron said it would be of the greatest benefit to this part of the country if such a bridge were constructed.—The Chairman thought the matter more in the province of the Highway Board than that Authority.—Mr. Aaron said the object was to memoria- lise the County Council and help the Runcorn Commis- sioners all in their power. At the present time the L. & N.-W.R. Co. had a monopoly of carriage in the district, and on the Cheshire Lines Railway at Widnes, hay and straw and other goods were carried at half the rate they had to pay in Runcorn. If in constructing the bridge they would follow the lines of the low level bridge at Newcastle, it would not cost more than one halt the amount now estimated.—Mr. Aaron moved that the clerk attend the conference.—Mr. Lewis agreed that the bridge would be of the greatest benefit, and seconded the motion which was carried.—Mr. Aaron gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board tie would move the re-appointment of Ir. Farrington as inspector of nuisances at an increase of salary of £2O a year.

div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.

I hear that it is not improbable thet new rub- ber works may shortly be started in Warrington. A number of London gentlemen who have bought the plant of the Fylde Rubber Works have been making inquries in Warrington as to the suitabil- ity of the town as the scene of their future opera- tions.

The Warrington bench seem to have got into a rather undignified position on Thursday. It is hardly becoming of licensing magistrate& to begin bargaining with big brewers, yet that is, practi- cally, what took place. Magistrates in. dealing with licenses now-a-days do not need to bargain. They are supreme, and can give or withhold licenses at their discretion. Their action, I take it, should be governed entirely by a desire to provide fcr the puLlic interest or convenience,, and to deal out even-hapded justice to the various applicants that appear before them.

The Warrington magistrates did not rise to that standard either in dealing with the public or the applicants.. In fact the public Seemed to be very little thought aboutosnd as for the applicants there was only one in it. In dealing with the applica- tions for new licenses for Battersby-lane and Bewsey districts, one might have fancied that the magistrates would have shown just a little anxiety to know what " Battersby-laners" and '`Bewsey- ites" thought about the matter. But that would have been a mistake. The licensing committee, or a majority of them, appeared to be only anxious to know what Messrs. Greenall and. Co. had to offer in order that they might freely, give. As a 'matter of fact, Messrs. Greenall and Co. had:nothing to offer, while the magistrates had everything to give. The licenses which it is proposed should be given up could be cancelled by the magistrates at their dis- cretion. But what can you expect when the bench condescends to bargain with the brewer P

Then how marked the contrast in the treatment of the different applicants ! You might have thought that if the magistrates had come to the conclusion ' that a full license was needed at Bewsey and another in Battersby-lane, it would have been granted to houses with off-licenses which were al2 ready established, and which had been conducted without complaint. But again, you would have been mistaken. When magistrates begin to barter, there can be no pretence of equal-handed treat- ment. If justice were to be sold, there would never a rich man be convicted; and, so, if valuable new licenses are to be Riven away to those who can offe: in exchange comparatively worthless old ones,there is chance for small men, like Councillor Bol- ton and Mr. A agstaffe.

I was much tickled and amused, whe.n forming ore of the crowd at the big fire, on Monday after- noon, to hear the confident and alarmed anticipa- tion expressed on all hands that the huge chimney stack which stands close to where the fire happened, was on the decline; and would presently fall. Quite a consternation was caused amongst the inhabit- ants round about, by this threatened catastrophe ; there were not very many people whose houses lay beneath the supposed tottering structure, who went to bed with • perfect composure on Monday night. There were individuals among the crowd who had persuaded themselves that the chimney was more and more departing from its perpendi- miler position, and speculating as to the time that would be necessary, at the rate at which the stack was declining, to bring it down with a crash. As a matter of fact the stack had never stirr.Ad, and considering its construction and its fireproof mater- ials, titere was no immediate danger of its fall- ing. But the force of imagination is great—its heat was as fervid as that of the fire—and once excited in individuals it is contagious. so that the fear of the chimney's collapse became almost uni- versal among the spectators.

Their excited conjuring up of this purely imagin- ary peril, even to the extent of fancying they saw the stack falling, reminded me of a famous exam- ple of the strong and catching power of imagina- tion in a crowd. A celebrated wit in the early part of this century played an extraordinary practical joke on the. public in London for the express pur- pose of illustrating to what a fevered pitch the imaginative faculty when once thoroughly aroused I can be worked up. lie stood looking intently at the lions at the foot of the • Nelson monument in 11 Trafalgar Square, and exclaimed, as if Co himself, 1" The tail does wag. lam sure it wags." Others beard his remark, and stared at the lions in turn. until first one Dystander and then another exclaimed " By heavens it does wag, I see it clearly," and so forth, and presently there was collected on the spot one of the largest crowds ever assembled in the metropolis, absorbed in the phenomenon of an inanimate lion wagging its caudal apppendage, the practical joker having meanwhile quietly slipped away, and being in delightful enjoyment, from a distance, of this rare exemplification of the gulli- bility of mankind.

Schoolmasters have a particular reason for wish- ing that fires may not be too frequent in Warring- ton. It is their arduous duty to teach tile youthful mind to shoot, and, what is more, their work is judged by that blessed measuring wand known as "results." Now, in order to get good results, a regular and punctual attendance of the scholars is highly desirable, in fact absolutely necessary. But a big blaze is a deadly attraction to the juvenile mind. It was so on Monday. The number of youngsters that were "on the scene" was legion, and they did not seem to be deeply impressed with the serious character of the conflagration. I am told that in one school only five lads out of two bow:red put in an appearance at the usual time on Monday afternoon. The staff, all told, in that de- part went was five scholars and eight teachers.

A curious awl rather unpleasant incident occurred at the lAgh-st. baths on Tuesday afternoon. From twenty to thirty individuals were disporting them- selves in the swimming bath, when one of them, who had come out of the water, and dressed, in- formed the keeper of the baths that his purse, con- taining about 155., had been stolen from his trousers pocket. It appeared that while he had been in the building no one had come out of it, and therefore the presumption was that someone still on the ptemises must be the thief. The police were com- municated with, and Inspector Spinks and a con- stable were presently on the spot. The swimmers, ' none of whom had left the place, were informed of what had occurred, and the proposal was made that they should all come out and dress and then sub- mit to be searched.

This suggettion was indignantly resented, and consequently the police proceeded to institute a rigid search themselves of all the clothes they could lay hands on, and of the building, but no purse could be discovered. At length when the excitement and indignation of those present had become very pronbunced, the individual who had caused all the commotion discovered that, he hav- ing a hole in his pocket between the lining and the cloth, the purse had slipped down into his trousers. He found the purse and he found also that his un- popularity had reached its climax, for he was ac- corded by way of a parting salute three hoots, alike loud, deep, and unanimous, from the exasperated company of swimmers. had the police not been present, he might possibly have left the building with larger holes in his clothing than thaz in his trousers pocket.

As an admirer of Ow poetry of Shelley, I have been pleased to see the interest excited by the centenary of his birth. Mr. Butler gave several interesting quotations last week by way of illus- trating the poet's views ; and I should like to add another or two. Speaking of death he says : Death is the veil which these who live call life ;
il-iTy—si-se-p---and it is lifted. To me this is as striking and as profound as Shakespere's lines :
We are such stuff As dreams are made on ; aud mur little life Is rounded with a sleep. Shelley has, too, said some charming things abou.t love, the following amongst others :

I know That love makes all things equal ; I have heard By mine own heart this joyous truth averred,— The spirit of the worm beneath the sod In love and worship blends itself with God. If this does not indicate a religious spirit, I am at a loss to know where it is to be found.

Seeing how quickly smallpox is spreading, the Sanitary Committee of Warrington has a serious task betore it in coping with and extirpating the dreaded disease. No doubt the committee will prove equal to the occasion. I notice that at the meeting of the Board of Guardians there was some disposi- tion to complain of the nearness of the proposed temporary smallpox hospital to the workhouse and other densely-inhabited places. div.head: COUNTY ASYLUM
div.p: THE COUNTY ASYLUM

Replying to a communication from the Clerk to tbe Guardians, Mr. Alexander Hornhy, Clerk of the County Asylum wrote stating that there are patients in the asylum from the City of Chester received under contract. —The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner said when the Committee appointed by the Board visited the asylum on the pre- vious Tuesday, the Asylum Committee were sitting and the question of the woman who had been returned to the Workhouse was raised, and the Chairman stated that she was sent away from the asylum comparatively cured and that the Guardians ought to have a proper ward to receive such cases with some person properly qualified to look after them or send them to Macclesfield asylum, which would cost the Un!on 25. a week more than Chester asylum. He(Mr. Tanner) remarked" Ho v is it you receive pauper lunatics from the City of Ches- ter ?' and the Chairman replied that they had had a contract with Chester for many years but it expired next November. At the time of the visit there were 550 patients in the asylum and there wasinot a single place unoccupied. During the discussion that followed Mr. Baxter said it was not fair that Runcorn Union should be put to the expense o sending their lunatics to Parkside Asylum, Maccleqfied for the conven- ience of the City Authorities of Chester. There had been a proposal before the County Co,incil to spend £70,000 in erecting another asylum, but it was opposed and he thought the matter would end in the enlarge- ment of Upton Asylum. It was thought that Chester, which was a county of itself, ought to pay for and maintain an asylum.—Mr. Brandreth said it cost between £2 and £3 to send a patient to Upton Asylum ; it would cost double that amount to send a patient to Maccles- field Asylum.—After further discussion it was decided that the Clerk should write to the Clerk of the County Asylum at Ur ton stating that if they were to send their patients to Macclesfield the extra expense ought to he paid by the authorities of Upton Asylum.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner remarked that the Chairman said it was very likely there would be plenty of room when the con- tract with Chester expired.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' ANNIVERSARIES.—On Saturday afternoon the various friendly societies in Newehurch, Cu!cheth, held their respective anniversaries, under favodrable circumstances, the weather being all that could be desired. The first on the list was "The St. Peter's Glory," Court No. 941, of the Ancient Order of loresters, held at the New Inn,Culcheth. The members met at the court at 230 p.m., and at 3 p.m. they sat down to a substantial dinner, served by Mrs. Lowe, the number being 50. At 430 they formed a procession, and were headed by the secretary (Mr. W. Yates), other officers, and several young members, then came the splendid banner of the court, bearing the arms of the or- der, borne by six members, and afterwards the Firs-lane Brass Band, followed by the remainder of the members. Each member wore a green rosette. At the conclusion of the procession, the band played a selection of music for dancing, conducted by Mr. Joseph Knowles, the bandmaster. The court is in a prosperous condition, having funds to the amount of £507 13e. 9d., and the , number of members is 79. The Friendship Lodge of the t United Order of Free Gardeners' Friendly Society,held at the Harrow Inn, Culcheth, met at 2 p.m., and at 3 p.m. partook of dinner, catered in excellent style by Mr. and Mrs. P. Unsworth. The number of members present was 45. At 4 p.m., a procession was formed, headed by the new banner of the lodge, borne by six members, followed by a band. This society is also in a prosperous condition, having 66 members, and funds to the amount of over £5OO. Mr. James Whittaker is the secretary, and conducted the arrangements of the procession in a satisfactory manner. The Union Friendly Society, held at the Paca Horse Inn, Newchurch, met at one p.m., and at 2.30 p.m. sat down to dinner, served by Miss Lowe, the hostess. At 5 p.m. the members formed a Iprecession, headed by the Golborne Brass Band. This society had at the 31st of December last 47 members, and funds to the amount of £467 10s. 2d.

Mr. Spinks remarked at the Guardians meeting that the Medical Officer of Health for Warrington, was not in favour of placing a temporary smallpox hospital so near the Workhouse. If this be so, the Sanitary Committee will be taking upon themselves a veryserious responsibility,if they do not act upon the advice of their own Medina] Officer,,, Too much precaution cannot be taken, seeing that the malady is spreading; and a blander ill placing the hospital too near the Workhouse or private dwellings may be the means of spreading rather than of stamping out the disease.

OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX AT WARRINGTON. Smallpox has become rather Seriously prevalent in IVarrington durieg the last week. A few weeks ago, it will be remembered, that two or three. per- sons who resided in Latchford,were found to be•suf- fering from the disease, but, by means of •careful isolation, that outbreak seemed to have been stamped out. However, on the 28th iof last month, a lodger at the " model " lodging-house on Friars-green was found to be affected with smallpox, and he was re- moved to the infectious diseases hospital. Ile was a navvy, and had come to the towu from Lincoln on the 17th or 18th July, accompanied by his brother, both of the men having stayed for a short tinueat Sheffield. This patient succumbed to the disease. on the sth of this month. For a short while no further outbreak was noticed, but on the 18t1 of this month it was found that a scullery maid at the hospital was suffering from the malady though not in a severe form, and, later on, another patient —a young man—bad to be admitted from., the model lodging house. It is worth mentioning that both this patient and the navvy who died walked through some of the streets to the hospital. At, the end of last week and the beginning of this it be- came apparent that the disease was spreading .vith a rapidity that was, to say the least, alarming. A young woman, a dressmaker by trade, living in Priestley-street, contracted the disease. Another case, that of a child at the Workhouse, was also re- ported on Saturday, and following this came the cases of a glass blower living at Bowling Green- terrace, of a girl, 16 years of age, from Guardian- street, and a further ease, on Tuesday, in Hayd ock- street . Vigorous efforts have been made by the sanitary authorities to check the spread of the dreaded malady. A consultation between Alderman Burr. gess (the chairman of the sanitary cornmittee),,the Town Clerk, and the Medical Officer of Health took place on Saturday morning, and on Sunday .evening a meeting of the Sanitary Committee was held. At this meeting it was decided that the medical.officer and others concerned should take all steps that they might consider necessary to meet the emergency On Monday night the Sanitary Committee again met, and ie was decided .to erect a temporary iron hospital on the ground owned by the Corporation near to the infectious diseases hospital. The Medi- cal Officer has also issued placards reccmmending vaccination and re-vaceination, and asking that notice should at once be given to the proper author- ities as soon as symptoms of smallpox become mani- fest. From later inquiries we find that the diseasocontinues to spread. Up to yesterday fourteen patients had been removed to the infectious diseases hospital, ,but as yet there has beenesnly one death, that of the navvy men- tioned above. Of the additional caseapne has occurred in Winwick-st., one in Winwick-road, one in Howard- st., one in Percy-st., and another in Guardian-st. In order to provide the additional accommodation needed at the hospital, the Sanitary Committee, at their meet- ing on Wednesday, decided to purchase one of Morton and Company's corrugated iron buildings, lined with wood, and intended to bold 20 patients. The build- ing 1813611 g erected on land which has been acquired this week adjoining that on Which the hospital stands and near the workhouse. For this land, we understand, the Corporation will pay the sum of £750: This is the severest epidemic of smallpox from which Warrington has suffered frit many yesrs. Since the infectious diseases hospital was erected in 1877, every case of smallpox that has occurred has been an imported CaSP, that is to say, the person suffering has brought the disease with him from some oetside place, and the treatment that has been given in Warrington at the hospital has been successful In checking any further spread of the disease. The origin of the present out- break is doubtless due to the navvy who was taken from the lodging house on Friars'-green, and who succumbed to tie. attack. He had been id Warrington a fortnight, and had wa!liA about the town while the disease was upon him, leo, not in an advanced stage, and indeed,the same may be also said of tha second person. who was admitted to the hospital from the Friars'-gteen lodging house. Thla man had been employed at the Gas Works, .a rid had moved about in the usual way prior to being admitted to the hospital. The monthly report of the Medical Superintendent of the Infections Diseases Hospital, presented on Jely lath,. 1892, contsins the following reference to making provis- ion for an outbreak of smallpox "I; think I may assume that the committee has already accepted the prin- ciple that further provision should be made for the recep— tion of small pox. ' As you are already aware, whenever a case of small pox is admitted, we are placed in great danger of transmitting this disease to the other patients in hospital, and to the inhabitants of the surrounding neighbourhood, in consequence of the nearness of the wards to each other, and the proximity ofithe adminis- trative department to the ward usually used for the reception of small-pox, as well as the nearness of this ward to the adjoining street. The recently erected Bradford smallpox hospital appears to me to have been constructed in such a manner as to prevent the danger of communication of the disease to others, and its exten- sion to the surrounding neighbourhood, special provision being made for the destruction of the germs of the dis- ease. We also require increased accommodation for the storing of clothing, and articles temporarily not in use. Of necessity a certain amount of personal clothing has accumulated since the ere ction of the Hospital in 1877, and we have no room for that purpose or for the proper storing of bedding, household linen, Sm. The sleeping accommodation for the St aff is rapidly becoming inade- quate to our present requirements. The following lists of streets will give an idea of the parts of the town in which cases have occurred, and something like the order in which they were discovered The " Model" Lodging-houseeFelaes-green. The Infectious Diseases Hospital. • " Model" Lodging-house. 56, Priestley-street. „. Workhouse.. • 23, Liverpool-road. 21, Guardian-street. Haydock-street. 46, Winwick-street. • 17, Win wick-road. 23, Guardian-street. , 58, Howard-street. 6, Percy-street. ANOTHER DEATH LAST El-ENING. We ascertained from inquiries lost evening that a second death from. smallpox has taken place at the Infectious Diseases Hospital:, one of the patients from Guardian-street having succumbed to the malady. THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS ON THE SMALLPDX OUTBREAK. At the, fortnightly meeting of Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, the Workhouse Master reported that, on Friday the doctor stated in his medical book that a child named Tosh. Ahern, aged four years, was suffering from variola, i.e. smallpox. The child was placed in isolation and the case reported to the Authorities at the fever N.-spied. Dr. Gornall, the medical officer of health, visited the workhouse and saw the case. Afterwards he (the workhouse master), received a note from the Town Clerk stating that the Urban authority refused to take the case into their hos- pital. All the drains and sewers had been thoroughly flushed and disinfected, and everything was done to prevent the disease spreading.—Mr. A. Jolley said he had seen in the newspapers that the case was one of, chickenpox and not of sinallpox.—The Chairman said Mr. Jolley should not believe everything he saw in the newspapers. With regard to the refusal of the Corpora- tion to take the case into their hospital, he said he was pleased that the poor of into, knew that they had a workhouse to go to if they were refused admission to the hospital.—Mr. Ratcliffe said the chairman should say the poor of the Union and mt. of Warrington only. (Laughter.)—The Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) said that as the question with regard to ad missionto the hospital might be- come an important one he would read the correspondence. 'rhe Town Clerk had written to the Workhouse Master as follows With reference to the case of smallpox reported from the Workhouse I am instructed by the Sanitary Committee to inform you that as the Guardians are required by article 92:0f the Consolidated Order of the Poor Law Commissioners of the 24th July, 1847, to provide accommodation in the Workhouse for sick paupers the Corporatien cannot consent to receive into the borough hospital paupers suffering from infectious disease resident in the Workhouse." Upon receiving that letter the Workhouse Master had ferwarded it to him (the clerk), and asked for advice. In reply he wrote to the Workhouse Master as follows :—" If it becomes sufficiently important to require the Urban Sanitary Authority of Warrington to receive from the

t Workhouse cases of smallpox I will advise the Guard- dians to adopt the necessary steps to that end ; mean- while the desire of the Guardians will be to assist the Urban Authority in view of the epidemic said to be now prevailing. The articla quoted by the Town Clerk is clearly against and not favourable to his contention. No doubt exists upon our standing in loco parentis as to the sick child, and whatever is the right or privilege of a parent, being an inhabitant of Warrington, is equally so of the Guardians. I notice from your letter a doubt has arisen as to the nature of the disease. My own view is that in any case brief isolation will see the child well in a few days, and that the inmates, so far as the child is concerned, have no cause, with such isolation, to fear any ill results."—The Workhouse Master asked for instructions as to whether people should be allowed to pass in or out of the workhouse as usual during the pre- valence of the epidemic. It was stated that the Catholic inmates were allowed out on Sundays to attend their places of worship, but that sometimes, instead of going to church, they went to the houses of friends which might be in parts of the town where the disease existed.—Mr. W. Houghton: Is nobody responsi- ble for them when they leave the workhouse? 1— The Workhouse Master said there yeas no check upon them.—Dr. Spinks (tha.Workhouse medical officer) said there were two cases of small-pox in Guard- ian-St., and the town seemed to be getting full of them. —Mr. HATCLIFEE said that, as Chairman of the House Committee, he should move that the leave of absence of the inmates should be discontinued for a time.—Mr. A. JOLLEY Inconded this proposal, which was agreed to.— Dr. SPINES then referred to the proposal of the Corpor- aticn to extend their hospital close to the boundary wall of the Workhouse. He thought this would be objectionable, and he advised the Guardians to oppose the proposal with all their strength. He thought it was too near the Workhouse to place a small-pox hospital, as, he added,the disease was communicable within 1,000 yards. He believed the Medical Officer of Health was .not in favour of the extension in that direction.—ln answer to the Chairman, the Clerk said he did not think they had any power to interfere. They must first suffer from a wrong before they had any remedy. They had members on that Board who were also mem- bers of the Corporation and they could try to quietly influence their colleagues on the Sanitary Committee. If in the opinion of the Medical Officer it was not a proper tying to do, he was sure the Committee would consider the matter. He would certainly advise that I Board not to do anything antagonistic to the Corpora- tion in the difficult position in which they were placed. —The discussion then ended.

div.head: MR. T. E.. ELLIS ME
div.p: MR. T. E.. ELLIS ME

A daily contemporary thus refers to Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P.,-formerly private secretary to Mr. J. T. Brunner, .M.P. :--•• Welshmen everywhere have received with the liveliest feelings of satisfaction -the news of Mr. Thomas Ellis's appoin.tment as Junior Lord of the Treasury. This is by no means the first time that a Welshman has become a mem- ber of the Government, but, as someone has already pointed out, it furnishes the first instance of the promotion to a Government . post of 'a man who habitually addresses his constituentsin the Welsh language. There are many other reaeons why Welshmen should rejoice in the appointment of Mr. Ellis. . He is the leadiuz .political .representative of the Nationalist revival which has done so much for Wales during the last few years. , liowbver pro- minent others among the younger Welsh members may become,no one can . deprive -Mr. Ellis of the glory of having been the pioneer of the 6' Young Wales" movement. As he is as yet but barely over tnirty, a brilliant political future may be safely predicted for him, provided his health keeps up. His office as one of the Whips places him in a particularly favourable position to advance the interests of Males."

Mr. Ellis has this week written as follows to Mr. W. Handley:of Runcorn:—"My dear Mir. Handley.— Many thanks for your very cordial congratulations. The memories of my association with the North- wich Division will ever be fresh in my mind, and I shall ever value the many friendships which I made there."

div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION,
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION,

The annual election of five members to Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners takes place on Thur-day next. The retiring members, who are eligible for re-election, are Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C. H. J. Grice, W. Hankinson, W. Timmins, and U. White. It will be regretted that Mr. Timmins does not intend to seek the suffrages of the rate- payers on the present occasion,and It is also stated, with every appearance of authentie information' that Mr. White will pursue a similar course. Of the others, the addresses of Mr. Chico and Mr. Hankinson appear in our columns to-day, and these gentlemen therein show forth reasons why their fellow townsmen should re-eleet them to the posi- tions they have so well filled in the past. Mr. Speakman .is away from home, but there is no reason to believe that he will retire from the sphere of public usefulness which which he has been as long connected. The new candidates are Mr. William Leach, of Albert-street, and Mr. Thomas Lea or Church-street, grocer, both of whom express their views and claims for support in their advertised addresses. Should no other can- didate put in an appearance before Thursday next, these gentlemen will pramtically have a walk over, although it will be necessary that votes should be recorded for them at the polling booth. The polling will take place at the Market Hall, where Mr, Wiswall the returning officer, is having the accom- odation made on &similar scale to last year, when Mr. Once bad charge of the arrangements, which gave as much satistaction as can be expected under the antiquated system of the Commissioners Act, to which Mr. Hankinson' aptly draws attention in his address. Bach candidate is fighting for his own hand, like Hal of the Wynd in Scott's novel the" Heart of Mid Lothian" and the ratepayers have free choice.

div.head: ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT
div.p: ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT
BURTON WOOD.

- At Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. White, a man named Thomas Dutton, wheelwright, of Burtonwood, was brought up on a charge of assaulting an old man named John Gar- van also of Burtonvrood From the evidence given by the police, Garvain being too badly injured to attend..it appears the latter some time ago did some drainage for Dutton, for which he alleges be has not been paid. On Saturday he met Dutton, and asked him for the money, but the latter seizing a spade which clarvain had in his hand, knocked him down with it,,and then jumped on him, injur- ing his chest, and breaking one of his legs. Dutton then went away leaving Garvain lying on the road, where lie was found by some people and conveyed home. Dr.. Starkey Smith of Warrington, was, called in, and found bim suffering from a com- minuted fracture of Abe leg, and other serious in-. juries. Dutton was afterwirds apprehended by Sergeant Devlin, and kcked up. lie was remanded until September sth on bail.
Yosterclay, before Mr. James Tinsley, William Mnnka. and Thomas Leigh were charged with tieing drunk.. at Croft, the previous night, and fined ss. and costs.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A. COACHMAN.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A. COACHMAN.

Yesterday afternoon an accident occurred to Robert Godwin, coachman to Mr. George Combr, J.P., of Middleton Hall. He was leading the limse attached to his employer's carriage in Hor,e- market-street, and the horse suddenly became restive, and in endeavouring to manage it he got under its feet. The animal kicked him, or trod on him, and lie sustained a scalp wounds and several bruises. Ile was conveyed to the Infirmary, and had his wounds dressed, and soon after was able to proceed home.

- - sEnars ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY STATION. Last evening a woman named Mrs. Ryanof Duke- st..Widnes,vnet with a serious accident at Bank Quay Station,Warrington. It appeared that she travelled by strain from Widnes to Warrington, intending, it is supposed, to travel on to Newton-le-Willows. The train by which she was travelling reached Warrington low-level station about half-past live. and Mrs. Ryan went from the low-level station to the high-level. Here she was.passing over the ii by the crossing at the t.outh end of the station when she was caught by a train which was coming into the station from Chester. She was thrown down upon the line and the traia passed over one of her legs. smashing it. in a terrible manner, and also fracturing her left arm and s.?me of her ribs, Mr. Ashurst, the stationmaster, and other railway officials were at once upon the scene, and rendered all the aid in their power to the unfortunate woman She was put upon an ambulance and conveyed to the Infirmary where it was follnd neceasary tt amputate the injured leg.

div.head: HALE OLD MAN.
div.p: THE HALE OLD MAN.
