div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATE.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATE.
THEFT OF A MUG.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Edward Smith, labourer, 12,Lythgoes-lane, was charged with stealing from the Soldier's Return public-house, a mug, about eight o'clock on Saturday night, the pro- perty of the landlord, Mr. Stirrup. The prosecutor missed the jug and sent for the police, and P.C. Chrimes came, and subsequently went to the prisoner's house and found the jug in his cupboard. The prisoner, who was drunk, said the jug was his property and had milk . .

in, but it Contained 'beer, and writn'ess 'took both him and the jug away.—The Chief Constable said had he or Inspector Spinks been at the police station when ths prisoner was brought in, he would, under the circum- stances have let him go, and advised the landlord to summon him.—Mr. Stirrup said he did not wish to press the case, and the Bench contented themselves with re- cording a conviction against the prisoner.

div.head: THEFT By A YOUNG GIRL.
div.p: THEFT By A YOUNG GIRL.

At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday, Ellen Aplin, aged 13, daughter of John Aplin, navvy, of 81 Welfield-street, was charged with stealing a silver brooch, value 23. 6d., from the shop of John Welsby, jeweller, 52, St. James's-street, Latchford, on Monday evening. The prisoner, it appeared, went to the shop and asked to be allowed to look at a brooch, but went out without purchasing anything, and then Mr. Welsby missed the stolen article. Ile went out for a policeman, and gave her into the custody of P.C. Newey, who took her to the police station. He found the brooch in a shawl belonging to the prisoner.—Mr. Welsby said he did not wish to press the case, because her parents were very respectable. —The chairman said that it was a very melancholy case, the prisoner now being there for the third time, and asked her whether she went to Sunday school, and she replied she went to church on Sunday night.— The Chief Constable: Her youth and apparent respect- ability have eot her out of several scrapes whea she has been before the magistrates.—The prisoner's father ap- peared, and said he did not know what to do with her. Be had used violence with her and tried every means.— The Chief Constable said the girl had not been well treated at h•lrne.—She was fined 10s. and costs. SELLING PAINTED SPA RROWS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday William Ford, a hawker, from Manchester, was charged with having cruelly illtreated some birds in 2uttermar- ket-st., at noon on Friday.—lnspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.C.A., stated that on Friday he followed the defen- dant into a public-house in Buttermarket-st., and found that the man had got several cages, each with a bird in, and that he had some thick brown paper round the cages in such a manner that the birds were quite ex- hausted from suffocation. The defendant told him that they were Norwich canaries, and cost 4s. 8.1. each. He (witness) on examination found that tie birds were painted, and this con- siderably added to the value of them. After the paint had been on the birds some time they would become irritated, and try to peck it off their wings. This would in time kill them. He also found that one of the birds was a sparrow, but it was painted so that it might be taken for a canary. On arrival at the Police Station, the defendant told him (witness) that the birds were German canaries, and were worth 2s. each.—The defendant stated that he bought the canaries from a person a day or two before.—The defendant's wife said that she did not know her husband had bought the birds.—Alderman Burgess: Who does the painting? (Laughter.)—Witness : I couldn't say that.—The defen- dant was fined 10s. and costs.

EXPOSING A CHILD SUFFERING FPOII FEVER. James Bead, 6 Catherine-street, was charged yester- day Dr. John H. lomall, Medical Officer of Health; with exposing his child in the neighbourhoodof Heath Side and Catherine-Street, while it was suffering frcm scarlet fever, without taking proper precautions to pre- vent the spread of the disease.—Mr. J. Lyon' Whittle, Town Clerk, said that technically the defendant was responsible but really his mother and sister with whom he lived, and who had charge of the child, he having to go to work every day. Under the local Act some noti- fication by the head of the family to the Medical Officer of the occurrence of such disease was required, but the defendant was not charged with having failed to comply with this Act. The Medical Officer of the town had always taken the necessary steps, and it was very seldom there was any notice from the head of the family. The child had been attending school while suffering from the fever, being in a state of desquamation, and, on the Monday following died. It behoved people to be exceedingly careful now when there was scarlet fever and smallpox raging in the town, and the case was brought as an example to the public, but he did not wish to press it.—The defendant was fined the costs.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH FOLIC & COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair) Mr. John Geddes, and Mr. L. Voisey. GAMBLING.—Edward Downey, Thomas Hardman, James Dickinson, and William Rate were charged with gambling in Horsemarket-st., on Sunday the 14th of August. They were each fined ls.—Wm. Richardson, James Cullen, and Wm. Henry Heath were also fined is. each for gambling in Blue Coat-st., on the 14th of

August. • SLEEPING Our.—Peter Sculley and Wm. Coyne were charged with having slept on the premises of Mr. Rich- ardson on. Saturday night. The defendants, who are quite young lads and who have only just come out of prison, were each sent to gaol foi Wait:Mal;

Moonoz.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenell) and, Aldermen Francomb and Harrison.' • .1 . DRI7NI IN CHARON OF HORSE AND. Parker, drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Bridge Foot, on Saturdaf night, 108 and costs. Damcg AND DISORDERLY.—Martin Curley, an Irish labourer, Friars' Green, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, also with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting William Curley, his brother, iu Jolley's Yard on Saturday night. P.S. Chantler said the defendant was without his Shirt, and had William on the ground, and he was covered with blood, and Martin was in the act of kicking him. On Sergeant Chantler telling him he would kill:his brother he said with an oath it was time he was dead. The defendant's shoe toes wgi-a covered with blood, with kicking his brother.— The defendant said his brother as abusing his mother I and struck witness several times.and he was only trying to get away from him. lie never used violence to biro, and he was bleeding through tumbling down.—Mrs. Cur- ley, the mother, said William struck Martin first, and then Martin struck him and knocked him again-st the fender. William tore Martin's shirt off.— Wm. was absent, and at the suggestion of the Chief Constable who said there were always disturbances with the Curleys, the charge of assault was adjourned for his appearance, and Martin who pleaded guilty of being drunk, was fined 103. and costs on that charge.— Daniel Cavaney, an Irish la bourer,drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Saturday night, was fined 38. Fanny Renshaw, married woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road and assault- ing Mrs. Daley of the lodging-house in that thoroUgh. fare. On Saturday night D.S. Monaghan said she was drunk and using filthy language, and seized hold of Mrs. Daley by the hair of the head.—The defendant said she wanted her husband out of the lodging-house. ss. and gosts.—Oswald Drinkwater, drunk and disorderly in
Horsemarket-street, on Sunday morning, 53., Bridget Atherton, in Stamford-st., on the 13th inst., 103. and costs.
ARMY DESERTION.—Patrick Burke was charged.with being a deserter since June 4th from H.M. Liverpool regiment stationed at Warrington. Be was handed over to the military authorities.

CRUELTY TO AN Ass.—John Thomas Robinson, huckster, Mill-st., a boy, was charged with cruelty to an ass in that street on the 7th bast. A constable and Inspector Dowty, H.S. P.C.A., proved that the lad pulled at the donkey's bit until its mouth was cut and bleeciing. It was stated that the donkey belonged to Mrs. Locker, with whom he lived. The defendant was let off with the record of a conviction against him. FIGHTINO.—Wm. Connor, fish hawker, 23, Brook-st., for fighting in Buttermarket-st., on the 13th inst., was bound over in £5 to keep the peace for six months. Doo CasEs.—Samuel Massey,farmer, Grappenhall, for allowing a dog to be •at large unmuzzled and without a collar in School Brow, was fined 2s. Bd.—Peter Law- less, fishmonger, Corporation-st., was charged with the like offence, and with keeping the dog without a license. —The defendant pleaded that he bought the dog to sell again, but a gentleman, whom he intended it for would not have k.—The cases were dismissed.—ElLin Warbur- ton, wife of Peter, 139, Mersey-st., was charged with allowing a dog to be at large unmuzzled, and without a collar. Her defence was that the dog had been left by a lodger, and she had now destroyed it, and she was fined 2s. 6d.—William Hickey, hawker, 3 Wakefield-st., was charged with keeping a dog without a license. He proved that he bad bought the dog on Sunday week the day before being summoned, and took out the license on the Tuesday, and was dismissed. - -
TIIESDAY.--Before_Mr. R.Garnett (chairman), Aldermen
_ .. . . Francomb and Chandley, Capt. Ridgway, and Messrs. E. M. Crosfield and J. White.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—MichaeI Walsh, in Butter- market-at., on Monday evening, was fined ss. and costs. —Daniel O'Laughlin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st. A constable said the man had broken the crockery at home, and struck his wife and mother, cutting them as though he had a knife in his hand. He was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.

THURSDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley (chairman) Sut- ton, Francomb, Burgess, and Holmes, Captain Ridgway, and Mr. 1. Monks. Amur DESERTION.—Patrick Ward and James Lumb, were charged with deserting FI.M. Liverpool regiment, stationed at Warrington. They were handed over to the military authorities. FRIDAY.--Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman) and Wright. _ . . .

ASSAULTS.—Joseph Royle, -24, Blue Coat-street, was charged by Alice Homes, married woman, his sister, 5, Charles-st., with assaulting her on the 20th inst.—The complainant said he came into the house and struck her, without provocation.—Mary Ann Wade and Annie Dooney deposed to his assaulting the complainant. Annie Dooney said she remonstrated with him and he said he was the complainant's brother and he could do what he liked with her, and told her to mind her own business. He struck his sister with his open hand, and pushed her after witness had spoken to him.—The de- fendant said his sister was getting goods unknown to her husband, and he went to ask her about it, and on his telling her what he had come for, she swore and said it was a lie that she had done so. He said" Get away," and struck her with his two fingers.—fle was bound over in his own recognizances fcr £sto keep the peace for six months.—Charles Roberts, of Twelve Houses, Howley, was charged with assaulting William Blackburn, of the saline street.—The complainant said he was walk- ing by the river side, when the defendant came up to to him and asked him what he had been saying to his little daughter. Witness replied that he had said no- thing to her, and the defendant knocked him down. Witness had said nothing to the child.—A female witness corroborated.—The defendant said the complainant had had a spite against him of late..--David Mannion deposed that lie was in company with Roberts when his child came up to them and complained that the defendant had been " agate of her" again.—The child herself and another little girl stated the complainant mot the former and shook her.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and to pay 1 costs.

WIFE DESERTION.—Joseph Lowe, Crosley-street, was charged with deserting his wife, Frances Lowe, and chil- dren, living in Knutsford-road. He was ordered to con- tribute 8s a week for their maintenance.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.

YESTERDAY WEEK.—Before Messrs. T. P. Norris (in the chair), Charles Lister, and John D. Dewhurst. A LANDLORD PROSECUTED.—James Potts Chapman, landlord of the Railway Hotel, Heatley, was charged with having on the 3rd August unlawfully kept his house open after eleven o'clock. A second charge was that the landlord at the same time and place permitted drunkenness,and Thomas Swain was charged with being drunk on tile licensed premises. Mr. Brown, of Stock- port, appeared to prosecute for the police, and Mr. flockin, of Stockport, was for the defence. On the second charge, Mr. Browne, Warrington, appeared for the defence. P.C. Howe stated that on the 3rd August at 11 20 at night, his attention was drawn to the Railway Hotel by a light Inside. He went in and found six men in the kitchen. He asked the landlady what ac- count she could give of the matter. She said they were only a few travellers. He called her attention to 'Swain. She replied that she had not noticed him. Swain said that he had come to Heatley by the 11 15 train, but he (witness) told him that he had not, as he had seen that train come in and depart. Swain then said that he had come by the 930 train.—Mr. Hockin said that he did not think when he came to Lymrn that he would have a case to defend. But there was no case for the prosecution whatever. Mr. Swain came to Heaney by the 930 train, and hearing that some friends of his were at the Railway Hotel, he went there and stayed with them. The bar was closed at five minutes to eleven, and no drink was sold after that. Mr. Brown, for the prosecution, then withdrew the firs 'i charge.—The second charge, namely, that of permitting drunkenness, was then proceeded with.—P.C. Howe said that when he went into the house he saw Mr. Swain sitting down. He was drunk. He was staggering on his way hame.—Mr. T. Swain said that he came from Warrington to Heatley ly the 9.20 train. He did not speak to the constable as to what train he came by. The officer did not charge him with being drunk. He was perfectly sober at the time.— Mrs. White also stated that Mr. Swain was sober., and the case was dismissed. ALLEGED GAMBLING.—Arthur Mills, Thomas Scott, Frederick Talbot, Alfred Brannighan, and Wm. Scott were charged with playing an unlawful game with coins on July 17th.—Sergeant Jor.es gave evidence, but the defendants were dismissed with a caution.

CHANGE OF POACHlNG.—Ricliard Forster and William Mantle were charged with having been on certain land about Lymm, on the 29th July, forar, unlawful purpose. —Sergeant Wynne proved the case.—The defendant Forster, on whom were found nets, stated that he had had them given to him to carry by a man.—lle was fihed 108., and the other defendant was dismissed. • RIDING ON THE FOOTPATH—PEAC Hodson, Ernest Jones, and Cornelius Smith were charged with riding their tricycles on the footpath, at Bollington, on the 7th inst.—The defendants gave as their reason that the road was a bad one, and that the footpath was not marked. —They were dismissed with a caution.

THEFT BY YOUTHS.—Two lads, named Roney and Carlan, were charged with Stealing 63. 21,1. from the pocket of a pair of trousers, left by a labourer named Foyle at the Widnes Baths on the 24th August. AN AFFILIATION ORDER. —Sarah Ann Flelsby obtained an affiliation order against Albert Clays of Frodsharn, in respect of her illegitimate boy. the amount of the order was 3.5. per week.—Mr. Burton was for the com- plainant and Mr. Linaker for the defendant, who admitted the ,aternity of the child.

WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER.—This return match , was played at Warrington, on Saturday. Splendid cricket weather prevailed, and there was a capital atten- dance, there being considerably over 1,000 present after lunch. Warrington won the toss, and elected to bat on a wicket which certainly did not favour the batsman, as the opening essays tended to prove. The start was indeed disastrous, Yonge and Clarke being dismissed with only a single on the board, whilst with an addi- tional run C. B. Voisey was well caught. With J. J. Crosfield as R. Smith's partner, a better aspect was put on the game, but runs came slowly, the bowling and fielding of the visitors being superb. With 24 runs on, of which Crosfield had made 11, he was tempted to hit out at Irving, and Mills brought off a fine catch at cover point. Bell came next, but was never at ease, and after contributing two was bowled by Irving, and Clark was taken in the slips, whilst L. A. Voisey experi- enced the hardest of luck, being bowled off his arm, the ball dropping on the top of the bails. At this point lunch was taken, R. Smith being not out 15—a patient display. Holland, who had relieved E3combe just before the interval, bowled with remarkable success. On resuming Dutton accompanied R. Smith to the wickets, but the latter started to force the game, and from the first ball sent down he was taken at mid-off. The remaining batsmen were easily got rid of, and the ven- ture closed for the miserable total of 35. Manchester started with E. Rowley and T. P. Bellhouse, J. J. Cros- field and Smith (pro) bowling. With nine runs on, the first-named bowler brought off a magnificent catch, , which dismissed Rowley. With Houldsworth in, runs came at a rapid pace, and in half-an-hour the Warring- ton total was passed. Previous to this R. Smith had relieved the professional, and had the satisfaction of taking Houldsworth, with 42 runs on, the latter having made 19 in capital style. J. J. Crosfield crossed over whilst Smith resumed at his end. His first ball saw Bellhouse caught at the wicket, whilst in his next over Lord was caught by C. B. Voisey. Mills was dismissed at 53, the professional having taken the last four wickets since resuming for a matter of 11 runs. Wood played freely, and, coupled with Escombe. took the total to 98 I before the former was bowled for 18. Irving and Hol- land were dismissed with successive balls,and the innings I closoci for 97. Warrimg,ton went in a second time, and fared much better. Smith hit Irving clean out of the ground for six, and after making 11 in as many minutes, was finely caught on the boundary. J. J. Crosfield and Clarke played free cricket, and defied all the attempts of five bowlers until, oil the call of time, Clarke was bowled off his pads, the score being 62, Clarke having made 25, whilst J. CRICKET.

Last week was very eventful One in the history of the contest for the county championship. The Notts Eleven, after passing through all their engagements until near the end of the season without a single defeat, were overthrown by the youngest of the first class counties, whilst the most formidable of their rivals, Surrey, were by a couple of victories placed on a level with them, and may, after all, retain the Blue Ribbon of cricket at Kennington Oval.

Lancashire has not improved its position ; a victory over Sussex, the holder of the " wooden spoon," was followed by a severe det2at at the hands of Middlesex, and the chance of making even a respectable figure in the list at the conclusion of the season appears to be very remote. The county is bracketed with Somerset in the third position, a long way behind the leaders. The Eleven have had the worst luck during the season, but it is to be feared that they were not in their hest form on Saturday at Lard's, when Middlesex wound up their season at headquarters with a brilliant victory ever Mr. flornby's team.

Those who deal in the curiosities of cricket—always interesting—will be amused, says a sporting correspon- dent, to note the fact that the defeat of Nottingham was almost exclusively due to the efforts of three left- handed players. Mr. H. T. Hewitt, the captain of the Somerset Eleven, who hit so brilliantly for 60 : Mr. V. T. Hill ; and Tyler, whose slow bowling was the feature of the second innings of Nottingham, all play what an old and prejudiced country cricketer once described as "contrary to nater." A collection—realizing £44— was made to celebrate Tyler's 15 Nottingham wicket for 98 runs.

The championship table as at present arranged offers some conundrums which the public will find not very easy of solution. Nottinghamshire has twice beaten Surrey ; Surrey has twice beaten Somerset, and Somer- set has proved herself the only county capable ot inflicting a thoroughly decisive deteat upon Notting- hamshire. By all the rules of sport, it would seem that Somersetshire should be accounted the champion county, but as a matter of fact she will occupy only a third or fourth position. Again, if Surrey should gain another victory and Nottingham he again defeated, the title of " champion of the counties" will be held by a team who have been twice decisively defeated by the second in the order.

In the year 1881 there was no room for doubt as to which was the champion of the counties. The title be- longed beyond dispute to Lancashire, which had gone through the season undefeated by any other county,and when Cambriige University supplied the only team capable of lowering the colours of the County Palatine. In that culminating year of triumph Lancashire won no fewer than six matches by an innings, one by ten wickets,one by eight wickets, one by 216 runs, and one by 50 runs ; whilst there was no doubt that the matches with Middlesex, Gloucester, and Notts would have ended in their favour if time and the weather had per- mitted. Such a record as that compares favourably with the performances of either Surrey or Notts this season.

The " stonewall" cricketer does not find much favour in London. In the Kent-Midilesex match Georg 2 Hearne was " safe," but intolerable. He occupied him- self for hours in" making a collection of runs," and when he went in the second time a spectator fairly brought down the house, says " The Cricket Field," by crying out very earnestly, " Now do be careful."

Mr. Sydney Crosfield, the captain of the Lancashire Eleven, is the subject of an interview in this week's number of " The Cricket Field." Referring to what must be so obvious to Southern observers—namely, the deadly earnestness with which the representatives of Lancashire play cricket,—Mr. Crosfield said : " I think there is more real rivalry than is usual in club matches elsewhere, and the players are very much in earnest. It is not at all an uncommon thing to find 5,000 or 6,000 spectators at a purely local match, and even at quite small villages there are often as many as 1,000. The fact is that each side plays to win, and the players are greatly disappointed when they lose. This, of course, makes run-qetting a matter of some difficulty, and, moreover, the wickets are often—perhaps generally— slow, so that bowling has the upper hand. One is struck with the difference in the scoring on a Saturday after- noon in the South of England and in the North, and we often have occasion to smile when men who have been easily making immense scores about London come up and play a few club matches in Lancashire—they find out then the reason why centuries are not so numerous with us.

" There are." he added, " always quaint things hap- pening. Roper tells a tale of a blacksmith who played against our club, Sefton, at Kendal. He was run out about ten yards, but this did not seem to trouble him much, and he went back to his wicket and proceeded to take guard again. Roper in his most affable manner intimated that the pavilion was a place more suitable to the batsman than the wicket just at the point of the game. However, the blacksmith settled the matter by slowly remarking that he was not going till one o' them there pegs was knocked down, and maybe not then,' meaning that to be bowled was his only idea of getting Out at cricket ; and for his cheek he was allowed to con- tinue his innings, which lasted for another ball or two. E. S. Carter has a tale of a man who was caught at the wicket. He was rather deaf, and leaned forward to catch the umpire's decision, which was Not out.' But , in leaning he lifted his foot, and the wicket keeper I promptly stumped him. As he was slowly and sadly 1 retiring he remarked, Eh, Mr. Carter, there are many I points in this 'ere game which requires to be carefully worked out before you understand it aright."

Asked if he could account for the occasional collapse of the team, Mr. Crosfield said :—" I can't account for them, nor can anyone else, I believe. We are stronger in batting than we have ever been, and twice have made over 400 this year and twice over 300 : but sometimes, for no particular reason, we go to pieces. The weather has been very much against us this year, and some of our drawn matches must have been wins but for rain. . . . There is a great deal of anxiety, but the Committee do all that they possibly can to make things pleasant for the captain, and that makes a lot of diffe- rence. Besides, the professionals are the most agreeable fellows that one could possibly have anything to do with, and are remarkable for their goad humour, even under the most trying circumstances. And you know when every man in the team is anxious to help a cap- tain as much as he can, it considerably lightens the onerous nature of the work."

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Warrington will open a splendid It of fixtures next Saturday by a home match with the strong Yorkshire Combhation from Dewsbury. There is every prospect of the coming season being the most successfulthe Warring- ton club has expsrienced. Last season the local players again took a leading place—it would,perhaps,be too much to say that they took tke leading place—amongst the Rug- by organisations of Lancashire, and,partly as a conse- quence of this, they have secured a list of fixtures of the most attractive kind. Another think which will most undoubtedly give a fillip to Rugby football in Lancashire during the coming season, is the forrsation of the Rugby League, composed of the eight leading clubs of the country, including, of course, Warriagton. The matches in onnection with this L.ague are sure to be great " draws" and the playerA on both sides may be relied upon to do their level, best to secure the verdict.

The teams will be composed pretty much as last year. Boscow will again diff)lay his smartness and cool judg- ment at full back. For three-quarter positions there will again be avairable Evans, Heesom, H. Webster, Potts, and Barnes. and at half-back the two Bates will be a w,dl-matched pnir. The fonvard combination will include H. Ashton, who captains the team. Fair Turner, Bandies, Nevins, J. Jolley, T. Donohue, Berry, and others who have heretofore done good service in that department.

In the course c.,1 the season the- first team will again do the" grand tour." They will ramble to Ireland on this occasion and there play matches with Dublin University and Lansdowne. The President, Mr. P. DaViOS, will pre- sent a cup and silver medal to the players who, as de- cided by the vote of their fellow members at tl.-13 annual meeting, shall he considered the best players in regard to merit and conduct.

WARRINGTON BREWSTER ' SESSIONS.

The annual licensing sessions at Warrington were opened at the Borough Police Colin on Tuesday, before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), Aldermen Fran- comb and Chandley. Mr. E. M. Crosfield, Captain Ridgway, and Mr. John White.

div.head: CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.
div.p: THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

" I have the honour to inform y7o-i.Fil;a-t.ilie annual Brewster Sessions for the borough will be held at the Sessions House, Warrington, at 10 a.m on Tuesday next, 23rd inst. The present number of license holders are : Licensed victuallers, 88 ; beer-house keepers, 48 ; and off licensed shopkeepers, 73; total 209. The transfers during the year were-12 licensed victuallers houses, 6 beerhouses, and 11 off-licensed shops ; total 29. Pro- ceedings have been taken against four licensed victu- allers during the mat year, three being dismissed and one paid costs ; and the number of persons brought up for drunkenness is 680, being 93 less than last year. The annual average for drunkenness during the last 25 years is 760." The report then gives a table contaiming the number of drunken cases during the past ten years. In 1883 the following persons were charged with drunken- ness : —Convicted, males 432, females 185 : discharged, males 47, females 53 ; or a total of 717. In 1891, 513 males and 166 females were convicted, and 50 males and 44 females were discharged ; while in 1892, 424 males, and 149 females were convicted, and 50 males and 57 females were discharged; making the total for 1891, 773 and for 1892 680.

The report contains the new applications, which are as follows :—For new victuallers' provisional licenses : Mr. Joseph Houghton Clarke, Battersbv-lane, new hotel to be built; Mr. George Pilling, Catherine-st., new hotel to be built. For full alehouse license: Mrs. Susan Beard, Bevrsey-road, the Grove House (six days' license) ; Mr. Wm. Bolton, 112 and 114, Battersby-lane, off-license premises. Wine. spirits, and sweets off the premises : Myles Frederick Catcheside, 12, Horsemarket-st., grocer. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, appeared to represent Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, and the Licensed Victuallers' Asso- ciation ; and Mr. H. Davies represented Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., but there being no objections to the renewal of existing licenses, there were no interests to defend, and the licenses were all renewed. The sessions were then adjourned till Thursday.

div.head: NEW APPLICATIONS. FRESH LICENSES GRANTED.
div.p: THE NEW APPLICATIONS. FRESH LICENSES GRANTED.

The adjourned licensing sessions were held on Thurs- day for the hearing of new applications,before Aldermen Holmes (chairman), Francomb, Burgess, and Chandley, Councillor Falselough, Mr. F. Monks, and Captain Ridg- way. Mr. H. B. White, magistrates' clerk,having some- what recovered from his long illness, was present, as he had also been at the opening sessions on Tuesday. Mr. R. Davies applied on behalf of Mr. Jos. Houghton Clarke, for a new hotel to be erected by him between Sharp and Scott streets. Mr. Cherlton, of Manchester, on behalf of Messrs. Joseph Titchard, Joseph Flornfield, Edward Davies,and other property-owners Mr. Davies said it was proposed to expend something like £2,500 in erecting the hotel, so that the Bench might rely upon it that everything that the architect or builder could do to accommodate the public for legitimate premises would be aone. The house would be situated where there was no accommodation, and it was the desire of the appli- cants to put up a house which would be a credit to those concerned. His clients were not only brewers, but very extensive property-owners ; and their desire was to im- prove their property, and at the same time to do it in a manner which they hoped would meet with the approval of the Bench and the public generally. It was not for the increase of the consumption of beer that they were making the application,but it was to pro- vide accommodation for cyclists, and travelling people, and that class who need inns for victualling purposes. They were even ready to make any changes, even such radical changes as were lately suggested by the Bishop of Chester. Some of the magistrates he (Mr. Davies) had heard, and the people of Warrington, took what might be described as extreme views, and this application was made with a desire to meet those who hell these views, with the object of reducing drunkenness by lessening, as they proposed to do,the number of houses in congested districts. Mr. Davies then referred to another applica- tion he had to make for a provisional license for a new hotel proposed to be built for Mr. George Pilling in Catherine-street, Bewsey-street, and said his re- marks wouid apply to both cases. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., considered that the most congested district was the site of the old Buttermarket ; and the local knowledge that the Bench possessed would enable them to follow him. Adjoining each other on the south side of Buttermarket-street there were belonging to his clients three old-established, well-frequented, and fully licensed houses named the Fox Inn, the Crown and Sceptre Inn, and the Curriers' Arms, on the north side a house of a similar charactet , called the Bear's Paw, and lower down the street on the southerly side there was a beerhouse called the White Bear. The naxt congested place was at the town end, where there was a beerhouse also belonging to his clients, called the Black Horse Inn, in Turner-street. His clients had in- structed him to say that if the Bewsey-road application were acceded to for building the new hotel they would be willing to give up the Bear's Paw, in Buttermarket-st. and the Black Horse lan, hr Turner-st. ; and if the iattersby-lane application were acceded to they would be willing to give up the Fox Inn and the White Bear beerhouse. He was sure it was not to the pecuniary advantage of his clients to give up any of these houses. When he was returning from the Sessions last Tuesday in the company of one of the directors of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., he ventured to suggest that another great improvement might be made by giving up the Curriers' Arms license and enlarging the Crown and Sceptre into a good and commodious house, and this his clients were prepared to do if their applications were granted. He suggested also that the off-license of a beerhouse near the site ot the house in Catherine-street., might be given up, which they were prepared to do. The effect of the applications being acceded to would be that all the six licenses he had mentioned would be abandoned, and two large, roomy, well-built, and commodious hotels built, and he was sure there would be an almost unanimous feeling that such an offer, which deaths and other changes might prevent ever being made again. should be accepted. Be thought the magis- trates would be of opinion that the acceptance of it would be for the public benefit. The population of Warrington had very largely increased, especially in those districts in which it was proposed to build the hotel. Considering this fact, and that no new license had been granted in Warrington, except one at the Cen- tral Station, for 30 years,, he thought the magistrates might feel sure the number of licensed houses in the future would not be more than the requirements of the town demanded. tie did not propose to go into general arguments about the need of public-houses, as he had done on previous occasions, as they did not wish to excite prejudice of any kind, but to offer something which they believed would be acceptable. It was a most liberal offer, and he hoped the magistrates would meet his clients, who did not look to any increase of emolumsnts or profit, bat desired to improve their houses and meet the views of the great majority of the people of Warrington.—William Wilson, assistant to Mr. Win. Owen,. architect, was called, in his employer's absence from home, to give evidence in support of the applications. The next beerhouse to the site of the proposed hotel was about 420 yards away, and the next 560, yards away. He had not heard of any enquiry round about as to the necessity of licensed houses. The old Fox Inn, the Currier's Arms, and the Bear's Paw were close together. —Mr. Chorlton : Two of them jpin.—Mr. R. Davies: Three of them join.—Cross-examination continued : The conversion of the three houses might provide accomoda- tion for as many as the three did. Ile did not know whether the workmen at Bewsey Forge had ever asked for a licensed house in that neighbourhood. The middle of the town was not quite such a residential part as 40 years ago, so that the people who formerly lived at the centre were now going to the outskirts. The men going to the waggon works or any of the large works from the cottages in the neighbourhood would go within reason- able distance of licensed houses. Mr. Cliorlton, in opposing the•application, said one did not like that bargaining which, had been submitted to the bench. The application was one that should rest upon its own merits; and it shouldscareely come before toe bench with the suggestion that if they granted that license the applicants would do awaly with some other licenses. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. were really giVing up nothing. At present they had four houses,. with four managements and four expenses going on,and they wanted to diminish those expenses by taking away three of them without suffering one sixpence of loss, because they were going to increase the one house that remained to such an extent that it would probably be, in its superficial area, equal to .two or. three of the pre- sent houses. Anybody would be very glad • to give tap two or three sources of expense and trouble if by enlaaig- ing another place under oneananagernent and at Dne uost they could do the same business. They would lose nothing by -giving up those houses,.for the person who had been in the habit of going to them wmald go to the exteuded "ailace near to them. They gave up nothing in order that they migbt get established in a populous district of,work- ingmen's. houses. The house that it was proposed to build wbs near to the barracks and near to the waggon works. Was it a wise thing to place additionali tempta- tion in a district like that ? Had the applicants brought , any rseornmendation fawn any commanding officer, or any acer,at the barracke,or had they brought any man there to say that the accommodation was wanted in the district ? Their worships were in a sense officers of Her Ma-Zesty and should have some care for Her Majesty's servants who were in the barracks and who did not need that additiona% temptation put in their way. They had e-at brought a manager of the wagon works, nor had they brought even one of those working-men whom, I, Messrs. Greeuall, Whitley, an ud Company were so anxios to supply to come there and say that they wanted that accomodation. Mr. Davies had said the honee was wanted for cyclists, travellers, and so on, voople who were running about, but that was surely not.the law. The law had been laid down many years ago by Mr. Justice Lush that vvhal should be considered was the interest and the welfare of the locality in which it I was proposed to license, the house. Re asked the Reach

to consider whether the well-being of the neighbour- hood wont] be improved by that new licensec and whether it would be for thr welfare of the soldiers at the barracks and of the working-men residents of the locality 'to pint any more temptations in their way than War- rington could already show them. He also asked them to consider the application not upon the proposition made by Xr. Davies but upon • the wants of the neigh- bourhood, and whether there was any evidence of the want of that license.

John Senior, of I, Scott-st., near Battersby-lane, them gave evidence against the applioation. He said that he had lived in that neighbourhood all Ms life. Theta were two houses not very far away, one being the Manx Arms and the other a beerhouse. In his opolion those were sufficient for the waits of the neighbourhood. His mother owned two houses near the site and the proposed new public-house. _ _

, Francis Teggin, of Sharpe-street, near Battersby-lane, said he lived the house next to the proposed new public. house. Be was opposed to the granting of the license and said he did not think it was needed.—Cross-exam- ined by Mr. Davies, he said he had never been a teeto- taller.—Mr. Davies : Why do you object to this house? —Witness : I don't want it next door to me.and I don't think you would like it next door to you. (Hear, hear, and some applause.) He wo.uld have no objection to the house if it were twenty or thirty yards away. Adam Horrocks, of Irlam-street, also objected to the license being granted. He had some cottage property near Battersby-lane, and he had never heard from his tenants or anyone else a request for a house of that kind.—Cross-miatnined by Mr. Daviee-: He lived next door to a beerhonse. _ _ PROPOSED NEW HOI7SE IN CATHRRINE-STREET. _

Mr. Davies next made the application on behalf of Messrs. Greenall. Whitley and Coy. for a full license for a new house proposed to be erected at the corner of Catherine-at. and Bewsey-road. Alluding to Mr. Chorlton's remarks he said they were not bargaining with the bench. / They were offering to give up certain licensee if two new hotels were allowed to be built. That was 'a practice that had been extensively followed at St. Helens wbere the magistrates did not object if there was a reasonab e offer to allow the applicants to build a good hotel. Mr. Chorlton had also spoken of managers, but it was perfectly well understood by the whole town that there was not a single house that his clients possessed, that was managed by a manager. They were all let to bona-fide tenants, and further than that, his clients had no interest in the sale of spirits or anything of that kind. Mr. Wilson produced plans of the proposed new house which he said was estimated to cost £2,800. He . also gave particulars as to the dimension of the house. Mr. Chorlton said he appeared to oppose the applica- tion on behalf of Councillor Greening, Mr. John Green- ing, Messrs. Rathbone, R. Roberts, Hesketh, and others. I He cross-examined the witness as to whether he was aware that there were already one off-license in Hoyle- st., three in Pierpoint-st.,and two in Pitt-street. Address- ing the Bench, Mr. Chorlton said there was less ground for the application in that case than in the other. He I pointed out that on the triangular space on which I Catherine-street and the adjoining streets stood there were already several licensed houses, including the Grove and an Indoor licensed house in Pitt-street. With I regard to Mr. Davies's statement as to Messrs. Greenall dnd Company not employing managers, they could at all events put extra rent on their tenants. Did the Bench suppose that after Messrs. Greenall and Company had given up two or three licenses and spent their money on enlarging the Curriers' Arms and increasing the accommodation they would not put att increased rent on that house? With regard to the Catherine-st., applic- ation he also pointed out that the applicants had not brought forward the slightest evidence that the license was wanted. That being so, he need not take up their- worships' time in calling witnesses agaihst the applica- tion.
THE" GROVIC " LICHNSN.

_ Mr. Seger, barrister, of Liverpool,next made an appli- cation for the full license to bo given to the " Grove" public-house, Bewsev-road, which is occupied by Mrs. Baird (late Mrs. Lawton), and owned by Messrs. Wag. gaffe, brewers, cf Manchester. He said that was, he be- lieved, the 15th application that had been made for that license. It had been granted on one occasion, but the confirming authority did not confirm it. He contended that they had a claim to a full license prior to that of Messrs. Greenall for the house in Catherine-st., seeing that the " Grove "was an already established house with an off-license. It had been there 18 or 18 years, and had always had an admirable charac- ter. He did not accept the view that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley,. and Co:, were making their magnanimous offer with the desire not to increase their trade. It was quite clear that that was a business offer, and that they had made a pretty good guess that the business they were likely to do in the new neighbourhood would compensate them for the licenses they were giv- ing up. It was absurd to look upon that as a generous offer. If they wanted to make a generous offer let them shut up the whole of their houses in the town and so oblige the teetotallers. (Hear, hear, and applause.) But do not let them dome there and pretend that that was other than a business offer. Arguing in favour of his own application, he said that the people who wanted piablie-houses were the working-men, and he alluded to the number of ironworkers and others that were em- ployed in the neighbourhood of the " Grove." This house, he added, had originally cost Messrs. Wagstaffe about 3,500 and if the present application were granted they would be prepared to spend another £1,500 in im- proving the accommodation. Alderman Wright was then called as a witness and put in plans of the proposed extensions that he hag prepared for the owners of the " Grfive." The cost of carrying these outle estimated at £1,500.—1n answer to Mr. Chorlton, he said he had himself submitted those plans to the bench five or six times. He did not think the population a the district had increased very much in that time. He had himself heard wcrking-men ex- press a wish that there was a fully licensed house in that neighbourhood. Mrs. Baird spoke to having occupied the-" Grove " . about 12 years. In answer Co Mr. Choriton she said business had not gone down lately but iacreased. She knew there waa an indoor licensed house about 150 yards away. e Mr. John Fair, commercial traveller, 97, Bewsey-road, said he theught a fully licensed house was required there.

IJQ,bn Wagstaff% of the firm of Messrs. Wagstaffe and Co., brewers, owners of the " Grove," said they were pail a rent of £3O or £4O for the house. There were About twelve barrels a week supplied to the house.

, ,Mr.Chorlton said this was an. attempt of a Manchester brewer to get a footing in Warringtou. That was the ISth application, and Alderman Wright himself adr mitted that there was no difference between this year field last. Be asked the i3enen not to grant ,he license. [ AYPLiCA.TION BY CO6NCILLOS BOLTON. Mr. Segar, barrister, of Manchester' applied on behalf of Councillor William Bolton, for full license to off. licensed premises,ll2.andll4,Battersby-lane.Mr.Chorlton opposed the application, on behalf of property owners. Mr. Segar said the accomodation there was insufficient, and Mr. Bolton was very well known to the Bench, cer- tainly to Warriugton,for the admirable manner in which his houses were conducted: In case the application were acceded to, Mr. Bolton would be willing to give up three licensed houses, and to spend £1,500 to .£2,000 on. [ the improvement of the house as to Which he applied. The nearest publicehouse • In one direction was about 580 yards-off. The district was thickly populated, and the accommodation sparse compared with other parts of the town. If anybody was to have a license in that locality it ought to be Mr. Bolton, who had bouzlit the hojse and had held a license to sell beer there for a number of years without any complaint having been made about it. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and tie., absolutely proposed to put a fully licensed house next door to Mr. Bolton's premises; And it did appear to. him that (Mr. Seger) that they were people of a certain amount of assurance to propose this: it was about as impudent a thing as they could do. • It showed a curions notion of propriety, and he hoped some of the deaths or alterations in Mr. Greenall's farm that Mt. Daviesspoke of would not make their principles any worse than this. Mr. Davies :. May I correct the learned counsel 2 Our house is on the opposite side of Battersby-lane, but there is a street between called Sharp-street.--Mr. Bolton was called, and conortned the statement. of his counsel as to his intentions. He said he received 12s. a week or £3l 14s. a year for the house. He had had the beer license since 1874. He had the right to prevent any licenses being held on Thacres of land in the neighbourhood, and would guarantee that he would exercise that right. l'be nearest public-house was about tl-611 yards away and the nearest fully. licensed house 570 yard away. He objected to name the three licensed houses he was prepared to close if his applica- tion were acceded to, because if he did, these houses might be said on that account next year he be not wanted; and he declined to name them, without a ' guarantee-from the magistrates that their licenses would be renewdd in future. They were valuable houses. In the district as to which he applied there were about 3,000 ieSabitants in a radius of about 2.40 yards, as far as. he could make out.—Mr. Davies denied that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and 0). were going. to take the trade out Of Mr. Bolton's hands.. They had made application years before hs• bought the property.—Witness eross-eeamined by Mr. ' Chorltola : This was the sixth application witness had made for the license. There had been an increase-of 200 cz 300 houses in tha.neighbouehood since his appli- cation last year. He paid the taxes._-Mr. Choelton contended that house was.not„• .ter deductiug taxes, of the-value defined by the see' .}...—Mr. Bolton, in reply to. Mr. Seger, said the hoe was worth inore than £4O a Yeax.—John E. Wright, • elitect„ said within a radius et au yards there were ,dOO people, 600 house*, and he allowed 5 to a hocee. the population had increased i since last application, and was steadily increasing. Mr. !Bolton, he should say, was a gentle-man who could,be well trusted witla a license. Witness owned SO to 60 cottages la the neighbourhood eendhe raised no objection, The house was worth £,55 a year.—Me. Chorlton said . the district seemed to be a sort of pleasant country where the brewers would like to congregate, but tlU•re were 'I public-houses enough already,and it was merely a matter of brewers wanting to increase their very large profits. Mr. Balton had mentioned that he would give up three housts if his application were su.ccessful, and the pre,

vious applicants made similar offers, but was It fat!' that they shOold come there and say they wiuld give UPe houses that welt' not paying them if they might fin. houses that would pay in another distrkt ? The d_L- trick was open ground at present. Be asked the mag," . . .

- THE TRUE POET.— The child of impulse and Passion, yet retaining all the simplicity and easy confiding faith of childhood ; impatient, impetuous, artd full of life, with the blood ever running races through his veins, yet ever under the guidance of reason—not cold and pale as she is wont to be Painted, but wise with an earnest wisdsm, and Warm with the glow and freshness of an earlier Clime ;—he must be skilled in human nature, and not only must he be familiar with the spoken word Riad the visible act, but with that philosophy according to which these are regulated. He must Ponder deeply the motives of the heart, and be able, by a quick and divining sympathy, to pene- trate into its very retirements. He must cherish his imagination, and cultivate his taste, by a care- ful study of all those whose works give evidence that they felt within them the strivings of the diviner mind; not to imitate, but to gain directions vial* may guide him to those guarded and en- chanted fountains of inspiration from whence they themselves have drawn. He must be learned in all the branches of human knowledge, that his mind taaY be full of associations. He must become • tauter of the most copious vocabulary, that copies ,sverlieruts, not less important to the poet than the ' , razor ; and not only take pains to acquire cora- ' Mend of words, but he must study into their powers, and busy himself in learning all those reflected thades and hues of meaning, with which they have °ten tinged by association, as if they had been dipt "in the warm flush of a rainy sunset :" for this is that distinguishing peculiarity of a poetio dialect, ihat its words not only suggest the single and • linatediate idea to the mind, but come linked with • I.!, thousand beautiful, though dim, remembrances. niut his most anxious labour ought to be to cultivate ',. his own heart—to cleanse it from all the taints which it acquires by coming in contact with the World. He must strive earnestly to purify his • ltuagination :to fill his mind with noble desires and ~ aintives ;to divest himself of every selfish, local, or Party prejudice; to become, in truth and in deed, a 'I citizen of the world; to ennoble and expand his heart till it become a great sea, which shall gather ' ~tribute from the fountains of the whole earth, to the and again give back their contributions in ' .""e shower and the fruitful dew. He must strive ' to make himself perfect in all good, wise, and great ' things and to become a living example of that ' Perfection upon which his soul's eyes should be for •• ever fixed. Thus educated, those restless yearnings Of the spirit, those unquenchable desires, ever thirst- ' g for satisfaction, yet never satisfied, which form "ne real moving power that impels the true poet ITward, will be left free to act; and those high stincts "haunting the eternal mind, a presence that will not be put by," will find for themselves a ' longue and a ready utterance.—North American .Ueviem. div.head: TEA DRINKING.
div.p: TEA DRINKING.

There is a certain class of people who take every opportunity of sneering at their neighbours for indulging in the " folly " of drinking tea which they tell you is poisonous, and for the use of which the Chinese, as they say, make a point of laughing at us. I have generally remarked, that those who in this manner condemn the use of tea are them- selves addicted to the drinking of intoxicating liquids of some kind or other, and that, in most Instances, they are not a bit more healthful or more innocent than the unhappy tea drinkers whom they affect to pity. In the way that tea is usually made with a large mixture of sugar and cream; both which ingredients are highly nutritious, it is fully more salutary, and a great deal more refreshing, than any other light liquid that could be poured into the stomach. With all due deference to Cobbett, milk, even entirely divested of its creamy particles, is heavy, and though it may be used with advantage as a meal, when work is done in the open air, it can never suit the appetites of the great mass of the people, who are confined by sedentary employments. Milk is the food of men in a rude state, or in child- hood ; but tea or well-made coffee is their beverage In a state of civilisation. It would seem that the civilised human being must use a large quantity of liquid food. Perhaps solid me3t is more nutritious; but there are cases in which a small degree of nutriment is quite sufficient. A lady or a gentle- man of sedentary habits does not require to feed like a ploughman, or a fancy man trainipg for a pedestrian excursion. They can subsist' in a healthful state with a small quantity of solid food, but they do not do well unless with a large quantity of liquids, and these of a light quality. Good bear has been recommended as a substitute for. tea; but beer is at the best a cold, ungenial drink, except to robust people who have much exercise. Beer may certainly be made almost as light as water i tself, but in that case it is filled with gaseous matter or con- fined air, and it cannot be drank with comfort as a simple refreshment. It will always be remembered that there are different kinds of tea, and that some are more salutary than others. Green tea ought by all means to be avoided by persons of weak nerves. Black tea is the preferable for general use, and, if properly made, will prove antispasmodic, and relieve pains or cramp in the bowels. In some instances tea does not suit the particular state of the stomach, and it should then be abandoned, the taste naturally pointing out when it should be taken. But no species of prepared fluid seems so suitable to the palates and the stomachs of the people of this country. No kind of drink is so refreshing after a journey or fatigue as tea. It restores the drooping spirits, and invigorates the frame for renewed exertion. No other kind of liquid with which we are acquainted has the same remarkable influence morally and physioally. Fermented or distilled liquors, taken under the same circumstances, either induce intoxication or sleep. It is preposterous to say that tea is poisonous. As there is an astringency in its properties, I believe it would be most injurious were we to live upon nothing else, or drink it as a tincture. But who does either? As it happens to be prepared and used, it answers merely as a refresh- ing aid p166.11ng drink, either to the solid hreaci and butter taken along Al it, or after a recent dinner of substantial viands. Hew idle it is to say that this harmless beverage is ruining the constitutions of the people of this coun- try 1 The very reverse can be demonstrated. The inhabitants of Great Britain use more tea than all the rest of Enrope pat together, and yet they are the healthiest nation on the face of the earth. . The North Americans are also great tea drinkers, and human life among them is of nearly an equal value. Who would for a moment compare the thin wretched wines of France and Germany, or the sour krout oi Russia, to the " com- fortable ' tea of Great Britain, and who would lose time in calculating the different effects of these liquids on the constitution?

Tea has other excellent properties. At this pre- sent moment it is putting down the pernicious practice of dram - drinaing, and evidently limiting the extent of after-dinner potations. It seems to be impossible that a regular drinker of tea can be a lover of ardent spirits; and it is generally observed that as a man (or woman either) slides into the vice of tippling, he simultaneously withdraws from the tea-table; so true it is that the brutalized feelings of the drunkard are Incompatible with the refined sentiments producedby
"The cup which cheers but not inebriates."

It is hence to be wished that tea, or some other equally simple prepared fluid, should be still more brought into use. Do not let it be urged as an objection that tea is expensive, for it is the cheap- est beverage in use. With respect to price, it should not be placed against water or milk. It comes in place of same other indulgence—intoxica- ting liquors for instance—respecting the price of which we never heard any complaints from the lower walks of life. Tea is thus not entirely a superfluity. The clamours as to its fostering habits of evil and light speaking are so antiquated as hardly to deserve notice. Formerly, when tea was exclusively a luxury among women, the tea-table was perhaps the scene where scandal was chiefly discussed. But while I suspect that the same amount of scandal would have been discussed if there had been no tea-tables whatever, I must observe that tea is now partaken of under greatly different circumstances. From being the favourite indulgence only of women, it is now an ordinary domestic meal, and there is no more dis- position to draw forth the failings of our neighbours over tea than over roast beef or punch, at seven o'clock any more than at five. In the upper classes of society, what with late dinners, routs, and frivolities of every description, tea-drinking may be put aside as a vulgarism; but as being, in point of fact, a powerful agent in humanising the harsh feelings of our,. nature, and cultivating the domestic affections, I trust it will long hold a place in the dietetics of the respectable middle and lower classes of Great Britain.—W.C.

FRIENDSHIP (says J. C. Hare) closes its eye rather than see the moon eclipsed; while malice denies that it is ever at the full. Mug is the sole civiliser ; for he has not only raised himself from barbarism, but he has tamed the lower animals in order that they might better serve his own needs, and is daily teaching his fel- low-men who have lagged behind in the raca of life to avail themselves of the garnered experience of bygone ages in the shape of books and of the advantages of living in communities ruled by cus- toms which are the well-considered outcome of ages of experiment. THERE are two things of a very peculiar charac- ter in Holland, which deserve to be noticed. One Is the enactment authorising husbands, wives, and children, to be imprisoned in a house of correction set apart for the chastisement of offences against the laws by which the relations of social life are governed—the other, a contrivance for compelling the incorrigibly idle to work. At one end of the room is a pump, and a stream of water runs in from the ceiling; so that unless the prisoner labour continually, he must inevitably be drowned.— Elliot's North of Europe.

THE advantage of good manners to the private individual who happens to possess them are very often overlooked; and the success of a man in life Is wrongly attributed to luck wheu it should have been ascribed simply to his affability and politeness. A hundred anecdotes have been related which prove the fallacy of the common idea, and show how men have been " made " by manners; bet perhaps not any of them exceeds in interest that of two notable English characters Raleigh, whose cloak is familiar to every child-reader of history, and Marl- borough, whose tremendous victories might never have enriched our military annals had he not first earned court favour and promotion by his consum- mate address.

Lim appears to me too snort to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs. We are, and must be, one and all burdened with faults in this world; but the time will soon come when, I trust, we shall put them off in putting off corrupti- ble bodies—when debasement and sin will fall from us with this cumbrous (tame of flesh, and only the spark will remain—the impalpable principle of life and thought, pure as when it loft the Creator to inspire the creature; whence it came it will return. perhaps to pass through gradations of glory, from the pale human soul to brighten to the seraph.— Charlotte Bronte. . _

HOOD never made a better pun than that of Hook, who waswalking with a friend, when they came to a toll-bridge. "Do you know who built this bridge ? " said he to Hook. "No," replied Hook: "but if you go over you'll be tolled!' ." MADAM," said a-husband to his young wife, in little altercation such as sometimes springs up in the best of families, "when a man and his wife have quarrelled, and each considers the other at fault, which of the two ought to be the first to advance toward a reconciliation r—" The best hearted and whitest of the two," said the wife, putting up her rosy mouth for a kin.
THE ASSAULT ON A• GAMEKEEER.
PRISONERS ALLOWED BAIL.

At Warrington O-C-c-a-sitcnal Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Barrop and Joseph Barrop, were charged on mand with trespassing in search of game on the 13th inst, on land at Grappenhallan the occupa- tion of Mr. Richard Barker. It will be remembered that in the affray which lc:Wowed upon the attempt made to take the two prisoners into custody, a gamekeeper, named Chinnock, was severely injured by being struck on the head with a stone. 'Elet was taken to the Warrington Infirmary, and for some time lay in a precarious condition. He is now understood to be pro- gressing favourably towards recovery, but he was still unable to le present at the court on Tuesday. The magistrate present was Mr. James Tinsley. Mr. Robert Davies again appeared to prosecute, and Mr. A. Browne defended. In the absence of Chinnock the proceedings were of a formal nature. Dr. Longdale,one of the house surgeons at the Infirmary, said that Chinnock was still suffering from the wounds described last week. He was going on very well, and would probably be able to at- tend court in another week. Mr. Davies said that under these circumstances he would ask for a further remand, and the Bench remanded the prisoners till Daresbury Sessions next Tuesday. Mr. Browne then applied that the prisoners might be liberated on bail, and this re- quest was acceded to. The bail fixed was the prisoners in £2O each and two sureties for each prisoner of £lO each. Bail was at once secured and the prisoners were liberated, Mr. Browne explained that on the case being previously before the Court he made a mistake in saying that the prisoners were employed by Messrs. Greening and Company. They were really employed by Messrs. Silcock.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 27, 1892.

The sixth annual sports in connection with St. Mary's Young Men's Society, Widnes, were held On St. Mary's Football Club ground, on Saturday after- noon. The weather was fine, and there was a large attendance. The officials were :—Handicapper, Mr. Walter Platt; judges, Messrs. T. Farrell,, W. Kelly, and T. Harding ; referee, Mr. T. Laws; starter, Mr. E. Farrell. The sports for the first 'lime were held under the rules of the N.C.A. A. The entries for the seteral events were very numerous, and there were some exciting finishes. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., distributed the prizes to the successful competitors. Afterwards dancing was indulged in until dusk, to the, strains of -St. Mary's Band,
11A.VDOCK FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS

Beautiful weither favoured the fiat annual athletic festival of the llaydock Football Club, on Saturday, when nearly 2,000 persons were present. There were seven events, for which prizes valued £35 were offered. Of the 100 entries, forty came from St. Helens, and seventeen from Haydock. Results _ _ _ _ _

Kenyon, St. Helens, 48 yards start; 2,F. Brown, Widnes,s4 yards ; 3, J. White- man, Earlestown, 35 yards. Very good race. Won en the tape by few inches ; two yards between second and t iird.

Two Miles Bicycle Handicap.-1, M. Bailey, St. Helens 215 yards ; 2, R. Dutton, Rainford, 325 yards; 3, W. Lowe, Rainhill, 325 yards. Time 6 mins. 10 secs. The Haydock brass band was present during the after- noon, and at the conclusion of the sprts played for dancing.
ALLEGED, ARSON BY A TRADESMAN.

On Saturday afternoon, at Frodsham Police Court before Mr. A. Thomas, Samuel Massey, greengrocer and postu3an, Main-st., was clinted under a warrant with having maliciously and feloniously set fire to the dwelling-house in which he resided, with intent to defraud the London and Lancashire Insurance Company, on Sunday night, August 14th. Mr. A. Linaker reptc sented the prisoner. George Jones, assistant overseer, Main-st., stated that on Sunday night he was in a lane at the rear of Massey's house when he perceived a smell of something burning. At first he thought it was a chimney on fire, but after- wards noticed smoke issuing from under the slates of the residence of the prisoner. He tried the doors, and finding them fast an entrance was effected through a broken window. Seeing no fire in the house he ran through the stable and climbed into the loft. He had to return on account of the heat and stifling smoke. Be obtained a long ladder,•placed it in front of the house, went up. pulled off a number of slates, got some water, and eventually succeeded in extinguishing the outbreak. Be observed the fire to be in three different places—in three ring-heaps—on the top of the ceiling of the front bedroom. On going up the first time he found a ladder reared out of the loft up to the place. Be had lived in the house for ten years, and bad never seen any hay there.
William Bullock, Church-st., Frodsbam, gave corro- borative evidence with reference to the extinguishing of the fire. _

Thomas Britland, Main-st., stated that about 8.30 on Sunday night he was passing Massey's house, and as the shop had been closed for a few days previously, he looked in, it being his intention to take it for his mother. He noticed the back and front doors open, and could see right through into the back yard. He went down the street about 100 yards, and then heard a scream. He walked a little further, then heard someone knocking, and returning to the place found it to be on fire. Sarah Dirnilo, wife of Samuel Dimilo, Main-st., said she lived next door to the Masseys. On Sunday night, shortly after eight o'clock, she saw the prisoner, his wife, and his wife's sister come down the street, and try to qplock the door. Some little difficulty was experienced, but ultimately they went in. She saw Mrs. Massey and her sister go down the street, and directly afterwards Massey followed them. When some eight or ten minutes had elapsed she heard a child cry "The house is on fire, my father will be burned." Ellen Jones, wife of William Jones, another neigh- bour, spoke to hearing cries of fire on Sunday night. She ran through her house and found all the doors at the rear of Massey's premises fast. The prisoner subse- quently came to the place with other men, some of whom got on the roof. P.S. Doyle deposed that shortly after eight o'clock on the 14th inst. he went to the housd of the prisoner, and turned off the gas at the meter. He then went to where the fire was. It was burning in two places, about five feet apart. A ladder was reared in the corner from the loft to the garret over the front bedroom. Witness sent for Massey, and asked him how he accounted for the fire. He replied that he had some; good neighbours; they had even poisoned his hens. The officer then asked whose ladder it was, the answer received being he believed it was his and was usually kept an the other side of the loft. He further stated, that he locked the door leading into the backyard when he turned the cow out that morning. He had been in possession of the key ever since. Asked if there had been previously any hay in the place where the fire was Massey said " No, it has been carried up by someone."—Cross-examined : The prisoner answered his questions readily enough. William Booth, insurance agent, produced the policy of insurance, and stated that it was dated July 27th this year. He gave the detailed amounts, which were £lOO for household goods, £3O in equal proportion on cow and pony, £lO on implements, &c., and £4O on hay. The latter amount was a mistake in being so large. Samuel Davies, architect and surveyor, Frodsham, stated that in accordance with instructions he had pre- pared the plan of the house produced, which was correct in every partieular. . _

- ; The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Cheshire Assizes. On the application of Mr. Lina- ker bail was accepted, himself in £5O and two sureties in £2O each. His defence was reserved.

THE LATE LAMENTABLE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Sir,— In view cf your well-known readiness to take up any cause that makes for the good of your fellow townsmen, and the public at large, I venture to solicit a small space in your valuable journal to advocate the needs of the surviving sufferers by the late disaster at Hutchinson's Works. It is proposed to start a public subscription, the fund accruing from which will be administered by a committee of gentlemen, to be here- after selected. The Committee proton. have already been offered a two night's benefit at the Alexandra Theatre. _ .

In addition toth.-.; above, a gentlemag in Wales has written to say that he will be very glad to send a sub- scription to any movement of the sort contemplated. I am also informed tta.t the, Widnes Cricket Club—and others—have taken the matter up, and are going to play matches for the benefit of the sufferers. I feel convinced that it only wants mentioning to induce the whole of the Chemical works—not only in Widnes—but all the sur- rounding district, to take up this good work. It is also desirable that all subscriptions should be paid into " Parr's Bank" to the Accident Fund; Hutchinson's Works. Thanking you in anticipation, I subscribe myself your obedient servant,
FRANK CAVE.

133, Mersey road, Widnes. P.S.—A committee of six Foremen, with Mr. A. G. Kyle—engineer of Entchinson's works—as treasurer, has now been formed- to administer the money raised by our artistic friend:, at the Alexandra Theatre; such money to be devoted to the immediate wants of the sufferers, pending the formation of a fund, by public subscription or otherwise. Albany Buildings, 47, Victoria-Street, Wostminster, S.W. August.l.Cth, 1892.
Sir,—Ttas World's Women's Christian Temperance Union for the British :Empire, has opened headquarters at the above address.

The growing interest in this wcrk has made it neces- sary to have a local habitation ; I shall have m7pwn office there ; the rooms will be pe,ned daily, and all friends are cordially invited to visit them. The litera- ture published by the Union will be there on sale. Many persons have written desiring to join the Union apart from affiliated Societies, .and for this purpose a special section has been provided. The Frances Willard Band, named in honour of the World's President, admits women in ail parts of the world into membership. The conditions of membership are the signing of the Total Abstinence Pledge and the payment of an annual tee of one shilling. Cards of membership will be scut, en which are por- traits of Miss Willard as World's-Presdent, and myself as President for the British ,Empire. All information concerning membership, the children's pledge cards for the Chicago Yair,?•the literature of the Union' its work and objects, can be o'4tained by sending to the headquarters. May I ask that you will ;oin wlth.us at the noon hour, wheia all the warla prayer ascends to,the throne of grace that a special blessing may rest up= this wide move- ment for humanity. We shall hold Weekly Prayer Mretmgs to which all women are cordally invited ,every Thursday, after the ;:.,15th of October.

div.head: TII.A.WKS TO TIM EDITOR,.
div.p: TII.A.WKS TO TIM EDITOR,.

Sir,—lt appears to be the fashion to congratulate you —to pat the Editor on the back. Mr. W. H. Butler has done it in his letter Leaded " Was Shelley an 4theiat ?" By the way it would be interesting to ;mow why as that letter written ? Te show an acquai ntenance with Shelley's verses, and, incidentally and uneonsciou‘ly, an entire ignorance of the man himself .? But itay " Great men are genera:7 misunderstood by their generation "says Mr. Butler. What a solace for taik- ative mediocrity! But was Stelley an atheist ? We!: he was to Mr. Butler, and he wtis not to mycelf. The fact of Shelley having rejected the popular /lumbo- 4mbc) of his time does not constit,ute an atheist. To see God in everything—even if you reject the blood-thirsty Jewish Javeh—is distinctly not to deny the existence of God. We have had the distinguish.ecT Advantage of perusing Mr. Butler's thoughts on Shelley, but as the Yankees say, "I should admire to" read those a Pll7anen B9l°F! 1.44 t; ii2Xteeds w¢ul4 have been I

an eye opener ; to have seen the theistic thinke; ten- derly turned inside out by "Poor Shelley, poor faithless Shelley," would have been one of the delights of litera- ture. Poor faithless Shelley, says Mr. Butler. How much better had the poet been if cut out after some smugly complacent Methodistic pattern, and been able to style himself a "theistic thinker !" How much less we should have heard of him under these conditions. He would have died, been suitably entombed, and speedily forgotten; lost among the stereotyped religious common-places of his time. Faithless ! Because he found the cut-and-dried traditional belief untenable? To my mind the man who rejects the mythology of his time—the crude imaginings of an age of ignorance and crass credulity—shows a larger,a more vital and vitaliz- ing faith in " the power not ourselves," than does the man who adheres to the dogmas of his day and so gives up his soul to be bound in the intellectual fetters, I rivett,ed by the ignorant dead. Your correspondent seems to have forgotten that faith—faith in the popular mythology—is generally in inverse ratio to knowledge and general culture ; so that after all to style Shelley " poor faithless" is to bestow upon the poet a merited if unconscious eulog,ium. My object in writing is to thank you, sir, for your advocacy of the cause of humanity in the treatment of , animals—in your powerful denunciation of the cruelties 1 involved in field sports. In this matter we have indeed ' much room for needed reform ere we can justly call our- selves a civilized nation. You would not need to scratch the modern Englishman very deeply to find an unwoaded Briton underneath. We have a deal of hale people in England,and you know what Dr. Watts said—" The devil finds work for idle hands to do." Now, while not so cock-sure as to the personality of the instigator, I quite agree with the Dr. as to the evil effects of idleness—it invariably leads to mischief—to bird-butchering,battues and the like. I have great faith in the speedy advent of better feeling toward, and better treatment of, animals from my fellow-men than they show at present. Coin- cidont with or consequent to the decay of that iniquitous idea that these creatures were "given to us to do with them as we pleased," I believe will come a juster appre- ciation of our responsibilities therein, and a kinder and mere rational treatment. At present the treatment of animals both those we use and those we abuse, as well as those we subject to the horrors of vivisection, is a dis- grace to our assumed civilization. Upon the latter :nal- practise of vivisection—cruel experimentation upon liv- ing animals—l shall, with your permission, feel it my painful duty to enlarge later ea.—Faithfully yours, JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 22 August, 1892.
