SENT TO PRISON.—A tramp named George Amscough was recently charged with begging at the Lymm Police Court, before Mr. W. P. Brabazon. P.C. Arthen, who proved the case, stated that the defendant was found begging at High Legh. He was sent to prison for seven days. M ARRIAGE AT OITORTRINGTON. —At St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington, on Tuesday afternoqn, the marriage of Miss Gibbons, of Sandy - lane, Lymm, and Mr. II arrop, late of the Heatley }Dote', was celebrated. The marriage service was conducted by the Rev. Mr. Locker, and Mr. 0. G. Smith officiated at the organ. The happy couple, who are well-known throughout the district, were the receiptents of the best wishes of their many friends on leaving the church. SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT HEATLEY.

Mr. R. Dobson conducted an inquiry at the Heatley Hotel, on Tuesday afternoon,teuching the death of Thos. Chorley, a youth who was on the previous day drowned in the river Bollin, at Warburton.—Naney Ellison,living at Rush Green, Lymm, widow, stated that she identified the body as that of Thomas Chorley. He was 17 years of age. He lived with his parents at Heatley, and worked as a clerk at Warrington, for the firm of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. She was living at the deceased's house prior to his death, on account of the parents' ab- sence. The parents had not yet arrived home. On Monday the deceased came home, and after partaking of his tea, he stated that he was going for a bathe, and asked for a tcwel. She (witness) tried to persuade him from going, but was unapt° to do so. James Travis, Heatley, said that he saw the deceased at Heatley Heath about a quarter-past seven o'clock. They then both proceeded to the Bollin for a bathe. He (wit- ness) entered first, and swam across. The deceased asked him if the water was warm, and on receiving a reply in the affirmative, he announced his intention of swimming across the river, although he had only learned to swim the previous day. He advised the deceased not to attempt it, but the unfArtunate lad would not be persuaded. When the deceased reached the middle of the water he put one hand up, and then sank. Witness went to his rescue, but was obliged to return, as the drowning lad caught hold of his ankle, and was pulling him under. He then sent for help, And his brother came up and brought the deceased, who was then dead, out of the water. James Travis deposed that hearing there was someone in 1 the water he ran to the place, taking off his clothing as he went along. He entered the river, and let himself down three times before he discovered where the body was. He then dived twice, and the seoend time suc- ceeded in bringing the body to the bank. He assisted in trying to restore consciousness. P.C. Howie stated that when he arrived on the scene the body was on the bank. He used Dr. Sylvester's method for restoring apparently drowned persons for three-quarters of an hour without success. The body was afterwards con- veyed to the deceased's late residence. The coroner, in summing up the evidence, commented on the bravery of the two'brothers, who had done all in their power to rescue the deceased. A verdict of " Accidental death whilst bathing" was returned.

The Penketh farmers are now in the midst of their havvesting operations, and if the weather keep fine they will secure a good crop. The corn is of good quality, but scarcely up to the average in quantity. In some parts it is badly beaten down by the recent rains. The root crops are exception- ally good. Mr. John Routledge, of Rose Farm, Barnton, near Northwich, and son of Mr. J. C. Routledge, of the Woodwards, Penketh, has been awarded the first prize at the Cheshire Agnicultural Show held at Warrington, for the best cultivated farm, limited to the residents of the County of Chester or within a radius of five miles from the boundary—to the resident tenant wholly depending upon farming of any farm not being less than 30 acres, nor exceeding 100 acres, who shall have the same in the best and most complete state of management. Mr. Rout- ledge also secured a gold medal valued at £5, given by Messrs. Bay and Sons, of Crewe, for the best farm in the above class.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY WHERE WEALTH ACCUMULATES AND MEN DECAY.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY WHERE WEALTH ACCUMU- LATES AND MEN DECAY.
BY IL WIIITHAM.

Well, I suppose you are done with the elections for a short time, and are now quietly moralizing about the results. A moral victory is all very well in its way, but its good results are in the shadowy distance. I must confess to being much disap- pointed with the Warrington voter. Possibly he will see, some day, how very foolish it is to have his Radical political measures find their way into the statute book through a Conservative filter. Its foolishness and its round-aboutness are so very apparent. It might be interesting to INTERVIEW SOME GOOD OLD TORY,

one who has seen, say half a century's politics pass before him--I couldn't recommend Sir Gilbert, be- cause I am not sure if he ever did see, or know, anything about politics—an i ask him what he thinks ot the politics of the past twenty years. If he answers candidly, he would say that he had passed the latter twenty years in undoing the work of the previous twenty years. Yes, every construc- tive measure of recent years has been destructive of the work of former years. What the Tories placed on the statute book, the Warrington voter thinks they should take off. How much had the Radicals to do with passing the equitable land laws? Surely the voter has heard enough and read enough to be sick of bearing the landlord's song:— . . _

"And the miner digs in the darksome cave Where the sun cloth never shine; Though they work and toil like the galley slave, The fruit of their toil is mine." Tories passed combination laws forbidding working- men to unite. It would have been impossible to- day to have had a Trades Council in Warrington could Toryism have ruled. The more you ill-use some dogs, and the better they like you. We have now entered upon

div.head: PRESIDENTIAL CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE PRESIDENTIAL CAMPAIGN.

For the next few months nothing but politics, or what passes here for politics, will be heard. Amidst it all, the papers wi:l contain interesting sketches of that peculiar product of Europe, known as the "Pauper Labourer." More especially will the Eng- lish pauper labour be trotted out, as he is intended to be shown up as the direct, and only possible product of Free Trade. Of course it would nut suit the American politician's purpose to give examples of German pauper labour, as the result of Protection, or to quote statistics from other nations in Europe where Protection rules. He quite ignores the fact that the immigration figures prove it is the Protective nations of Europe that are now flooding the American labour market. Yet this is so,saving in the ease of Ireland. England's figures stand the lowest. No doubt the solial question in England is watched keenly by the sociologists on this side,as well as by the rest of the civilised world. Nine mil- lionaires have died during the last three years in England; two of them worth two millions and a half pounds. I wish my readers would turn to "Black- wood's Magazine" for July, and read Mr. Abram's article on the Lancashire Cotton Trade. .It is sad reading. I remember in the "Examiner" years ago, foretelling what Mr. Abrams says has now come to pass. The markets of India, China, and Japan are within measureable distance of being lost to Lan- cashire, and what will England be without Lanca- shire? The same will surely be very soon said of the Yorkshire woollen trade. In spite of present appearances, I can foresee the time is very near when Protection will be thrown to the winds in this country. Forced by the immense immigration into this country, we shall have to find other mar- kets for our woollen goods, and then, what of York- shire? What can be done to stop this? How pre- vent the individual from growing criminally rich ? I say nothing as to the workman growing poorer, or standing still, as the case may be. I have just had the very great pleasure of A VISIT FROlf MR..WILLIAU BIBBY,. .

_ a brother Oddfellow, and one of Warrington's rising sons. With him I have spent two days in Boston. With him I paid a visit to another of Warrington's sons, ono of the brightest geniuses that ever left Old England's shores. The meeting was one of great mutual pleasure. To me it was one also of sadness. Here I found, in Boston, Mr. James Roberts, the son of Mr. John Roberts, the tanner, holding a high position, as designer and special inventor, in one of the largest American wood machinery manufactories. How for years he has been quietly maturing his wonderful inventive faculties, until now, not only the factories of the State: 4 contain evidences of his skill and steady per- severance, but even the side walks show evidences of his power to place cheap mechanical toys for I children on the market. He has risen so high in the estimation of his fellow citizens of Boston as to receive a deputation from them asking him to become a candidate for a seat in the Council room of " the Hub of the Universe." SEATED IN MR. ROBERTS' ROOM,

surrounded with drawings, and models, were four Warringtonians, one a Mr. Bibby, who left the old town forty years ago, talking over England's position as the market of the world.; what she should do to retain that proud position; what she could do, and that easily, to keel) her sons at home and so make use of her own native talent. When you read of America's inventive genius, make no mistake. The native American is nowhere.; go where you will you will find it is the Britisher, either English or Scotch, who is on top. Now I ask, why do you drive him away! Carnegie is Scotch, Mr. Frick is not American—by the way, I shall have something to say of these worthies in my next; and the head workmen at Homestead are none of them of American birth. My own argument is that you elect, as legislators, men who prefer to see commerce die rather than lose the old nobility men who care not one toss as to how complex or costly your patent laws are ; men who think they have a divine right to own not only the land, but all that it contains ; men who would bottle up the air and sunshine for sale, so that it would enable them to get. into Parliament, as a stepping stone to the peerage. Men only should be sent to Parlia- ment who have proved by their unselfish, and dis- interested lives, that they are patriots in the true sense of the word, men who care not to maintain an Established Church,because it provides positions for their dull and stupid sons, or who See only in a huge standing ,army a means of thrusting themselves, and their sons, deep down into the nation's purse. I spent a few of the happiest hours I have had since I came over here with the Bibbys and Mr. Roberts, and shall, if .I can decently, refer to the latter and his work on future occasions.

THE NEWCASTLE CAMPAIGN.
MR. AIORL.EY AND THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.

There was great enthusiasm at Newcastle on Saturday, when Mr. John Morley appeared in the city for the first time during the present contest. The right hon. gentleman was wel- comed by a large crowd at the station, and most cordi- ally greeted on his arrival at the Liberal Club, where he made a brief speech. Again In the evening he had a splendid reception at a great npeting held in support of his candidature at the Townllall. This gathering was presided over by Mr. Burt, M.P. Mr. Morley, in the course of a powerful speech, while not complaining of the Tories for opposing him on the present occasion, severely criticised the methods which had been adopten to influence the'electors against him. The real question for them, after all, was whether he had fulfilled his pledges and kept his promises. They did not want an echo, a parasite, a sycophant, and a flatterer to represent them. On all important and pres- sing questions there was agreement between them. On labour matters he was not against an eight-hour work- ing day, but the question was not whether a period of eight hears was enough for a man to labour. It was whether it was expedient that an eight-hour day should be got by voluntary arrangement or by Act of Par- liament. A good many tricks could be played in mere politics without the State being much the worse, but here they came to a question of wages and tariffs and hours and markets, where a mistake might mean a cup- board without bread, a grate without fire, children with- out clothes, and hearts without hope. Mr. Belli, his opponent, xi:light promise what he pleased, but he, come what might, would not barter the Interests of the working people by holding up those interests to an auction of rival politicians. In his opinion the eight kours.question was not yet ripe for legislative treat- ment.

On Wednesday, the candidates for the representation of _Newcastle drove round the constituency and delivered brief addresses to groups of workmen. The Irish Secretary and Mr. Ralli were interviewed by a Civil Service Federation representative on Wednesday, and the result is that the support of that body will be given to Mr. Morley.

div.head: LABOUR DEPUTATION.
div.p: A LABOUR DEPUTATION.

Mr. Morley on Saturday received a deputation from the Labeur party in Newcastle. Several trade represen- tatives made speeches impressing upon the right hon. gentleman that the object they bad in view was to obtain an eight-hour working day by legal enactment, and one of the speakers warned Mr. Morley that if be could not support the proposal the working men of Newcastle would oppose him. In reply, Mr. Morley said there was not a man in Europe who had expressed more deeply than he had his sense of the social misery now existing. As for the remedy now proposed—an eight-hour ivorking day—he could not find that it had been thought out by the labour conungnity of Great Britain. He did not find that the balance of argument was in favour of the principle, and the more they thought of the complexities which it would introduce I into modern industry the less would it be supported. He was willing to listen to szew arguments, but at present he was exactly in the same position as before the Gen- eral Election. In reply to a question, the right hon. gentleman said he could not support an Eight Hours Bill for miners. THE UNITED TRADES AND MIL MORLEY.

Another manifesto has appeared, the authors of which are the United Trades Societies of Newcastle. They say in their address to their fellow workmen :—" No measure can be a complete measure that the present Parliament may give us,and the only possible means by which the representation of labour can be improved is by the payment of members and the payment of election expenses out of the pnblic funds. This the Liberal party are pledged to give us at the first opportunity. and as the Right Hon. J. Morley, the representative of that party, is pledged to the question, we ask you to give your votes to him at the ensuing election. Apart from the foregoing considerations, we urge upon you the fact that the question of Ireland has to be first ' taken into consideration, and under present circumstances no ques- tion affecting our interests can be reached until that has been dealt with and effectively settled. Consequently, a vote given to Mr. Ralli is a vote given in direct opposi- tion to our best interests. Mr. Ralli is opposed to the payment of members, and also opposed to the question of Ireland. True he has partially promised to vote for an eight hours day, but is deadly opposed to every other question directly affecting the cause of labour, and it is because we feel thae the cause of labour will be best served by returning Mr. John Morley that we confid- ently appeal to you to cast your votes foe him."

div.head: POLLING.
div.p: THE POLLING.

The poll at Newcastle-on-Tyne opened at eight o'clock on Thursday n3arning. The rival colours of the candid- ates were even at that early hour very generally worn by persons on the way to their daily occupations. The register on *hich the seat was (ought contains 32,117 voters of whom 24,588 were accounted for at the recent general election. From estimates made as to the probable strength of Thursday's vote it is doubtful if the lower figure will be reached. A not inconsiderable number of electors of the Sestrond Ward, a residential quarter, are away for holidays. In addition an allow- ance has to be made for deaths and removals, because the register is a year old. Mr. Morley was abroad as early as nine o'clock and drove through some of the more central parts of the city including Northumberland-street. Mr. Rani. with his postilion gaily apparelled in red, started on a round of the city shortly after nine. Both candidates were heartily received by their supporters. . THE RESULT.—GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The result of the Dolling at Newcastle-on-Tyne was de- eared yesterday as follows : Mr. J. Morley (L)... 12,983 Mr. P. Rath (C)... 11,244

Majority 1,739 The result of the contest at the general election was as follows : C. F. Hammond (C) 13,823 Right Hon. J. Morley (L) 10,905 J. Craig (L) . • 10,888 A scene of the wildest enthusiasm followed the de- claration of the poll, and Mr. Morley was accompanied to the Liberal Club by a vast cheering multitude. The unsuccessful candidate and Alderman Hamond,M.P.,left the Town Hall, a few minutes later, but had a some- what mixed reception. The crowds were so great as to black the thoroughfares in the vicinity of the Municipal buildings, and even the roofs of the houses were occupied. Many hundreds of people were parad- ing the streets, singing the Morley election songs. In his speech from the balcony of the Liberal Club,Mr. Morley said the whole electoral history of the country had not furnished such a fact as that of to-day. A minority of 5,000 had been turned into a majority. Mr. Morley left at 5.20 for tjae North.

div.head: AUGUST 4)7. 1892.
div.p: AUGUST 4)7. 1892.
FREE EDUCATION IN
RUNCORN.

The Government examinations of the various elementary schools in Runcorn took place about two months ago, and at some of the schools the report of her Majesty's Inspector has already been received. The managers are compelled by law to permit the ratepayers to peruse these reports in some convenient place and'at some convenient time, and they have also to fix in some prominent. posi- tion a statement of the receipts and expenditure for the previous year. We are thus enabled to supply our readers with the following interesting reports :

div.head: .GIIBENWAY-RD. BOARD 'SCHOOL.
div.p: .GIIBENWAY-RD. BOARD 'SCHOOL.

The Inspedtor states: BOYS SCHOOL: The school has made good progress during the past year and is now in a highly efficient condition ; the arithmetic of the fourth standard is weak but this is the only defect; the first class does remarkably well. English and geography are well taught. Order very good. GIRLS' Smoot :—The girls are in excellent order and the work of the lower standards is very good. Above the third standard the work falls off. The fourth stand- ard is rather weak in spelling and very weak in arith- metic. The arithmetic of the -fifth standard is not good. English good. More attention should be paid to mental ' arithmetic; the neglect of this subject probably causes the failure in the arithmetic problems. The average attendance 'must not again exceed the prescribed limit in either department. The plans of the existing buildings were approved for 274 children in the mixed school ; now used by the boys and for 207 girls. Tux GRANT.—The total amount of grant earned by the school is £5OO 4s. 6d., of which £293 2s. 6d.'was ob- tained in the boys department and £207 2s. in the girls' department. The grant per head of total average attendance is boys 203. 6d., and girls 19s. In the boys' department the school earned the maximum of the principal grant, viz., 14s. per head,and the girls depart- ment 12s. fld. per head. Both departments obtained the highest grant of is. 6d. per bead for• discipline and organisation. The actual average attendance on which grant is paid was boys 285, girls 218. The sum of £32 83. Bd. had been deducted under article 107 (b) reducing the grant to £467 15s. 10d. The fee grant amounts to £209 lie. Bd.

The boys' school was examined in drawing in June last by the Inspector from the Science and Art Depart- ment and the" Excellent "grant has been awarded. MILL Baow HIPANT SCHOOL.—The Inspector states: "An exeellent school." There was an average attend- ance of 621 in the boys' department and 608 in the gills department • total 123. The school has earned the highest filed principal grant of 9s. per head and also the the highest grant of 6s. per head for discipline and organisation. The grant per heed on average attend- ance is 17s. ; and the total grant £lO4 Ils. The fee grant on an average attendance of 123 is £44 12s. 6d.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS.
div.p: PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS.

The Inspector states: Bars' SCHOOL: Elementary work Is generally good in the four lower standard.; the third and fourth standards do very well. The fifth standard which was a very weak class last year, is again weak both in composition and in arithmetic. The latter sub- ject fails badly in the seventh standard aad less badly in the sixth standard. English and geography good on the whole. Algebra is•well taught. The discipline is not so gaod as it might be. The first standard is a very large class and very difficult for any one teacher to keep in perfect order; the boys are rattier restless and are addicted to prompting one another. Both the first and second classes have the bad habit of simultaneous answering; this should be checked at one:

Gums &Roof.: The girls are in excellent order and do very creditable work. The seventh standard fails in arithmetic and problems, and the third standard are almost a total failure ; in other respects there is much to praise. English is good except in the fourth standard. Needlework is always good here. The school is greatly over-crowded. It is much to be wished that managers would provide a separate junior school for thh boys and girls in the first standard; there are 150 in the two departments. INFANT SCHOOL: The school has improved; the general result may perhaps be called good. Elementary subjects are well taught on the whole ; the first class work is decidedly good.' Object and natual history lessons are much less successful, Kindergarten work good. Musical drill taught with success. The children are rather noisy; in so large a school this is an important matter. Tan GRANT: The total amount of grant earned by this school is £747 55., of whieh £343 3s. 6d. was obtained in the boys' department £229 18s. in the girls' depart- ment and £lBO 15s. in the infant department. In the boys' and girls' department the school earned 12s. 6d. per head of the principal grant,the maxi mum being 145.; and the infants earned the maxium of N. Of the grant for discipline and organisation, the boys' department earned is. per head and the girls is. 6d. per head, the latter figure being the maximum. The infants earned , 45., the maximum being 6s. The actual average atten- dance on 'Which grant is paid was boys 371.3, girls ' 241.9 ; infants : boys 141. girls 99 7 ; total average atten- dance 854. The sum of £l2 11s. 6d. had been deducted from the grant under article 107 (A). The lee grant amounts to £355 155., but this has been reduced under sectien 1 (2) of the Elementary Education Act, 1891, by £lo3s. 9d. on account of the excess of fees received dur- ing the ten months ended 30th June, 1892, for which the same is liable under section 2 (2). "My Lords have satisfied ;,hemselves that there wasreasonable excuse for failure to comply with the section of the Act for the months in question." The report for the boys' school last year (1891)reads as fallows : This is on the whole an excellent school. One class the fifth standard, by its weakness in arithmetic and in English, and by its laxity in its discipline Im- perils the grant under the three articles dealing with these subjects. But the other seven eighths of the school is so good that this standard may be regarded as an important ineldent." The sum of £6 was earned in the specific subject of algebra.

div.head: BATHING FATALITY AT .RUNCORN.
div.p: BATHING FATALITY AT .RUNCORN.
GALLANT CONDUCT OF BOYS:

Mr. R. Dobson. the deputy coroner for the honor and fee of Halton, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday evening, on the body of Alfred Cox, aged 16 years, who Waii drowned in the OW Quay Canal on Sunday afternoon whilst bathing. It appeared that the deeeased, who was employed on the Ship Canal Works as tool carrier, and came from the neighbourhood of Wolverhampton, went, on Sunday at four o'clock, to bathe in the reservoir formed by the blocking of the Old Quay Canal above Wigg's works. He was accompanied by Charles Jones, a point turner from Gas-st. and another youth named John Wilson. After bathing about twenty minutes the deceased got beyond his depth and sank, and Wilson went to help him,but the deceased seized him and pulled him under the wster. By great struggling Wilson fried himself and succeeded in reaching the bank, when he fell down exhausted. ,Tmnes then attempted a rescue. fle seized hold of the drowning youth by the arm, but could not move him, and, not being able to swim, would have been drowned in his efforts to save his companion but for the timely aid of Robert Roland Harrison, aged 13, of Thomas-st., who tools off his shirt, and, throwing Jones one end of the garment, dragged him ashore. The witnesses stated that Cox did not rise in the water, and after their unavailing efforts they went for help and a man named Henry cragg of back Mersey-st., dived into the vgater sevezal times and ultimately recovered the dead body of the unfortunate youth. Harrison had been previously bathing and could swim a bit.—Tbe Coroner spoke in high terrea of praise of the heroic conduct ot fiarrison and Jones,and the foreman of the jury said the agreed that something should be don jurors were e to reward the boys for their noble conduct.—The Coroner I promised to bring the subject, before the attention a the Royal Binnane Society.—A verdict of drowned wlsilst bathing, ,

div.head: FEAriED GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: FEAriED GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

A terrible colliery explosion took place yesterday morning at the Park Slip Colliery, Aberhenflg near Bridgend, South Wales. One hundred and forty one men are entombed in the pit, and it is feared that the loss of life will be enormous. The day shift of nearly 150 hands had gone down when an explosion occurred wrecking the workings, and destroying the ventilation .Up to the time of writing it has been found impossible to reach the men below, as the pit is believed to have fired. The whole airways are blocked with debris. The scenes on the surface are distressing. The vibration of the explosion was felt tin ee miles away. It is hoped to reach the interior of the Park slip work- ings. The flames from the pit burned the fan wheel and other structures on the pit-head. All the works for miles round have stopped, and their is no lack of relief gangs. who are fortunately still able to get ingress by the pit shaft. Two hauliers have been rescued from the road. way, one all but asphyxiated by gas, and ths other with his face badly burnt. No hope is felt for the recovery of the men in the workings. It is now reported that no one was killed on the surface, and the fire below is slight. Five brothers are among the entombed, most of whom have families, many large ones. The colliery is in a very inaccessible district, and there is therefore great difficulty in obtaining news therefrom. Up to six o'clock last evening no bodies had been re- covered. The main roads are completely blocked by enormous falls, and the efficials are hopeless of anybody baying escaped death.

div.head: , CHOLERA.
div.p: THE , CHOLERA.
SERIOUS RAVAGES AT HAMBURG.

A telegram from Hamburg says no official reports have yet been issued, and those published by newspapers differ widely. The "Hamburger Nachricten," for in- stance, states thgt up to the present there have been 300 cases, of which 120 ended fatally, 85 deaths occurring on Tuesday. The patients are immediately tranferred to special wards of the hospitals, while the dead are conveyed without delay to the public mortuaries. Several fatal cases of Asiatic cholera have also occurred at Altona.

, Official statistics published on Thursday state that 82 case of cholera and 32 deaths occurred in Hamburg on Wednesday. Dr. Koch has expressed the opinion the opinion that though the actual number of cases is small in proportion to the population, the character of the outbreak is such as to warrant the gravest appre- hensions. Elaborate precautions against he spread of infection are announced from every country in Europe. All through railway traffic between Germany and Austria has been stopped, and the conveyance of steer- age passengers from Hamburg is to be entirely suspended. A Teheran te!egram states that ' cholera cohtinues to rage thee, the deaths being estimated as reaching at least 500 daily. _ .

A Berlin correspondent telegraphs that the news of the appearance of Asiatic cholera at Hamburg was officially confirmed. Up to Tuesday afternoon there had been 219 cases of various choleraic diseases, arid 75 deaths since last Thursday. Three cases of Asiatic cholera ap- peared on Wednesday, at Altona. The disease prevalent at Antwerp has now also been declared to be Asiatic cholera. Much alarm is felt at Berlin and at Vienna,and rigid precautionary measures are being adopted all over the Continent. A Paris correspondent telegraphs that a fatal case has occurred at Rouen. The daily official return at St. Petersburg shows that there were 5,505 cases and 2,659 deaths in Russia on the 21st inst. The situation at Antwerp remains unchangel. The total number of deaths since the appearance of the disease is 14. One suspicious death occurred at Berlin on Wednesday. The number of cases in Russia on Monday was 5,679, and the deaths amounted to 2,753. The epidemic is spreading in St. Petersburg. The cholera cases in Havre since the 30th ult, have num- bered 365 and the deaths 104, but the doctors express an opinion that no Asiatic cholera has appeared. A steamer arrived at Pauillac (Bordeaux), on which one person had died of cholera, and two men on board are ill. A violent epidemic has broken out in the province of Lublin on the Austro-Russian frontier. A case of chGlera has appeared at Grosswardein in Hungary. There has been one suspicious case in Vienna and one at Bude-Pest.
PARIS, FRIDAY.—A telegram here from Havre reports that there have been 28 cases of cholera in that town,ten of which were fatal. • PRECAUTIONS IN' ENGLAND.

The Customs Board have issued instructions to their officers regarding the treatment of foreign warships and other Government vessels flying Government pennants, with reference to chclera. Concerning vessels arriving from infected ports, Custom officers are supplied with a set of cholera questions. SUSPECTED CASES ON A. LONDON STEAMER.

On Thursday at noon the steamer (lemma arrived off Gravesend from Hamburgh, having on board sixty alien emigrants. Her captain reported that three of them were suffering from illness. The vessel was then in- spected by Dr. Whitecombe, of Gravesend, who found three aliens suffering from illness, the symptoms pointing to cholera. Dr. Collingridge, chief of the Port of Lon- don Medical Staff, inspected the persons, who were removed to the Port of London Sanitary Hospital. The Gemma was placed in quarantine.

div.head: TWO DEATHS AT GRAVESEND.
div.p: TWO DEATHS AT GRAVESEND.

Two of the three aliens immigrants who were received from the steamer Gramm°, on Thursday, at the Port of London Sanitary Hospital, near the Ship and Lobster, Gravesend; suffering from symptoms of cholera, have since died, onin expiring on Thursday night and the other yesterday morning. They were both women. The other patient, who is a male, is stated to be improv- ing.
THE SHOP HOURS' INQUIRY. REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.

The Special Committee appointed to inquire into the shop hours have presented a report, stating' that they have amended the Shop Hours Bill by limiting it to the same protected classes as those to which the Act of 1886 applied. The committee do not recommend the inclu- Mon of adult women. They have modified the 1886 Bill so as to make tne enforcement of its previsions by inspectors a matter of local rather than imperial res- ponsibility. The only remaining alteration is the express exclusion of domestic servants.

The following telegrar, was received on Thursday morning from Lloyd's c..icutta agent : The Anglia steamer, belonging to tl. _t Anchor Line,homeward bound, capsized in Jelßrigham channel, river lionghly. Thirty- two lives saved, 15 missing. A steamer is io atten• dance. , The Anglia was a steel screw steamer of 3,287 tons gm:4, and was built at Glasgow in 1888. She left Cal- cutta on the mornim, of August 23rdl bound for London. On Thursday night Messrs. Bender-son Bros., of Glas- gow, received a telegram from Messrs. Graham and Co., their agents in Calcutta, stating that the Anglia touched the ground, capsized. and is a total loss. Twelve lives I we lost.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT ACT, 1852. ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a MEETING of persons entitled to vote at the Election of Com- missioners under the above-named Act will be held in the MARKET HALL, BRIDGE STREET, RUNCORN, ON THURSDAY, the FIRST HAY OF SEPTEMBER, 1892, for the ELECTION OF FIVE COMMISSIONERS in the place of Mr. Philip Speakman, Mr. Walter Timmins, Mr. William Hankinson, Mr. Henry J. Grice, and Mr. Henry White, who then retire from office, but are eligible for re-election. The voting will commence at nine o'clock in the forenoon and close at four o'clock in the afternoon. E. MARSHALL Secretary to the said Commissioners, Town Hall, Runcorn, August,l7, 1891

ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS. FELLOW RATEPAYERS or RUNCORN.—The time is again near at hand when you will be called upon to cheose five gentlemen to represent you and your interests on the Board of Commissioners that have the management of our common interests as ratepayers. Having now leisure time at my dis- posal, and having been a resident and a ratepayer of the town during the last 40 years, and being also well acquainted with the wants and requirements of the town, both theoreti- cally and practically, I should consider it a great honour If you conferred upon me the priviledge of being one of your representatives to the above Board. I don't wish to make you great promises which may never be fulfilled. I would wish to hold myself free to deal with every question that Mlles before the Board on its own merits, and according to the circumstances that give rise to that particular question, and will vote for or against it, according to the wishes of the ratepayers, so far as I know them, and also the best of my own judgement. Every question that has for its object the good of the town and the efficient carrying out of all the modern improvements of the town requirements, sanitary and, otherwise, at the smallest cost to the ratepayers, shall haye my strongest sup- port. Most of my fellow ratepayers know who and what I am. I place myself unreservedly in your hands, and shall consider it a great honour if, by your votes, you return me as one of your representatives to the above Board. I am sincerely, Your obedient. servant, WILLIAM LEACH. 20, Albert street, Runcorn, August 24, 1892.

THE ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS. TO THE RATEPAYERS OF RUNCORN. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The time being near when you will be called upon to elect Five Members to your Board of Improvement Commissioners, it is again my privilege to come before you as a candidate for your suffrages. During the term in which I have had the honour of being one of your representatives it has been my atm,independent of any party, to promote the interests of the town of Runcorn. There are very important questions at the present time requiring serious consideration by the Board. The establishment of a Technical Institute is a most interesting question, and which, lam pleased to say, is in a promising stage of ad- vancement. The proposed Vehicular Bridge across the River Mersey : This very important scheme, which will very materially aft ect the future of the towns of Runcorn and Widnes, and confer permanent advantages upon the coun- ties of Lanes eh ire and Cheshire, is not by any means being overlooked or given up. The interest taken in the matter by our Widnes friends through their Local Board, and by your own Board of Commies loners. is very encouraging, and there is reason to believe that the strenuous efforts being put forth to secure this object will be successful. The con- venience to the people of Runcorn which would result from the erection of a bridge over the Bridgewater Canal. near the crane in Halton -road, will be worthy of every consider- ation by the Commissioners. Having, as a member of the Board, dealt to some extent with these matters in the past, should you do me the honour of again electing me, my best efforts will be directed to th e successful Completion of these, and every other business which will be to the advantage of our town. Soliciting a continuance of your confidence, and the sup- port of your votes at the poll on Thursday next. I have the honour to be, Ladies and Gentlemen, 'Yours respectfully, HENRY J. Gill CE. 59, Bridge-street, Runcorn.

RUNCO DI ELR.ENcTioNOPPROCOVMEMMIESNSITONERASC 11892. 1832. To THE ELECTORS.—As one of the retiring Commissioners, I respectfully appeal to you for a renewal of the confidence you were pleases to repose in me six years ago, and again in 1889 when you honoured me by electing me one of your represent- atives on the Board of Commissioners. During my membership I have always tried to discharge faithfuily the pledges I first made you, by giving to every mhasure brought forward unb lamed consideration, and voting thereon only as I thought your interests best served. lam greatly in favour of a Vehicular Communication be- tween tha towns of Runcorn and Widnea, and would, if re- elected, do my do my utmost to induce the County Councils of theshire and Lancashire to make the question one of the most prominent items in their respective programmes. I believe a Bridge across the Bridgewater Canal, 'n the neighbourhood of Halton-road, would be much appreciated ty the residents there, and should be pleased to have the honour of participating in the promotion of a scheme for cal rying out this work. I feel that our Improvement Act, 1,52, is too antiquated for the town and district, and if re-election would introduce or strongly support a scheme for its amendment, or perhaps, better still urge for a Charter of Incorporation for Runcorn and contiguous townships. I have long felt that the water and gas supplies should be under the absolute control f the Governing Body of the Town but would hesitate in advocating their purchase until after a thorough inspection by, and upon the advice of, an eminent expert. If you honour me by again re-electing me, my mental energies shall be at your service in all matters affecting your health, prosperity, and welfare, and as in the past, so in the future, my interests shall be, in all respects, identical with your own. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours respectfully, WU. IIANKINSOI7. Camden Cottage. High-st., Runcorn. Aug. 27th, 1892.

• DEEMING'S WILL The relatives of Deeming, the perpetrator of the Rain- bill and Sydney tragedies, have received an intimation that the authorities in Australia have decided to carry out the instructions contained in the will made in gaol in Sydney as to the disposal of his property. Ile leaves a gold albert to one of his brothers, but the remainder of his effects, including some, land in Australia, he leaves to Mr. Lyle, his solicitor, Miss Rounsevell, some gacil officials, and others. The will is a somewhat singu— lar document. • • SHOCKING GOLF ACCIDENT. A shocking accident was reported on Wednesday from county Clare. The wife of Mr. O'Donnell, a magistrates was taking part in a golf match with her cousin, Mr. Frost, when by some terrible misadventure the stroke of his club, which he weilded with great force, instead of propelling the ball caught the forehead of Mrs. O'Donnell, who fell unconscious, blood gushing from a frightful wound. The agony of Mr. Frost on seeing what be had done was painful to witness. Mrs. O'Donnell wall taken home, but there is little hope ot her recovery. . • .1 THE LEICESTER SHOE TRADE Disrtr.Tß - The Press Association telegraphs :—Sir Henry SaMes's award as to the restriction of boy labour in tfie shoe trade was received in Leicester on Thursday. Sir Henry decides that one boy to three men shall be em- ployed in clickers', pressmens', !asters', and finishers' departments • but exempts factories in which nursery and low-priced goods are made, the Local Arbitration Boards being left to decide in these cases. The award d is a compromise between the views of the employers an those of Trade Unionists.
